flashcards.back: Confidentiality keeps information from unauthorized disclosure, integrity keeps it accurate and unaltered by unauthorized change, and availability keeps it usable when authorized users need it. Nearly every security requirement, threat and control can be traced back to one or more of the three.
flashcards.detail: Exam scenarios usually name a symptom (data leaked, record silently changed, service down) and expect you to name the property that failed, then pick the control for that property.

flashcards.back: Authentication proves who or what is making a request, authorization decides what that identity may do, and accountability (auditing) records what it actually did so actions can be traced back to it. They are separate steps and one does not imply the next.
flashcards.detail: A classic trap is treating a valid login as permission; being authenticated says nothing about being authorized for a specific record or function.

flashcards.back: Non-repudiation is assurance that a party cannot credibly deny having performed an action such as sending a message or approving a transaction. In software it is typically built from strong authentication, digital signatures and tamper-evident audit logs.
flashcards.detail: Encryption alone does not give non-repudiation; a shared symmetric key cannot show which of the two holders acted, whereas an asymmetric digital signature can.

flashcards.back: Every user, process and component should be given only the access it needs to do its job, for only as long as it needs it. This limits the damage from mistakes, bugs and compromise.
flashcards.detail: Applies to code too: a web service running as an administrator or with a database owner account violates it even if no user is over-privileged.

flashcards.back: No single person should be able to complete a sensitive process end to end, so critical tasks are split among people or roles (for example, the developer who writes code is not the one who approves its release to production). It makes fraud and undetected error require collusion.
flashcards.detail: Often confused with least privilege: separation of duties splits one sensitive process across roles, while least privilege trims each role to the minimum.

flashcards.back: Defense in depth layers independent controls (for example, input validation, authorization checks, encryption and monitoring) so that if one layer fails another still protects the asset. No single control is trusted to be perfect.
flashcards.detail: The key word is independent: two layers that share the same flaw or the same credential add little. Do not confuse it with simply buying more tools.

flashcards.back: Access decisions should default to denial, and a component that fails or errors should land in a secure state rather than an open one. Permission is granted explicitly instead of excluded explicitly.
flashcards.detail: Fail secure protects data (lock on failure), while fail safe protects human life (unlock on fire alarm). Exams usually mean fail secure for software.

flashcards.back: Every access to every object must be checked for authority, every time, rather than checking once and caching the result. Without it, a permission that is revoked or changed can still be used.
flashcards.detail: A typical violation is checking authorization only in the user interface or only when a session starts while the underlying API or later requests are unchecked.

flashcards.back: Security mechanisms should be as simple and small as possible, because simple designs are easier to understand, verify and test than complex ones. Complexity is the enemy of security.
flashcards.detail: Sometimes called keep it simple; it explains why a small, well-reviewed security component beats a sprawling custom framework.

flashcards.back: The security of a system should not depend on keeping its design or algorithms secret, only on protecting keys and other secrets. Designs that rely on obscurity fail once the design leaks, which it eventually does.
flashcards.detail: This is Kerckhoffs principle applied to software: use public, peer-reviewed algorithms and keep only the key secret. Obscurity may be a thin extra layer, never the foundation.

flashcards.back: Security mechanisms must be easy enough to use that people apply them correctly and do not bypass them. If a control makes the job hard, users will find a workaround that defeats it.
flashcards.detail: Appears when a scenario describes users writing down passwords or disabling a prompt; the better answer redesigns the control rather than scolding the users.

flashcards.back: A threat is a potential cause of harm, a vulnerability is a weakness that a threat can exploit, and risk is the likelihood and impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability. Without all three there is no meaningful risk.
flashcards.detail: Fixing a vulnerability reduces risk but does not remove the threat; a threat with no exploitable vulnerability produces little or no risk.

flashcards.back: Risk can be mitigated (reduced with controls), transferred (shifted by insurance or contract), avoided (by dropping the risky activity or feature) or accepted (knowingly tolerated within appetite). The choice depends on cost versus impact and on the organization appetite.
flashcards.detail: Acceptance is a decision made by the accountable business owner after being informed, not a default that happens when nobody acts, and not a way to ignore the risk.

flashcards.back: ALE is the expected yearly loss from a risk, calculated as single loss expectancy multiplied by annualized rate of occurrence. A control is cost-justified when the reduction in ALE exceeds the annual cost of the control.
flashcards.detail: Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor. Questions often give three numbers and ask which one is missing or whether a safeguard is worth buying.

flashcards.back: Privacy by design builds privacy protection into systems from the start, not as an add-on: collect only what is needed, make privacy the default setting, and keep protection throughout the data lifecycle. GDPR calls the legal duty data protection by design and by default.
flashcards.detail: Retrofitting consent screens late in development is the opposite of it; the early-requirements answer is usually the correct one.

flashcards.front: Secure by design and secure by default
flashcards.back: Secure by design means the vendor takes ownership of customer security outcomes by building security into architecture and engineering, and secure by default means the product ships already hardened without customers having to configure protections. CISA promotes both as manufacturer responsibilities.
flashcards.detail: The contrast is with shipping an insecure default configuration and publishing a hardening guide, which pushes the burden onto the customer.

flashcards.front: Secure software development lifecycle (secure SDLC) and shift left
flashcards.back: A secure SDLC integrates security activities such as requirements, threat modeling, secure coding, testing and review into every phase of development instead of testing security at the end. Shift left means finding and fixing defects as early as possible, when they cost the least to correct.
flashcards.detail: The cost of fixing a flaw rises steeply the later it is found, which is the standard justification for earlier security activities in any exam answer.

flashcards.back: The Microsoft SDL is a set of security practices grouped around training, requirements, design, implementation, verification, release and response, and is a prescriptive model that teams adopt to build more secure software. It popularized threat modeling and the STRIDE method.
flashcards.detail: SDL is a prescriptive process, whereas BSIMM is a descriptive measurement of what firms already do.

flashcards.front: NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF, SP 800-218)
flashcards.back: The SSDF is a set of high-level secure development practices organized into four groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software and Respond to Vulnerabilities. It is outcome-based and works with any SDLC model, and US federal software acquisition draws on it.
flashcards.detail: Remember the four groups by their verbs: prepare, protect, produce, respond. It describes what to achieve, not a step-by-step methodology.

flashcards.back: SAMM is an open, prescriptive maturity model with five business functions (Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations), each with three security practices and three maturity levels. Organizations assess where they are and plan a roadmap tailored to their own risk.
flashcards.detail: It is used to measure and improve a program deliberately, in contrast to BSIMM, which reports what peers are observed doing.

flashcards.back: BSIMM is a descriptive model built from observing the real software security initiatives of many organizations, organized into practices and activities across four domains: Governance, Intelligence, SSDL Touchpoints and Deployment. It lets a firm compare itself with peers in its industry.
flashcards.detail: Descriptive versus prescriptive is the standard contrast: BSIMM says what others do, SAMM and SDL say what you should do.

flashcards.front: Waterfall, agile and DevOps security implications
flashcards.back: Waterfall has distinct phases so security activities map to phase gates, while agile and DevOps iterate quickly so security must be embedded in short cycles through user-story acceptance criteria, automated tests and continuous feedback. The security goals are the same; only the scheduling and automation differ.
flashcards.detail: A wrong answer typically proposes a one-time security review at the end of a sprint-based project; the better one automates checks in each iteration.

flashcards.back: DevSecOps extends DevOps by making security a shared responsibility and automating security checks, such as static analysis, dependency scanning and policy checks, into the continuous integration and delivery pipeline. It aims to keep release speed without releasing unchecked code.
flashcards.detail: The point is automation plus shared ownership, not adding a separate security team that blocks the pipeline at the end.

flashcards.back: Security champions are developers or team members who take on extra security responsibility within their own teams, acting as a local point of contact, promoting secure practices and helping triage issues. They scale a small central security team across many product teams.
flashcards.detail: Champions are not a replacement for the security team and do not own approvals; they are a community-building and early-detection mechanism.

flashcards.back: Maturity models describe how repeatable and managed a process is, from ad hoc work up to optimizing, using levels. The Systems Security Engineering Capability Maturity Model (SSE-CMM, ISO/IEC 21827) applies the idea specifically to security engineering processes.
flashcards.detail: A higher level means the process is defined, measured and improved, not that the software is guaranteed secure.

flashcards.back: A gate is a checkpoint where defined security criteria must be met before work moves to the next phase or release, such as completed threat model, no open critical findings or a passed scan. Automated pipeline gates apply the same idea to builds.
flashcards.detail: Gates should be based on risk-based criteria; a gate that anyone can routinely override or that has no clear criteria provides no real control.

flashcards.front: Change management and the change advisory (control) board
flashcards.back: Change management ensures changes to requirements, code and environments are requested, assessed for impact including security, approved, tested and recorded before they are made. A change control board approves significant changes and keeps the baseline trustworthy.
flashcards.detail: Security impact analysis is part of every change request; emergency changes are still documented and reviewed afterward rather than skipping the process altogether.

flashcards.back: Security metrics such as defect density, percentage of code covered by scanning, time to remediate vulnerabilities and number of open findings by severity show whether the program works and where to improve. Good metrics are tied to goals and trend over time.
flashcards.detail: A count of vulnerabilities found can reflect better testing, not worse code; look for trends and mean time to fix rather than a single raw number.

flashcards.back: Developers, testers, architects, product owners and operators need different security knowledge, so training is tailored to each role and refreshed regularly. It supports the Prepare the Organization group of the SSDF and the training practice of the SDL.
flashcards.detail: One generic annual awareness video does not satisfy a role-based requirement; a developer needs secure coding, an architect needs threat modeling.

flashcards.front: Policy, standard, guideline and procedure hierarchy
flashcards.back: A policy states management intent and is mandatory and high level, a standard sets specific mandatory requirements, a guideline gives recommended but optional advice, and a procedure lists the step-by-step actions. Together they translate governance into practice.
flashcards.detail: Tested by asking which document is mandatory and technology-specific (standard) versus optional (guideline).

flashcards.back: Functional requirements describe what the software must do, while non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, availability and security. Security requirements are mostly non-functional constraints, but some, such as a login feature, are also functional.
flashcards.detail: If security requirements are missing from the specification, nobody builds or tests them; the first move is to elicit and document them.

flashcards.back: An SRTM maps each security requirement to its source, design element, implementation and test case, so the team can show that every requirement was built and verified. It also shows which controls are affected when a requirement changes.
flashcards.detail: Traceability works in both directions: from requirement to test for coverage, and from test back to requirement to justify why the test exists.

flashcards.back: A misuse or abuse case describes how an attacker or careless user could deliberately make the system behave badly, written as the opposite of a use case. They are used to discover security requirements and to build negative tests.
flashcards.detail: Use cases say what the system should do; abuse cases say what must not be possible and drive requirements like lockout and rate limits.

flashcards.back: Data classification assigns data to levels such as public, internal, confidential and restricted based on sensitivity and the impact of disclosure. The level drives requirements for encryption, access control, retention, logging and handling.
flashcards.detail: Classification is done first by the data owner and drives controls; it is not decided by the developer or by what is cheapest to protect.

flashcards.back: The data lifecycle runs from creation or collection through storage, use, sharing and archival to destruction, and security and privacy requirements must cover every stage. Data is often most exposed in transit and at disposal.
flashcards.detail: Requirements that stop at storage miss archival copies, backups and test environments, which are common sources of leaks.

flashcards.back: Data minimization means collecting and keeping only the personal data actually needed, and purpose limitation means using it only for the purpose stated when it was collected. Data never collected cannot be breached.
flashcards.detail: The best requirement for risky data you do not need is usually not to collect it, ahead of encrypting it.

flashcards.front: Privacy impact assessment (PIA) and data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
flashcards.back: A privacy impact assessment analyzes how a system collects, uses, shares and protects personal data and identifies privacy risks to individuals and the controls to reduce them. Under GDPR a DPIA is mandatory for processing likely to result in high risk to individuals.
flashcards.detail: Do it during requirements and design, before launch, so that findings can change the design cheaply.

flashcards.back: PII is information that can identify a person directly or when combined with other data, such as name, government identifier, biometric record or precise location. Laws define personal data differently, but all require extra care in handling it.
flashcards.detail: Pseudonymized data can often still be re-identified and is generally still regulated, while truly anonymized data is not.

flashcards.front: Regulatory and compliance requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX)
flashcards.back: Software must meet the laws, regulations and contractual standards that apply to its data and market, for example GDPR for personal data of people in the EU, HIPAA for US health information, PCI DSS for payment cards and SOX for financial reporting controls. Requirements work begins by identifying which apply.
flashcards.detail: PCI DSS is an industry contractual standard, not a law, but non-compliance still has real consequences such as fines and loss of card processing.

flashcards.back: FIPS 199 rates the potential impact of loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability as low, moderate or high for an information type or system, and the highest rating drives the baseline of controls. This is the first step in the NIST risk management approach.
flashcards.detail: The system takes the high-water mark: one high impact on any of the three properties makes the overall category high.

flashcards.front: Security user stories and acceptance criteria
flashcards.back: In agile development, security is captured as user stories or as acceptance criteria and a definition of done attached to every story, for example that all inputs are validated and access is checked. This makes security requirements testable inside each sprint.
flashcards.detail: A vague story like the system must be secure cannot be tested; the answer with a measurable criterion is better.

flashcards.front: Identity and access requirements (RBAC and ABAC)
flashcards.back: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles tied to job functions, while attribute-based access control decides using attributes of the user, resource and context such as department, time or device. Requirements should say which model and which roles or rules apply.
flashcards.detail: RBAC is simpler to administer; ABAC is more flexible and fine-grained but harder to audit and reason about.

flashcards.back: Requirements should state which security-relevant events must be logged (such as logins, access failures, privilege changes and data exports), what details to record, how long to keep logs and how to protect them from tampering. Sensitive data such as passwords must never be written to logs.
flashcards.detail: Logging requirements support accountability and incident response, and they must be defined early since retrofitting them is costly.

flashcards.front: Recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO)
flashcards.back: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after disruption, and RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. Availability and resilience requirements are derived from these targets.
flashcards.detail: RTO is about time to recover; RPO is about how far back the restored data may be. They are set by the business, not by IT.

flashcards.back: Retention requirements say how long data must be kept to satisfy law and business need, and disposal requirements say how it is securely destroyed afterward. Keeping data longer than needed raises breach impact and can violate privacy law.
flashcards.detail: Retention and the right to erasure can conflict, so requirements must say which data is kept for legal reasons and which must be deleted on request.

flashcards.back: ASVS is a catalog of testable application security requirements with three verification levels, from baseline (level 1) to the highest assurance for critical applications (level 3). Teams use it as a source of requirements and as a basis for testing and procurement.
flashcards.detail: The level is chosen by the risk of the application; level 3 is for the most sensitive applications, not a default for everything. ASVS 5.0 (2025) is the current stable version and keeps the three levels.

flashcards.back: Threat modeling is a structured way to identify what could go wrong with a system, decide how serious each threat is and choose mitigations, ideally during design. A basic version asks what we are building, what can go wrong, what we will do about it and whether we did a good job.
flashcards.detail: It is done early and repeated whenever the design changes; a threat model made once and filed away goes stale.

flashcards.back: STRIDE categorizes threats as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. Each maps to a violated property: authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorization.
flashcards.detail: Used by walking each element of a data flow diagram through the six categories. STRIDE finds threats; it does not rank them.

flashcards.back: DREAD is a scheme for rating threat severity by scoring Damage potential, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability. The scores are combined into a ranking used to prioritize which threats to address first.
flashcards.detail: Remember that STRIDE classifies and DREAD ranks; DREAD is subjective and has been dropped by some of its originators, but it remains in exam material.

flashcards.back: PASTA, the Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis, is a seven-stage risk-centric threat modeling method that starts from business objectives and technical scope and ends with risk analysis and countermeasures. It connects threats to business impact through attack simulation.
flashcards.detail: Pick PASTA when the question stresses business risk and attacker simulation; pick STRIDE when it stresses categories of technical threat per element.

flashcards.back: An attack tree shows an attacker goal as the root and the different ways to reach it as branches, with AND and OR nodes and often a cost or probability on each path. It reveals the cheapest or likeliest path an attacker would choose.
flashcards.detail: Attack trees begin from the attacker goal and work downward, while a data flow diagram starts from the system and its components.

flashcards.front: Data flow diagram (DFD) and trust boundaries
flashcards.back: A data flow diagram shows processes, data stores, external entities and the flows between them, and trust boundaries mark where data crosses between zones of different trust or privilege. Threats concentrate where flows cross trust boundaries.
flashcards.detail: When asked where to look first in a design for threats, the answer is the points where data crosses a trust boundary.

flashcards.back: The attack surface is the sum of all the entry points, interfaces and data an attacker could reach, and reducing it means removing unneeded features, ports, accounts and code. Less exposed surface means fewer places to attack and to defend.
flashcards.detail: Disabling an unused feature beats trying to harden it; code that is not shipped cannot be exploited.

flashcards.back: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust based on network location and requires every request to be authenticated, authorized and continuously evaluated using identity, device state and context. A policy decision point decides and a policy enforcement point applies the decision at each resource.
flashcards.detail: Being inside the corporate network grants nothing; this principle is often tested against a perimeter-only or VPN-only design.

flashcards.back: Mechanisms shared among many users or components should be minimized, because shared resources create paths for information to leak or for one party failure to affect others. Designs should isolate components rather than share state.
flashcards.detail: It is the reason multi-tenant systems isolate tenant data and why shared global variables or temp files are risky.

flashcards.back: Microservices need strong service-to-service authentication (often mutual TLS), authorization at each service, an API gateway as a controlled entry point, secrets handled outside the code and centralized logging. The many network paths mean the old trusted internal network assumption no longer holds.
flashcards.detail: Authorization checks are needed in every service, not just at the gateway, or an attacker who gets inside can call services directly.

flashcards.back: Secure APIs authenticate every caller, authorize at the object and function level, validate input against a schema, limit rates and avoid exposing excess data. The top OWASP API risk is broken object level authorization, where a caller changes an identifier to reach someone else data.
flashcards.detail: Hiding an identifier behind a long random value does not replace an actual authorization check on the object.

flashcards.back: In cloud computing the provider secures the underlying infrastructure and the customer secures what they put on it, with the split depending on the service model: the customer owns more in infrastructure as a service and less in software as a service. Data, identities and configuration are always the customer responsibility.
flashcards.detail: Misconfigured storage buckets are a customer-side failure, not the provider, which is the standard example for this concept.

flashcards.back: Secure container design uses minimal trusted base images, scans images, runs as a non-root user with limited capabilities, keeps secrets out of images, and applies network policies and role-based access control in the orchestrator. Containers share the host kernel so isolation is weaker than virtual machines.
flashcards.detail: The image is immutable and replaced rather than patched in place, so fixing a vulnerability means rebuilding and redeploying the image.

flashcards.back: In serverless computing the provider manages the servers, so the developer focuses on securing function code, event inputs, dependencies, narrowly scoped identity permissions and secrets. Every event source is an input that must be validated.
flashcards.detail: Per-function least privilege is the key control; one over-broad role shared by every function gives an attacker the keys to everything.

flashcards.back: Security design patterns are reusable solutions to common design problems, such as a reference monitor or single access point that mediates all access, input guards, secure logger and role-based access control. Using proven patterns avoids reinventing flawed security.
flashcards.detail: The reference monitor concept is tied to complete mediation: always invoked, tamper-proof and small enough to verify.

flashcards.front: Federated identity and single sign-on (SAML, OIDC, OAuth 2.0)
flashcards.back: Federation lets one trusted identity provider authenticate users for many applications. SAML and OpenID Connect carry authentication, and OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access to resources; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0.
flashcards.detail: OAuth 2.0 by itself is authorization, not authentication; that distinction appears often.

flashcards.back: Design should use vetted algorithms and libraries, protect data in transit, at rest and where needed in use, and manage the whole key lifecycle: generation, storage, rotation, revocation and destruction. Keys are best held in a hardware security module or managed key service, separate from the data.
flashcards.detail: Strong encryption with keys stored next to the data or in the code gives little protection. Crypto agility, the ability to change algorithms, is a design goal.

flashcards.front: Security design review and architecture risk analysis
flashcards.back: A design review examines the architecture against security requirements and principles, checking trust boundaries, authentication, authorization, data protection and failure handling before coding begins. Findings are tracked to resolution and feed the threat model.
flashcards.detail: Design flaws are the most expensive to fix later; this review is where insecure design (an OWASP category) is caught.

flashcards.front: AI and machine learning system security considerations
flashcards.back: AI-enabled software adds threats such as prompt injection, training-data poisoning, model theft, leakage of sensitive data through outputs and over-trusting model output that drives actions. Design controls include input and output filtering, least-privilege tool access, human approval for high-impact actions and provenance of training data.
flashcards.detail: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and NIST AI RMF catalog these; treat model output as untrusted input to downstream systems.

flashcards.front: Data protection by design: at rest, in transit and in use
flashcards.back: Sensitive data should be protected wherever it exists: encrypted in storage, encrypted on the network with current TLS, and, for the most sensitive cases, protected while processed using techniques such as tokenization, masking or confidential computing. Which control to use depends on classification.
flashcards.detail: Tokenization replaces a value with a surrogate and keeps the real value in a vault, reducing how many systems fall under compliance scope.

flashcards.back: Input validation checks that data is of the expected type, length, range and format before it is used, and it is most reliable as an allow-list of what is acceptable rather than a block-list of known bad values. It must happen on the server side, because client-side checks are easily bypassed.
flashcards.detail: Validation reduces attack surface but is not a complete defense against injection; it pairs with parameterization and output encoding.

flashcards.back: Output encoding converts data into a safe form for the context in which it will be displayed or interpreted, such as HTML body, attribute, JavaScript or URL, so that it is treated as text and not as code. It is the primary defense against cross-site scripting.
flashcards.detail: Encoding must match the output context; HTML encoding does not protect data that is placed inside a JavaScript string.

flashcards.back: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into a query so that it changes the query structure. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) keep code and data separate so input is always treated as a value, which is the preferred defense.
flashcards.detail: Escaping and stored procedures built with string concatenation are weaker than true parameterization; least privilege on the database account limits damage.

flashcards.back: XSS lets an attacker get a victim browser to run attacker-supplied script in the context of a trusted site, in stored, reflected or DOM-based forms. Defenses are context-aware output encoding, input validation, and a content security policy as a backstop.
flashcards.detail: Stored XSS persists on the server and hits every viewer; reflected XSS needs the victim to follow a crafted link.

flashcards.back: CSRF tricks a logged-in user browser into sending an unwanted state-changing request to a site that trusts the browser cookies. Defenses are anti-forgery tokens, SameSite cookie attributes and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions.
flashcards.detail: XSS abuses the site trust in the browser content; CSRF abuses the site trust in the browser requests. Do not confuse the two.

flashcards.front: Broken access control and insecure direct object reference (IDOR)
flashcards.back: Broken access control means users can act outside their intended permissions, for example by changing an identifier in a URL to read another account. It is the top category in the OWASP Top 10, and the fix is server-side authorization checks on every request, enforced by default deny.
flashcards.detail: Hiding a link in the interface is not access control; the server must check authorization for the specific object each time.

flashcards.back: SSRF makes a server send requests to a destination chosen by the attacker, often reaching internal services or cloud metadata endpoints that the attacker could not reach directly. Defenses include allow-listing destinations, blocking internal address ranges and restricting the server network egress.
flashcards.detail: It was its own OWASP Top 10 category in 2021 and is now treated under broken access control in the 2025 list.

flashcards.back: A buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a fixed-size memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially letting an attacker run code. Prevention includes bounds checking, safe functions, memory-safe languages, stack canaries, data execution prevention and address space layout randomization.
flashcards.detail: Mitigations such as canaries and ASLR make exploitation harder but do not remove the bug; fixing the code or changing language does.

flashcards.back: Use-after-free occurs when a program continues to use memory after it has been released, which can allow data corruption or code execution. Memory-safe languages such as Rust, Go, C# and Java prevent whole classes of these flaws, and government agencies encourage moving to them.
flashcards.detail: Memory-safety errors are consistently a large share of serious vulnerabilities in C and C++ codebases.

flashcards.back: A race condition is a flaw where the outcome depends on the timing of concurrent operations, and time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) is the case where state changes between a security check and the later use. Fixes include atomic operations, locking and checking and acting on the same handle.
flashcards.detail: A file permission check followed by a separate file open is the textbook TOCTOU example.

flashcards.back: Applications should fail securely, show users generic error messages and write detailed diagnostics to protected logs, never revealing stack traces, queries or system details to users. Logs must not contain secrets or sensitive personal data and must be protected from tampering and log injection.
flashcards.detail: Verbose error messages are an information disclosure that helps attackers map the system; the answer is generic to the user, detailed in the log.

flashcards.back: Use well-vetted libraries and current algorithms, never invent your own, generate random values with a cryptographically secure generator, and store passwords with a slow salted hash such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2. Hard-coded keys and outdated algorithms such as MD5 or SHA-1 for security purposes are defects.
flashcards.detail: Passwords are hashed, not encrypted, because there is no need to ever recover them; fast general hashes make guessing cheap.

flashcards.back: Secrets such as passwords, API keys and certificates must be kept out of source code, images and logs and held in a dedicated secrets manager with access control, rotation and audit. Detection tools scan repositories for leaked secrets.
flashcards.detail: A secret committed to a repository must be treated as compromised and rotated even if the commit is deleted, since history and clones keep it.

flashcards.back: Secure code review examines source code for security flaws, using a mix of manual peer review against checklists and automated tools, focusing on high-risk areas such as authentication, input handling and cryptography. It finds logic flaws that scanners miss.
flashcards.detail: Automated tools find patterns at scale and humans find design and business-logic flaws; the strongest answer usually combines both.

flashcards.back: Hardening removes unneeded services, accounts and features, changes default credentials, applies least privilege and sets secure configuration to an approved baseline such as a CIS Benchmark. Security misconfiguration is among the most common weaknesses.
flashcards.detail: Default credentials and verbose debug modes left enabled in production are the standard examples of misconfiguration.

flashcards.back: Protect the repository with strong authentication, least-privilege access, branch protection that requires reviewed pull requests, signed commits and an audit trail of changes. The repository is a high-value target because whatever is committed gets built and shipped.
flashcards.detail: Requiring a second reviewer for merges enforces separation of duties and defends against a single compromised developer account.

flashcards.back: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness list of the most critical web application security risks; broken access control has been first in both the 2021 and 2025 editions. The 2025 edition lists, among others, security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection and insecure design.
flashcards.detail: It is a list of risk categories for awareness, not a complete standard; use ASVS when you need verifiable requirements.

flashcards.back: CWE is a community catalog of software and hardware weakness types, such as improper input validation or use of hard-coded credentials, identified by CWE numbers. It classifies the underlying flaw, while CVE identifies a specific vulnerability in a specific product.
flashcards.detail: Weakness (CWE) is the type of mistake; vulnerability (CVE) is a particular instance in a product; CAPEC catalogs attack patterns.

flashcards.back: SAST analyzes source code, bytecode or binaries without running the application to find flaws such as injection patterns and hard-coded secrets. It works early in the lifecycle and pinpoints the line of code, but can produce false positives and cannot see runtime or configuration issues.
flashcards.detail: White-box and early: the choice when the question says source code is available and the goal is to find flaws before the build runs.

flashcards.back: DAST tests a running application from the outside by sending crafted requests and observing responses, much like an attacker, without needing source code. It finds runtime and configuration issues, but it cannot point to the line of code and covers only the paths it reaches.
flashcards.detail: Black-box and later in the lifecycle: the choice for a deployed or staging application with no source access.

flashcards.back: IAST uses agents or sensors inside the running application while it is exercised by tests, combining insight into the code with runtime behavior to give accurate findings with fewer false positives. It needs the application to be running with test traffic.
flashcards.detail: IAST sees only the code paths the tests exercise, so coverage depends on the quality of the functional tests.

flashcards.back: RASP embeds protection inside the application runtime to detect and block attacks as they happen, using knowledge of the application own context. It is a protective control used in production, not primarily a testing technique.
flashcards.detail: A web application firewall sits outside the application at the network edge, whereas RASP lives inside it.

flashcards.back: Fuzzing feeds large amounts of malformed, unexpected or random input to a program to trigger crashes, hangs and memory errors that reveal vulnerabilities. Coverage-guided fuzzers evolve inputs to reach more code, and fuzzing is especially effective on parsers and protocol handlers.
flashcards.detail: It is the best technique for finding unknown input-handling and memory-safety flaws; it is automated and needs no knowledge of the code.

flashcards.back: A penetration test is an authorized, time-boxed simulated attack that actively exploits vulnerabilities to show real impact. It validates that controls work together and is performed by skilled testers, often from an independent party.
flashcards.detail: A vulnerability scan lists potential weaknesses, whereas a pen test proves exploitability by actually exploiting them.

flashcards.front: Rules of engagement and testing authorization
flashcards.back: Rules of engagement are the written agreement that defines the scope, targets, techniques, schedule, contacts and boundaries of a penetration test, along with authorization from the system owner. Testing without it can be illegal and can cause outages.
flashcards.detail: Written authorization comes first; a scope not covered by the agreement must not be tested.

flashcards.back: Code coverage measures how much of the code is executed by tests, for example by statements, branches or paths. It shows what has never been tested but does not prove the tests check the right behavior.
flashcards.detail: High coverage with weak assertions gives false comfort; security test cases should cover abuse cases and error paths, not only happy paths.

flashcards.back: Regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to confirm that fixes and new features did not break previous behavior, including security controls. Automated suites run on every build make this practical.
flashcards.detail: Every fixed vulnerability should get a regression test so it cannot silently return.

flashcards.front: Unit, integration, system and acceptance testing
flashcards.back: Unit tests check individual components, integration tests check interactions between components, system tests check the whole assembled system against requirements, and user acceptance testing confirms the software meets business needs. Security checks belong at every level.
flashcards.detail: Authorization flaws often appear only at integration or system level, where components pass data between trust boundaries.

flashcards.front: Security test plan and test cases from requirements
flashcards.back: A security test plan defines what will be tested, how, by whom and with what pass criteria, and it derives its test cases from security requirements, abuse cases and the threat model. Traceability shows every requirement has a test.
flashcards.detail: Test cases built only from functional requirements miss security; negative testing of abuse cases is what finds the gaps.

flashcards.back: Negative testing deliberately supplies invalid, unexpected or hostile input and actions to confirm the software rejects them safely, such as boundary values, wrong data types and attempts to skip steps. It checks that the software does not do what it should not do.
flashcards.detail: Functional testing proves the right thing works; negative testing proves the wrong thing fails safely.

flashcards.back: Vulnerability scanning is an automated, broad and repeatable check for known weaknesses and missing patches, while penetration testing is a manual, goal-driven attempt to exploit weaknesses in combination. Scans suit frequent checks, and pen tests suit periodic deep assurance.
flashcards.detail: Scanners produce false positives that need validation; a pen test finding is usually exploited and so is more credible but costly.

flashcards.back: A bug bounty program invites outside researchers to find and responsibly report vulnerabilities in exchange for rewards under defined scope and rules. It complements internal testing with many diverse skills but needs triage capacity and a safe harbor policy.
flashcards.detail: It does not replace internal testing; a program with no triage process creates a backlog of unresolved reports.

flashcards.front: Test data management and data masking
flashcards.back: Test environments should not use real production personal data; use synthetic data or data that has been masked, anonymized or tokenized. Test systems are usually less protected, so real data there creates a breach and compliance risk.
flashcards.detail: Copying production into test without masking is a classic privacy finding, even if the test network is internal.

flashcards.back: A false positive is a reported issue that is not real, and a false negative is a real issue the test failed to report. Tools trade one for the other, and false negatives are more dangerous because they create unwarranted confidence.
flashcards.detail: Teams that ignore a noisy tool because of false positives may miss real findings; tuning and triage are part of a testing program.

flashcards.front: Security acceptance and test exit criteria
flashcards.back: Exit criteria are the predefined conditions that testing must meet before the software can be released, such as no open critical or high vulnerabilities, required scans completed and sign-off from the risk owner. Residual risk that remains is formally accepted by the business owner.
flashcards.detail: Releasing on a deadline despite failing criteria requires documented risk acceptance by the accountable owner, not a quiet exception by the project team.

flashcards.back: Release management controls how software moves into production through approvals, tested builds, versioning and rollback plans. Code signing applies a digital signature to the released artifact so users and systems can verify its origin and that it was not altered.
flashcards.detail: A signature proves who published the code and that it is unchanged; it does not prove the code is free of vulnerabilities.

flashcards.back: Configuration management identifies, controls and tracks the configuration items of software and environments, with an approved baseline against which changes and drift are detected. It supports repeatable builds, auditing and fast recovery.
flashcards.detail: Unauthorized changes to a baseline are a security signal; the baseline is also the reference for hardening and compliance checks.

flashcards.back: In a blue-green deployment two identical environments run, and traffic is switched from the old to the new in one step with easy rollback. A canary deployment sends the new version to a small share of users first and expands only if it behaves well.
flashcards.detail: Both reduce deployment risk and allow fast rollback; canary limits exposure of a flaw to a few users.

flashcards.back: A pipeline builds and ships code, so it must be protected: least-privilege and short-lived credentials, isolated and ephemeral build runners, protected secrets, signed artifacts and logged changes to pipeline definitions. A compromised pipeline lets an attacker insert malicious code that looks legitimate.
flashcards.detail: The build system is a prime attack target; the SolarWinds compromise inserted malicious code during the build process, not in the source repository.

flashcards.front: Infrastructure as code (IaC) security and drift
flashcards.back: Infrastructure as code defines environments in version-controlled files, so security checks can scan templates for misconfigurations before deployment and changes get reviewed. Drift is when the real environment diverges from the code, and is corrected by redeploying from code.
flashcards.detail: Scanning IaC templates before deployment catches open storage and permissive rules earlier than finding them in production.

flashcards.back: Before go-live, confirm that the software installs with secure defaults, is hardened, has documented and tested operations and recovery procedures, monitoring in place and a signed security acceptance. An operational readiness review gathers these checks.
flashcards.detail: Release approval should depend on completed security acceptance, not only on functional sign-off.

flashcards.back: Vulnerability management continuously discovers vulnerabilities, assesses and prioritizes them by severity and context, remediates or mitigates them, verifies the fix and reports. Prioritization uses CVSS severity together with exploitability data such as EPSS and the CISA known exploited vulnerabilities catalog.
flashcards.detail: CVSS measures severity, not risk to you; a medium score on an internet-facing, actively exploited flaw may outrank a high score on an isolated system.

flashcards.back: Patch management identifies, tests, deploys and verifies updates on a risk-based schedule, with an expedited path for actively exploited flaws, and a rollback plan. NIST SP 800-40 frames it as preventive maintenance of the enterprise.
flashcards.detail: Testing patches before broad deployment avoids breaking production; compensating controls such as virtual patching bridge the gap when a patch cannot yet be applied.

flashcards.front: Incident response for software and coordinated vulnerability disclosure
flashcards.back: Software incident response follows prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate and recover, then review lessons learned. Product teams also operate a process to receive vulnerability reports, often via a product security incident response team, and coordinate disclosure with the reporter.
flashcards.detail: Preserving evidence and containing the problem come before cleanup; lessons learned feed back into requirements and testing. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) now frames incident response around the CSF 2.0 functions rather than the four-phase lifecycle of Rev. 2.

flashcards.back: Production monitoring collects logs and metrics, centralizes them in a system such as a SIEM, and alerts on suspicious events so incidents are detected quickly. Detection requires that the application writes meaningful security events in the first place.
flashcards.detail: Security Logging and Alerting Failures is itself an OWASP Top 10 category (A09 in 2025); attackers often remain undetected for long periods.

flashcards.front: Root cause analysis and post-incident review
flashcards.back: After an incident or serious defect, the team finds the underlying cause rather than the symptom, records what happened and fixes the process and code so it does not recur. Findings should update requirements, tests and training.
flashcards.detail: A good answer fixes the class of problem, for example adding a test and a coding standard, not only the single instance.

flashcards.front: Software end of life (EOL) and decommissioning
flashcards.back: End of life is when a vendor stops providing support, including security patches, and decommissioning is the planned retirement of the software with notice to users, data migration or archival, access removal and secure data destruction. Running unsupported software leaves known flaws unfixable.
flashcards.detail: Plan retirement early; leftover accounts, credentials, DNS entries and data in retired systems are common sources of later compromise.

flashcards.back: Media sanitization ensures data cannot be recovered, using clear, purge or destroy methods depending on the sensitivity of the data and the media. Cryptographic erase renders data unreadable by destroying the encryption key. The current guideline is SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (September 2025), which replaced Rev. 1 and keeps the clear, purge and destroy methods.
flashcards.detail: Simply deleting files or reformatting is not sanitization; the method must match the sensitivity and whether media will be reused.

flashcards.front: Operational security controls: backup, recovery and continuity
flashcards.back: Operations maintains tested backups, protected from tampering and ransomware, along with recovery and business continuity plans that meet the RTO and RPO. Software should be designed so that restoring it, and its data, is practical.
flashcards.detail: A backup that has never been restored is an unverified assumption; testing recovery is part of operational assurance.

flashcards.back: A software supply chain attack compromises something a victim trusts, such as a dependency, build system, update mechanism or vendor, to reach the victim downstream. Examples include SolarWinds (build tampering), Log4Shell (a flaw in a widely used library) and the xz Utils backdoor.
flashcards.detail: The danger is that the malicious or vulnerable code arrives through a trusted channel and often with a valid signature.

flashcards.back: An SBOM is a formal, machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies in a piece of software, including names, versions and suppliers. It lets owners find affected products quickly when a new vulnerability in a component is announced.
flashcards.detail: An SBOM lists what is inside; it does not by itself tell whether the component is vulnerable or exploitable in your product.

flashcards.back: SPDX (from the Linux Foundation, also an ISO standard) and CycloneDX (from OWASP, now an Ecma standard) are the two main machine-readable SBOM formats. The NTIA minimum elements, such as supplier, component name, version and dependency relationships, apply to either.
flashcards.detail: Know both names and that either is acceptable; the exam asks for the purpose of an SBOM more than the syntax.

flashcards.back: SCA tools identify open-source and third-party components in a codebase, report their known vulnerabilities and licenses, and can generate an SBOM. Running SCA in the pipeline detects newly disclosed flaws in components already shipped.
flashcards.detail: SAST looks at the code you wrote; SCA looks at the code you imported.

flashcards.back: A VEX statement is a supplier assertion about whether a known vulnerability in a component actually affects a product, for example not affected because the vulnerable function is never called. It lets customers filter SBOM-based alerts.
flashcards.detail: VEX reduces noise from vulnerabilities that exist in a component but are not exploitable in the product.

flashcards.back: In dependency confusion an attacker publishes a public package with the same name as an organization internal package, at a higher version, so the build tool fetches the attacker version. Typosquatting uses names that resemble popular packages and relies on typing mistakes.
flashcards.detail: Defenses include scoped or reserved internal names, private registries with controlled resolution, pinned versions and lock files, and checking hashes.

flashcards.back: SLSA is a framework of incrementally stronger requirements for build integrity and provenance, so consumers can verify where and how an artifact was built. Higher levels require a hosted, tamper-resistant build with signed provenance.
flashcards.detail: Provenance is a verifiable record of the source, build process and builder that produced an artifact.

flashcards.front: Open-source license types: permissive versus copyleft
flashcards.back: Permissive licenses such as MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 allow broad reuse with few conditions, while copyleft licenses such as GPL require derivative works to be distributed under the same terms. AGPL extends this to software offered over a network.
flashcards.detail: License compliance is a legal risk found through SCA; mixing a copyleft component into proprietary software can force source disclosure.

flashcards.back: Before adopting a supplier or component, assess its security practices, vulnerability history, maintenance activity, certifications and reports such as SOC 2, and rate the risk against the importance of the function. Continue monitoring after selection, not only before.
flashcards.detail: Selection is not the end; monitoring for new vulnerabilities, ownership changes and end of support continues for the whole life of the dependency.

flashcards.back: Contracts and service level agreements can require security standards, breach notification, the right to audit, secure development practices, vulnerability handling timelines and exit provisions. These are the enforceable part of third-party risk management.
flashcards.detail: A questionnaire is evidence, but a contract term is what lets you act when the supplier falls short.

flashcards.back: Software escrow places a copy of source code, build instructions and related materials with a neutral third party, to be released to the customer if the vendor fails, goes out of business or stops support. It protects continuity for critical custom or proprietary software.
flashcards.detail: Escrow is only useful if the deposit is complete and verified as buildable; an untested deposit gives false assurance.

flashcards.front: Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) and evaluation assurance levels
flashcards.back: Common Criteria is an international standard for evaluating the security of products against a Security Target, optionally conforming to a Protection Profile, and results are given as an evaluation assurance level from EAL1 to EAL7. A higher level means more rigorous evaluation, not necessarily more security features.
flashcards.detail: EAL measures confidence in the evaluation, with EAL4 (methodically designed, tested and reviewed) being a common commercial level; EAL7 is formally verified design and testing.

flashcards.back: A reproducible build produces bit-for-bit identical output from the same source, so independent parties can verify that a released binary matches the published source. Signed provenance and artifact signing, such as with Sigstore, let consumers check integrity and origin.
flashcards.detail: This is the control that detects tampering inside the build step, which a signature alone cannot, since a compromised builder can sign malicious output.

flashcards.back: A blockchain or other append-only ledger links records together with cryptographic hashes, so changing an earlier entry breaks every later link and is detectable. Combined with a digital signature on each entry, it supports non-repudiation and a trustworthy audit trail.
flashcards.detail: It gives tamper evidence, not secrecy or correctness of what was recorded: the signature shows who wrote an entry and the hash chain shows the history was not rewritten.

flashcards.front: Availability engineering: redundancy, replication, clustering and scalability
flashcards.back: Redundancy duplicates components so one failure does not stop the service, replication keeps copies of data in step across nodes or sites, clustering lets several nodes act as one service with failover, and scalability lets capacity grow with demand. Together they protect availability.
flashcards.detail: Replication copies corruption and accidental deletions too, so it is not a backup; availability controls answer outages, integrity controls answer bad changes.

flashcards.front: Authentication factors, MFA, IAM, SSO and biometrics
flashcards.back: Authentication proves identity with something you know, have or are, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines at least two different factor types. Identity and access management (IAM) centralizes accounts and policy, single sign-on (SSO) lets one login serve many applications, federation extends that trust across organizations, and biometrics are a probabilistic something-you-are factor.
flashcards.detail: Two passwords are one factor twice, not MFA; a biometric match has false accept and false reject rates and cannot be changed if the template leaks.

flashcards.front: Authorization: permissions, entitlements and access controls
flashcards.back: Authorization decides what an authenticated identity may do. A permission grants a specific right on a resource, an entitlement is the bundle of rights a user or role holds across systems, and access controls enforce them when the request is made.
flashcards.detail: Entitlements accumulate over time (privilege creep), so they need periodic review, and enforcement must happen on the server for every request.

flashcards.back: GRC aligns three activities: governance sets direction, ownership and policy, risk management identifies and treats uncertainty, and compliance shows that regulatory, legal and industry obligations are met. In software it determines which authorities and standards shape the requirements.
flashcards.detail: Compliance is not the same as security: passing an audit shows required controls exist, not that the software withstands current threats.

flashcards.front: Split knowledge, dual control and secret sharing
flashcards.back: Separation of duties can be enforced technically. Split knowledge means no one person holds the whole secret (two custodians each know half of a key), dual or multi-party control means two or more people must act together to perform an operation, and secret sharing schemes such as Shamir split a key into shares of which a threshold is needed to rebuild it.
flashcards.detail: Split knowledge limits what one person knows, dual control limits what one person can do; answer choices often swap the two.

flashcards.front: Resiliency: fail safe, no single point of failure and failover
flashcards.back: A resilient design keeps working or degrades in a controlled way when parts fail. It removes single points of failure with redundancy, fails over automatically to a standby, and decides deliberately for each failure whether to fail safe (protect people) or fail secure (protect data).
flashcards.detail: Failover paths are themselves attack surface and must be tested; a standby that shares the primary credentials or flaw is not independent.

flashcards.front: Technical and geographic diversity in layered defense
flashcards.back: Defense in depth is stronger when layers use different technologies, so that one flaw in one product or algorithm cannot defeat every layer, and when critical services are spread over geographically separate sites so one disaster or regional outage cannot take everything. Distributed systems add resilience but also add trust boundaries to protect.
flashcards.detail: Layers that share the same code, credential or vendor flaw are not truly independent; diversity has a cost in complexity and skills.

flashcards.back: Passwordless methods such as passkeys (FIDO2 and WebAuthn) replace a memorized secret with a private key held on the user device, which improves both security and usability. A CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) separates bots from people but can hurt accessibility and conversion.
flashcards.detail: Complexity rules that users defeat with predictable patterns are a psychological acceptability failure; passkeys resist phishing because they are bound to the genuine site.

flashcards.back: Reusing vetted components and shared security services, such as one authentication service, one logging library and one cryptographic module, means each control is built, reviewed and patched once and applied consistently. The trade-off is that a flaw in a reused component spreads to every system that uses it.
flashcards.detail: Reuse supports economy of mechanism; the safeguards are an inventory of where each component is used, an owner who patches it and vetting before adoption.

flashcards.front: Security milestones, control gates and break/build criteria
flashcards.back: A security roadmap places milestones where defined evidence must exist, such as a completed threat model, a reviewed design or clean scans. A control gate holds the release until the criteria are met, and break/build criteria automatically fail a build when a finding crosses an agreed threshold, for example any critical vulnerability or a new high-severity dependency flaw.
flashcards.detail: Criteria are written in advance and exceptions go to a named risk owner; a threshold that is quietly raised whenever it fires is not a control.

flashcards.back: A strategy states what the software security program must achieve and why, and a roadmap sequences the work (training, tooling, process changes) against time, budget and measurable maturity targets. It starts from an assessment, for example a SAMM or BSIMM comparison, and the organization risk appetite.
flashcards.detail: A roadmap that is only a shopping list of tools is weak; each item should answer a risk or maturity gap and have an owner and a date.

flashcards.back: Security documentation records policies, standards and procedures, requirements, threat models, architecture and design decisions, test plans and results, risk acceptances, operational runbooks and incident plans. It is the evidence for audits and the memory that lets new staff and responders act correctly.
flashcards.detail: Documents need an owner, version control and updates when the code changes; stale documentation is a hazard because people follow it.

flashcards.front: Security KPIs, OKRs and metrics (remediation time, criticality, complexity)
flashcards.back: A key performance indicator (KPI) is an ongoing measure of how well a process performs, such as average time to remediate by severity, while objectives and key results (OKRs) pair a goal with a few measurable results for a period. Other useful measures are vulnerability criticality distribution, defect density and code complexity.
flashcards.detail: A metric must feed a decision; a rising count of findings can mean better testing, and average remediation time is far more informative when split by severity.

flashcards.front: Security reporting: reports, dashboards and feedback loops
flashcards.back: Reporting mechanisms turn security data into decisions: periodic reports for management, dashboards for delivery teams, and feedback loops that carry findings from testing, operations and incidents back into requirements, design and training. The audience sets the content, so executives see risk trends and developers see actionable findings.
flashcards.detail: A dashboard nobody acts on is decoration; the loop is closed only when a finding changes a standard, a test or a requirement.

flashcards.back: The Software Assurance Forum for Excellence in Code is an industry nonprofit of software vendors that publishes free, practical guidance on secure development, including its fundamental practices for secure software development and material on training and threat modeling.
flashcards.detail: In the outline it sits beside OWASP (community), NIST (government), ISO and PCI (standards) and SAMM and BSIMM (maturity models) as a source of regulations, standards and guidelines.

flashcards.front: Software security standards: ISO/IEC 27034, PCI SSF and NIST
flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 27034 is a multi-part international standard on application security processes and controls, the PCI Software Security Framework (Secure Software Standard and Secure Software Lifecycle Standard) covers payment software, and NIST contributes the SSDF (SP 800-218) and the SP 800-53 control catalog. The right one depends on the regulator, contract or market involved.
flashcards.detail: They differ in kind: ISO and PCI standards are assessed against, the SSDF is a framework of practices, BSIMM is a measurement and SAMM a maturity model.

flashcards.back: Technical risk describes the likelihood and technical effect of a flaw, such as a remotely exploitable injection bug, while business risk states what that means to the organization in financial loss, legal exposure, reputation or mission impact. Acceptance decisions belong to whoever is accountable for the business risk, so findings must be translated for them.
flashcards.detail: A technically critical flaw on an isolated test system may be a small business risk, and a moderate flaw in the payment path a large one; report both views.

flashcards.front: Risk assessment and risk analysis (qualitative and quantitative)
flashcards.back: Risk analysis estimates the likelihood and impact of identified threats, either qualitatively with ratings such as high, medium and low or quantitatively with money values (single loss expectancy, annualized rate of occurrence, annualized loss expectancy). Risk assessment is the wider process of identifying, analyzing and evaluating risks against criteria before treatment.
flashcards.detail: Quantitative figures look precise but rest on estimates; qualitative scales are faster and common for software findings, and both feed risk treatment.

flashcards.front: Legal considerations: intellectual property and breach notification
flashcards.back: Software teams must respect copyrights, licenses, patents and trade secrets in what they use and produce, and meet breach notification laws. GDPR requires telling the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, and the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule requires notifying affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery.
flashcards.detail: The clock starts at awareness or discovery, so the incident plan must name who decides that a breach occurred and who notifies; US state laws add their own deadlines.

flashcards.front: Assessment and authorization (A&A) and authority to operate
flashcards.back: Assessment and authorization is the formal process of testing a system controls (assessment) and having a senior official accept the remaining risk by granting authority to operate (authorization), as in the NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37 Rev. 2). The authorizing official, not the developer or the tester, signs the decision.
flashcards.detail: Authorization is a risk decision made on assessment evidence, and it is revisited through continuous monitoring when the system or threat changes.

flashcards.back: Verification asks whether the product was built right, by checking work against specifications, requirements and standards, and validation asks whether the right product was built, by checking that it meets real user needs in its real environment. Independent V&V uses a party that is organizationally separate from the developers.
flashcards.detail: Reviews, static analysis and requirement-to-test tracing are verification; acceptance testing with representative users is validation.

flashcards.front: Application decommissioning checklist and data disposition
flashcards.back: Retiring an application means removing credentials, keys, service accounts and certificates, deleting configuration and secrets, canceling licenses and external subscriptions, honoring the service-level agreement end dates, notifying users, archiving what retention rules require, destroying the rest and checking dependencies such as DNS records and integrations.
flashcards.detail: Order matters: confirm retention obligations and archive before destroying; orphaned accounts and dangling DNS records enable later takeover.

flashcards.back: Security awareness promotes secure behavior among everyone who touches the lifecycle through onboarding, communications, simulations, security champions and recognition, while training builds specific role skills. Both aim to make secure choices the normal ones.
flashcards.detail: Measure behavior such as reports made and repeated mistakes, not course attendance.

flashcards.back: Non-functional requirements include security (authentication, auditing, encryption), operational (monitoring, supportability, log formats), continuity (RTO, RPO, failover) and deployment requirements (hardening baseline, installation privileges, supported platforms). They are written alongside the functional ones that come from business requirements, use cases and stories.
flashcards.detail: Missed deployment requirements surface as default credentials and open ports at go-live.

flashcards.front: Compliance sources: regulatory, legal, industry and company-wide
flashcards.back: Compliance requirements come from regulators and their rules, from law (statutes, privacy laws, contracts), from the industry sector (defense, healthcare, financial services, payment cards under PCI) and from the company itself (approved languages, frameworks, tools, protocols and coding standards). Identify all four before design starts.
flashcards.detail: Company-wide standards, such as an approved cryptographic library, are easy to forget yet often drive design and tooling choices.

flashcards.front: Data ownership: data owner, data custodian and data dictionary
flashcards.back: The data owner is the accountable business role that classifies data and approves access, the data custodian operates and protects it day to day under the owner rules, and a data dictionary catalogs each field with its definition, type and sensitivity so requirements can be set per data element.
flashcards.detail: Developers and administrators are custodians, not owners, so they do not decide classification.

flashcards.front: Data labeling and handling (sensitivity, impact, PII, public data)
flashcards.back: Data labeling tags data with its classification, based on sensitivity or the impact of disclosure, so people and systems know the handling rules for storage, transmission, sharing and disposal. Handling rules differ for personally identifiable information, regulated data and publicly available information.
flashcards.detail: Labels must travel with the data as metadata or headers, or tools such as data loss prevention cannot apply the rules automatically.

flashcards.back: Structured data fits a defined schema, such as database rows, so each field can be classified, encrypted and access-controlled separately. Unstructured data such as documents, email, images, chat and logs has no schema, so sensitive content is hard to find and needs discovery and classification tools.
flashcards.detail: Unstructured data is where uncontrolled copies of sensitive information pile up; discovery has to come before classification.

flashcards.back: Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with a code while a key or table can restore the link, so it remains personal data under GDPR, whereas anonymization removes identifiability so the person cannot reasonably be re-identified, which takes the data outside privacy law. Masking a few fields is neither by itself.
flashcards.detail: Combined quasi-identifiers such as birth date, postcode and gender can re-identify people, so claims of full anonymity need to be tested.

flashcards.front: Data collection scope and lawful basis
flashcards.back: Collection scope defines which personal data is gathered, from whom, for what stated purpose and on what lawful basis. GDPR lists six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Collecting beyond the defined scope breaks purpose limitation and data minimization.
flashcards.detail: Consent must be specific and withdrawable; if the feature can work without a data element, the requirement is not to collect it.

flashcards.back: Privacy law gives individuals rights such as access, correction, erasure (the right to be forgotten), objection and portability, and users also set preferences on marketing, sharing with third parties and terms of service. The system must be able to find, export, change and delete one person data, including copies held by processors.
flashcards.detail: Requirements must reach backups, logs and third-party processors, or an erasure request cannot actually be completed.

flashcards.front: Cross-border data requirements: residency, jurisdiction and transfers
flashcards.back: Data residency says where data must be stored, jurisdiction decides which country law applies and who can compel access, and multi-national processing needs a lawful transfer mechanism; GDPR transfers to third countries rely on adequacy decisions or safeguards such as standard contractual clauses. The architecture must be able to keep a region data in that region.
flashcards.detail: Residency is an architecture requirement covering regions, key location, backups and support access, not just a contract clause.

flashcards.front: Data access provisioning: users, service accounts and reapproval
flashcards.back: Provisioning grants new users and service accounts only the access their role needs, through an approved request, and removes it on role change or departure. Service accounts need an owner, narrow scope, non-interactive use and rotated credentials, and periodic reapproval (recertification) by the data owner strips access that has accumulated.
flashcards.detail: Orphaned service accounts and privilege creep are the typical findings; access that is never reapproved only grows.

flashcards.back: When a supplier will build, host or process part of the system, security requirements go into the requirements baseline and the contract: development practices, vulnerability handling and notification, data protection, limits on subcontractors, audit rights and evidence such as certifications.
flashcards.detail: Requirements come first, written before selection; assessing and verifying the supplier happens later, in the supply chain domain.

flashcards.back: SABSA is a business-driven, risk-based framework for enterprise security architecture. It works down through layers (contextual, conceptual, logical, physical and component, with an operational layer for running the result) and traces every control back to a business requirement.
flashcards.detail: Its strength is traceability from business need to control; it is a method for designing the architecture, not a list of controls.

flashcards.back: In this design pattern a request passes along a chain of handlers, such as authentication, authorization, validation and logging filters, and each handler either rejects the request or passes it on. It makes security checks modular, ordered and easy to add or reorder.
flashcards.detail: Order matters (authenticate, then authorize, then run business logic) and no path may bypass the chain, otherwise complete mediation fails.

flashcards.back: Controls are identified from requirements, threat models and risk assessments, drawn from catalogs such as NIST SP 800-53 or the OWASP ASVS, and prioritized by the risk they reduce, their cost and effort, and their dependence on other controls. Cheaper preventive controls on the highest-impact threats come first.
flashcards.detail: A control that cannot be tied to a threat or a requirement is hard to justify, and one that mitigates a top risk cheaply belongs at the head of the queue.

flashcards.front: Distributed computing: client-server, peer-to-peer, message queuing and N-tier
flashcards.back: Client-server puts logic and data on a server that must authenticate and validate everything clients send, peer-to-peer has no central authority so trust and integrity are harder, message queues decouple senders from receivers and need authenticated senders and protected messages, and N-tier splits presentation, logic and data into tiers with controls between them.
flashcards.detail: Never trust the client tier, and treat every tier boundary and every queue as a trust boundary.

flashcards.front: Service-oriented architecture (SOA): enterprise service bus, web services and microservices
flashcards.back: SOA builds applications from loosely coupled services with published interfaces. An enterprise service bus mediates messages between them, web services (SOAP with WS-Security, or REST) expose them, and microservices are a fine-grained form. Security applies per message and per service: service authentication, message-level protection, schema validation and central access policy.
flashcards.detail: A compromised bus or broker sees or alters all traffic, so it is a high-value component, and transport security alone does not protect a message after a hop.

flashcards.back: Rich internet applications, such as single-page apps, run much of their logic on the client, which moves code onto untrusted devices. Threats include client-side tampering, script injection, secrets or business logic exposed in downloadable code, remote code execution through components and plug-ins, and constant connectivity that widens exposure.
flashcards.detail: Every control that matters must be repeated on the server, because client code can be read and modified by the user.
