flashcards.front: Pervasive and ubiquitous computing (IoT, RFID, NFC, sensor and mesh networks)
flashcards.back: Pervasive computing embeds small connected devices everywhere: Internet of Things devices, wireless and location-based services, RFID tags, near field communication (NFC), sensor networks and mesh networks. They are resource-constrained, physically reachable, hard to patch and often privacy-invasive, so they need device identity, encrypted channels, secure update and data minimization.
flashcards.detail: RFID and NFC can be skimmed or relayed at short range, and unique per-device credentials beat shared defaults.

flashcards.front: Embedded software security: secure boot, secure memory and secure update
flashcards.back: Embedded software runs on dedicated devices with limited resources. Secure boot verifies each boot stage signature from a hardware root of trust, secure memory protects keys and code from reading or modification, and secure update delivers signed, version-checked firmware with rollback protection.
flashcards.detail: A device that cannot be updated securely carries its flaws for its whole life, and anti-rollback stops attackers reinstalling an old vulnerable image.

flashcards.front: Cloud service models: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS
flashcards.back: Software as a Service delivers a finished application, Platform as a Service delivers a runtime to deploy code onto, and Infrastructure as a Service delivers virtual machines, storage and networks. The further down the stack the model sits, the more the customer must secure: the guest operating system and up in IaaS, the application and data in PaaS, data, identities and configuration in SaaS.
flashcards.detail: Moving up the stack hands patching to the provider but never hands over accountability for the data.

flashcards.front: Mobile application security design (implicit data collection)
flashcards.back: Mobile apps run on devices the organization does not control. Design for minimal permissions, secure local storage (keystore or keychain), certificate validation on network calls, resistance to tampering and reverse engineering, and awareness of implicit data collection: location, contacts, device identifiers and analytics libraries that gather data the user never knowingly entered.
flashcards.detail: Third-party SDKs often collect data the app owner never intended, which is a privacy requirement as much as a security one; the OWASP MASVS is the verification standard.

flashcards.front: Hardware platform concerns: side channels, speculative execution, secure elements, firmware and drivers
flashcards.back: Hardware leaks secrets through side channels (timing, power, cache behavior) and speculative execution flaws such as Spectre and Meltdown, mitigated by constant-time code, isolation and microcode or operating system updates. A secure element or hardware security module keeps keys in tamper-resistant hardware, while firmware and drivers run with high privilege, so unsigned or buggy ones undermine everything above them.
flashcards.detail: Software cannot fully repair a hardware flaw, so mitigation is layered, and keys belong in dedicated hardware where possible.

flashcards.front: Cognitive computing, virtual reality and augmented reality
flashcards.back: AI and cognitive systems add risks such as model poisoning, prompt injection and opaque decisions, while virtual and augmented reality add sensor-based privacy risks (cameras, spatial maps, gaze and biometric data) and physical safety risks from manipulated displays. Controls include data minimization, consent for sensor data, input and output filtering and human oversight.
flashcards.detail: Treat model output and sensor input as untrusted, and remember headset sensor data can be biometric and highly sensitive.

flashcards.front: Industrial IoT and operational technology (medical, automotive, robotics)
flashcards.back: Industrial IoT and operational technology cover facility controls, automotive systems, robotics, medical devices and software-defined production. Safety and availability dominate, devices live for decades, patching is slow and a failure can harm people or processes. Security relies on segmentation, minimal exposure, secure remote access and standards such as IEC 62443.
flashcards.detail: Confidentiality is often secondary to safety and availability, so even a security patch may need safety testing before it is applied.

flashcards.front: Secure management interfaces, out-of-band management and log interfaces
flashcards.back: Administrative interfaces are high-value targets: keep them apart from user traffic (often on an out-of-band management network), require strong authentication and MFA, restrict them by source and role, and log every action. Log interfaces must also be designed so logs travel over protected channels and cannot be altered or read by those who do not need them.
flashcards.detail: A management console reachable from the internet or the user network defeats other controls, and so do unauthenticated debug ports.

flashcards.front: Upstream and downstream dependencies and key/data sharing
flashcards.back: Upstream dependencies are what your software relies on, such as libraries, services and data feeds, and downstream dependencies are the consumers that rely on you. Interfaces need agreed authentication, rules for how keys and data are shared, who can change them, and a plan for when one side fails or is compromised.
flashcards.detail: A key shared between applications turns one breach into several; use per-application credentials and rotate them.

flashcards.back: Data loss prevention tools inspect data at rest, in motion and in use against policies built on classification labels, patterns and fingerprints, and can alert, block, quarantine or encrypt when sensitive data is about to leave. Software design supports them by labeling data and avoiding unprotected export paths.
flashcards.detail: DLP reduces accidental and careless leakage; it cannot reliably stop a determined insider or encrypted exfiltration.

flashcards.front: Trusted computing: TPM and the trusted computing base (TCB)
flashcards.back: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a hardware chip that stores keys, measures boot components and attests platform state, and the trusted computing base (TCB) is all the hardware, firmware and software that must work correctly for the security policy to hold. A smaller TCB is easier to verify.
flashcards.detail: Everything inside the TCB must be trusted, so design to shrink it; a reference monitor is a small TCB element that mediates every access.

flashcards.front: Database security design: encryption, views, triggers, privileges and secure connections
flashcards.back: Protect databases with encryption at rest and TLS connections, least-privilege roles per application, views that expose only permitted columns or rows, parameterized access and stored procedures, and triggers that enforce rules or write audit records. Keep database administrator duties separate from application accounts.
flashcards.detail: Views and triggers are security tools as well as conveniences, and an application should never connect as the database owner.

flashcards.front: Programming language environments: managed runtimes, virtual machines and scripting
flashcards.back: Managed environments such as the .NET common language runtime and the Java virtual machine provide memory safety, type checking and bytecode verification, while scripting languages such as Python and PowerShell are powerful but need controls such as signed scripts, constrained execution modes and logging. Native code has no such safety net.
flashcards.detail: Runtimes remove classes of memory flaws, not logic flaws, injection or unsafe deserialization, so language and runtime choice is a security decision.

flashcards.back: Applications inherit protection from the operating system: file and process permissions, mandatory access control frameworks such as SELinux and AppArmor, account separation, memory protections, host firewalls, auditing and secure update services. Design should use these rather than reinvent them, and run with least privilege.
flashcards.detail: Disabling unneeded operating system services and applying a hardening baseline shrinks the attack surface before any application code is considered.

flashcards.back: Virtualization lets many virtual machines share hardware under a hypervisor, which becomes a critical trusted component: a hypervisor flaw or VM escape can expose every guest. Controls include patching the hypervisor, isolating management networks, limiting VM sprawl and protecting images and snapshots.
flashcards.detail: Virtual machines are isolated by the hypervisor, containers only by the shared kernel, so a VM is the stronger boundary.

flashcards.back: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity and is signed by a certificate authority, forming the basis of TLS server and client authentication and of code signing. Credential management covers issuing, storing, rotating, revoking and expiring certificates, passwords and tokens, and single sign-on reduces how many credentials users and applications hold.
flashcards.detail: Expired or unrevoked certificates cause outages and risk, so automate renewal and keep private keys in protected stores.

flashcards.front: Flow control: proxies, firewalls, protocols and queuing
flashcards.back: Flow control governs what data may move where. Firewalls filter traffic by policy, proxies mediate and inspect connections on behalf of clients or servers, protocol choices decide what can pass, and queues buffer and rate-limit traffic between components. Together they enforce trust boundaries and limit the damage of floods.
flashcards.detail: A reverse proxy or API gateway gives one place to authenticate, rate-limit and log, but it supplements and never replaces checks in the service itself.

flashcards.back: Backups need the protections of the data they hold: encryption, access control, separation from production credentials, immutable or offline copies against ransomware and integrity checks. The plan states what is backed up, how often (set by the RPO), how fast it must be restored (the RTO) and how restores are tested.
flashcards.detail: Backups are a second copy of data attackers also want, and an untested restore is only an assumption.

flashcards.front: Secure data retention, retrieval and destruction design
flashcards.back: Design for the whole retention rule: keep data only as long as law and business require, keep it retrievable for authorized legal or business needs, and destroy it with a method suited to the media, such as cryptographic erase or physical destruction. Systems must be able to delete across replicas, backups and archives.
flashcards.detail: If the design scatters data into unmanaged copies, the destruction schedule cannot be met, so build deletion in from the start.

flashcards.back: Threat intelligence is evidence-based knowledge about adversaries, their tools and tactics, used to identify credible and relevant threats to your software and predict likely attack paths. Sources include commercial feeds, information sharing communities, government advisories and the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base.
flashcards.detail: Intelligence helps when tied to your assets and technology stack; raw feeds with no relevance only create noise.

flashcards.front: Common threats: advanced persistent threats, insiders, malware and suppliers
flashcards.back: An advanced persistent threat (APT) is a well-resourced, patient adversary that stays hidden for long periods, insider threats come from people with legitimate access whether malicious or careless, malware covers viruses, ransomware, trojans and backdoors, and third-party suppliers are a path through compromised dependencies and services.
flashcards.detail: Insiders are countered by least privilege, separation of duties and auditing rather than perimeter defenses, and APTs call for detection and response, not only prevention.

flashcards.front: Hybrid Threat Modeling Method (hTMM) and Trike
flashcards.back: The Hybrid Threat Modeling Method, from the Carnegie Mellon Software Engineering Institute, combines the SQUARE requirements method, security cards and Persona non Grata attacker profiles, while Trike is a risk-based method that builds a model of assets, actors and rules and derives threats from it. Both are alternatives to STRIDE and PASTA.
flashcards.detail: Several methods exist; choose by emphasis: categories for STRIDE, business risk for PASTA, attacker personas for hTMM.

flashcards.back: CVSS is an open standard from FIRST that scores the severity of a vulnerability from 0.0 to 10.0 and records it in a vector string. Version 4.0 has Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental metric groups, and version 3.1 has Base, Temporal and Environmental. Ratings are None 0.0, Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical 9.0 to 10.0.
flashcards.detail: The base score is intrinsic severity, not risk to you; add threat and environmental context, because a base score alone ignores exposure and exploitation.

flashcards.front: Modeling non-functional security properties and constraints
flashcards.back: Non-functional security properties, such as confidentiality levels, availability targets, the performance cost of encryption and latency budgets, are modeled in the design (for example in deployment diagrams and constraint tables) so trade-offs are visible before building. A constraint such as a battery budget or a legacy protocol can rule out a control.
flashcards.detail: A design that never records its constraints quietly drops controls later; make each property measurable, for example 99.9 percent availability or latency with TLS enabled.

flashcards.front: Secure operational architecture: deployment topology and operational interfaces
flashcards.back: The operational architecture shows how the software is deployed and run: network zones and segmentation such as a DMZ, where each component sits, which operational interfaces administrators and pipelines use, how CI/CD delivers changes and where monitoring and backups connect. Security reviews it as part of design, before deployment.
flashcards.detail: A sound application design deployed on a flat network with shared administrator access loses its protection.

flashcards.front: Protocol and API design choices (REST, SOAP, GraphQL, statelessness)
flashcards.back: Protocol choices shape the attack surface. REST APIs are typically stateless, which eases scaling but means every call must carry and validate credentials, SOAP offers message-level security through WS-Security, and GraphQL needs query depth and cost limits and per-field authorization. Common weaknesses are verbose errors, missing rate limits and excessive data exposure.
flashcards.detail: Prefer short-lived tokens validated on every request, and use the API schema as the basis for input validation.

flashcards.back: Declarative security states access rules outside the code, in configuration, annotations or policy files, so they can be reviewed and changed without recompiling. Programmatic (imperative) security enforces rules with explicit checks in code, which handles fine-grained, data-dependent decisions. Most applications need both.
flashcards.detail: Declarative rules are easier to audit and harder to forget, but a rule such as only the owner of this order may change it needs a programmatic check.

flashcards.front: Concurrency, thread safety and database concurrency controls
flashcards.back: Concurrent code that shares state without proper synchronization can corrupt data or slip past checks. Thread-safe code uses locks, immutable data, atomic operations or message passing, and databases keep concurrent updates consistent with transactions, locking (pessimistic) or version checks (optimistic).
flashcards.detail: Security effects include double spending, limit overruns by parallel requests and time-of-check to time-of-use flaws, so test with simultaneous requests.

flashcards.back: Sanitization removes or transforms dangerous parts of input, while canonicalization first converts input to a single standard form, decoding URL or Unicode encodings and resolving path sequences, so that disguised variants cannot slip past a check. Validate after canonicalizing, and prefer rejecting bad input over repairing it.
flashcards.detail: A double-encoded path such as ..%252f beats a check that runs before decoding; canonicalize, then allow-list.

flashcards.front: Output sanitization: encoding, obfuscation and encryption compared
flashcards.back: Output encoding, such as HTML or URL encoding, changes the representation of data so it is displayed as text and is the injection defense, obfuscation makes code or data harder to read without making it secret, and encryption protects confidentiality with a key. Base64 is an encoding and gives no protection.
flashcards.detail: Obfuscation is a speed bump for reverse engineering, never a security boundary or a place to hide keys.

flashcards.front: Secure logging and auditing: confidentiality and privacy of logs
flashcards.back: Logs should record security-relevant events with who, what, when, where and outcome, but never secrets, session identifiers or needless personal data. Protect them in transit and storage, restrict who reads them, neutralize newline and control characters in logged input, and keep them for the defined retention period.
flashcards.detail: Logs are evidence and also a leak risk: a log full of tokens and personal data is itself a breach target.

flashcards.back: After authentication the application issues a long, random session identifier, regenerates it at login to prevent fixation, sets the cookie attributes Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite, applies idle and absolute timeouts and destroys the session on the server at logout. Token-based sessions need short lifetimes, signature checks and a revocation path.
flashcards.detail: Session fixation is fixed by issuing a new identifier at authentication, and logging out must invalidate the server-side session, not just delete the cookie.

flashcards.front: Trusted and untrusted APIs and libraries
flashcards.back: Treat code and APIs from outside your trust boundary as untrusted: validate what they return, run them with least privilege, pin and verify versions, and avoid risky features such as deserializing untrusted data or loading code dynamically. Trusted components still need vetting and patching.
flashcards.detail: Trust is a decision backed by evidence such as source, signing and maintenance, not a default for whatever is popular; data from a partner API is still input to validate.

flashcards.front: Resource management: memory, compute, storage and network
flashcards.back: Software must acquire, limit and release resources deliberately: free memory correctly and avoid leaks, close files and connections, and set quotas, timeouts and limits on request size, concurrency and recursion, handling exhaustion gracefully. Poor management leads to denial of service and memory corruption.
flashcards.detail: Unbounded input sizes and missing timeouts are classic availability bugs, and cleanup must happen on error paths as well as the normal one.

flashcards.back: Tokenization replaces a sensitive value, such as a card number, with a random surrogate that has no mathematical relationship to it, while the real value stays in a protected token vault. Encryption transforms data reversibly using a key. Tokenization reduces how many systems fall within compliance scope, for example under PCI DSS.
flashcards.detail: Tokens are worthless without the vault, but the vault becomes the crown-jewel target; format-preserving tokens let legacy systems keep working.

flashcards.front: Isolation: sandboxing, virtualization, containerization and separation kernels
flashcards.back: Isolation limits what a compromised component can reach. Sandboxes restrict a process permissions and resources, virtual machines and containers separate workloads, and a separation kernel, evaluated against a Separation Kernel Protection Profile, enforces strict partitioning of components on shared hardware.
flashcards.detail: Pick the isolation by the sensitivity of the data and the trust in the code; virtual machines are a stronger boundary than containers, which share a kernel.

flashcards.front: Cryptography in implementation: levels, algorithm selection and agility
flashcards.back: Encryption can be applied at several levels: field-level for individual sensitive fields, payload for message bodies, transport for links such as TLS, and storage for disks, files or databases. Choose current standardized algorithms and key sizes, retire weak ones, and design for crypto agility so algorithms can be swapped without a redesign.
flashcards.detail: Transport encryption does not protect data at rest, and field-level encryption protects against database administrators; agility matters as NIST post-quantum standards (FIPS 203, 204 and 205, 2024) are adopted.

flashcards.front: Access control models: DAC, MAC, RBAC and trust zones
flashcards.back: Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the owner of an object grant access, mandatory access control (MAC) enforces labels and clearances set by policy that owners cannot override, and role-based access control (RBAC) grants rights through roles. Trust zones group components by trust level, with function permissions checked at each crossing.
flashcards.detail: MAC suits high-assurance settings, DAC is flexible but leaks through owner decisions, and RBAC eases administration of many users.

flashcards.back: Modern processors offer hardware features that software can use: no-execute memory protection, hardware shadow stacks and control-flow enforcement (Intel CET), pointer authentication and memory tagging (Arm), and trusted execution environments such as Intel SGX enclaves, Arm TrustZone and AMD SEV for encrypted virtual machines.
flashcards.detail: These make exploitation harder or isolate secrets but do not remove bugs, and some have themselves been hit by side-channel attacks.

flashcards.back: Reuse vetted internal libraries and well-maintained open source rather than writing security functions yourself, but select, pin, scan and patch what you reuse and know its license. Copying snippets from forums into production code brings unreviewed flaws and unknown licensing.
flashcards.detail: Reused code inherits its flaws and license terms; keep an inventory so one advisory can be traced to every product that uses it.

flashcards.front: Vulnerability lists: OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25 and CVE
flashcards.back: The OWASP Top 10 lists categories of web application risk, the CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses (published by MITRE with CISA, in the tradition of the original SANS Top 25) ranks weakness types, and CVE identifies specific vulnerabilities in products. Teams use them to focus reviews, training and tests.
flashcards.detail: Top 10 is categories of risk, CWE is the type of coding mistake and CVE is one flaw in one product; none is a complete standard.

flashcards.front: Inspecting for malicious code: backdoors, logic bombs and high entropy
flashcards.back: Reviews and tools look for deliberately hidden harm: backdoors that give secret access, logic or time bombs that trigger on a condition or date, hard-coded credentials, unexpected network calls and blocks of high-entropy data that suggest encrypted or packed payloads. Detection combines peer review, static analysis, binary analysis and behavior monitoring.
flashcards.detail: Malicious code is hidden on purpose, so independent review and signed commits matter as much as scanners.

flashcards.front: Code-level controls: watchdogs, file integrity monitoring and anti-malware
flashcards.back: A watchdog timer or process monitor restarts or alerts when a component hangs or dies, file integrity monitoring detects unauthorized changes to binaries and configuration by comparing hashes with a known-good baseline, and anti-malware scans for known malicious code. Software can build in integrity checks and heartbeat signals.
flashcards.detail: Detective controls need someone responding to the alerts, and file integrity monitoring is only as good as its trusted baseline.

flashcards.front: Addressing identified security risks (risk strategy for findings)
flashcards.back: Each finding gets a documented treatment: fix it, compensate with another control, accept it with owner sign-off, transfer it, or avoid it by removing the feature. The choice weighs severity, exploitability, cost and business impact, and a fix is verified by retesting.
flashcards.detail: Closing a ticket without retesting leaves the fix unproven, and an accepted risk needs a review or expiry date.

flashcards.back: When systems are combined, each interface needs an explicit trust contract stating what the other party may send and do, how it authenticates and how the link is protected. Integration security testing checks that a weakness in one system cannot propagate through the connection.
flashcards.detail: The combined system is only as strong as its weakest trusted connection, so treat data from a partner system as untrusted until validated.

flashcards.back: Build flags can add protection or reveal defects: high warning levels with warnings treated as errors, stack protection with canaries, position-independent executables that work with ASLR, non-executable stack and DEP support, FORTIFY_SOURCE checks, read-only relocations (RELRO) and control-flow guard options. Warnings should be fixed, not suppressed.
flashcards.detail: Flags mitigate exploitation but do not repair the code, and a compiler warning about an unchecked buffer is a free bug report.

flashcards.front: Anti-tampering: code signing, obfuscation and integrity checks
flashcards.back: Anti-tampering raises the cost of modifying shipped software: code signing proves origin and integrity, runtime integrity checks verify the code has not changed, obfuscation hinders reverse engineering and anti-debugging checks detect analysis. Signing is cryptographically strong, while obfuscation is only a delay.
flashcards.detail: Never rely on obfuscation to hide keys, and never embed secrets in client code, because they can be extracted.

flashcards.back: This category, new in the OWASP Top 10 for 2025, covers improper error handling, logic errors, failing open and other mishandled abnormal conditions, for example an unhandled exception that skips an authorization check. Prevention means handling errors specifically, failing closed, releasing resources and returning generic messages.
flashcards.detail: The exam link is to fail-safe defaults: an error path that grants access, or leaks detail, is a defect even when the normal path is correct.

flashcards.back: Handle exceptions at the right level, catch specific error types, never leave an empty catch block, release resources in a finally block or equivalent, return generic messages to users with detail in protected logs, and make the default outcome of any unexpected failure a denial.
flashcards.detail: A swallowed exception inside an authorization routine can turn an error into access, so test the error paths as carefully as the normal ones.

flashcards.front: Security testing strategy, plan and standards
flashcards.back: The strategy chooses which techniques at which stages address which risks, and the plan details scope, environments, tools, data, roles, schedule, entry and exit criteria and reporting. Reference sources include ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 for software testing, the Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual (OSSTMM), NIST SP 800-115, the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide and Software Engineering Institute guidance.
flashcards.detail: The strategy comes from the risk assessment and security requirements, not from whichever tool the team already licenses.

flashcards.back: Known-environment testing (formerly white-box) gives testers design information, source code or credentials, unknown-environment testing (formerly black-box) gives them nothing and simulates an outsider, and partial-knowledge testing sits between. Known environment finds more per hour, while unknown environment shows what an outsider could discover.
flashcards.detail: Source available and depth wanted points to known environment; realism of an external attacker points to unknown environment.

flashcards.back: Functional security testing checks that security features behave as specified, such as login, role checks and business-rule logic, including that forbidden actions are refused. Nonfunctional security testing examines qualities such as reliability, performance and scalability under attack-like conditions, for example behavior under load or resource exhaustion.
flashcards.detail: A control that works functionally can still collapse under load, so test both.

flashcards.front: Testing environment: interoperability and test harness
flashcards.back: A test environment should mirror production closely enough to expose real problems (versions, configuration, network, integrations) while staying isolated and protected. A test harness drives the software under test with scripted inputs, stubs and mocks and records the results, and interoperability testing checks it works securely with other systems and protocols.
flashcards.detail: When test and production differ, for example with debug settings or missing controls, findings do not carry over, and test environments must still not hold real data.

flashcards.back: Testing includes checking installation and setup instructions, error messages, user guides and release notes for accuracy and security: instructions should produce a secure configuration, error messages should not leak internals and release notes should disclose security fixes and changed behavior.
flashcards.detail: Documentation that tells administrators to disable a security feature, or shows a default password, is itself a defect.

flashcards.back: Undocumented functionality such as hidden administrative pages, debug interfaces, backdoor accounts, easter eggs and unused parameters can be an attack path. Teams find it by code review, comparing behavior with the specification, reverse engineering, traffic analysis and fuzzing, then remove or document it.
flashcards.detail: Anything absent from the requirements and documentation is unreviewed attack surface, so strip debug code before release.

flashcards.front: Analyzing the security implications of test results
flashcards.back: Results are triaged for severity, exploitability, affected assets and business impact, deduplicated and compared with the release criteria. The analysis decides between fix now, fix later with mitigation and accept, and informs product management about prioritization and about break/build outcomes.
flashcards.detail: Priority combines CVSS with exposure, data sensitivity and evidence of exploitation, and the release decision belongs to the accountable owner.

flashcards.back: Defects, errors and vulnerabilities are recorded in a bug tracker with severity, a risk score such as CVSS, an owner, a due date, a status and links to the requirement or test. Classification, for example by CWE type, supports trend analysis and root cause work.
flashcards.detail: Security issues need restricted visibility until fixed, and every closed item should be verified by retest.

flashcards.front: Secure test data: generation and reuse of production data
flashcards.back: Generated test data should keep referential integrity across tables, have statistical quality that resembles reality and be representative of production. If production data must be reused it is first obfuscated, sanitized, anonymized or tokenized, and data aggregation is considered because combining harmless-looking datasets can reveal sensitive facts.
flashcards.detail: Synthetic data avoids the privacy risk, whereas masked data keeps realism but can leak through re-identification or inference.

flashcards.front: Independent verification and validation and acceptance testing
flashcards.back: Independent verification and validation (IV&V) is done by a team separate from the developers and gives unbiased assurance, internal V&V is done by the project team, and acceptance testing confirms the software meets the agreed requirements, including security acceptance criteria, and is fit for its users before release.
flashcards.detail: Independence is what makes IV&V credible, and acceptance is where requirement-to-test traceability is checked.

flashcards.back: Mutation-based fuzzing alters valid sample inputs, flipping bits or truncating fields, to create test cases, while generation-based fuzzing builds inputs from a model or grammar of the format or protocol. Mutation is quick to start and generation reaches deeper structure. Coverage-guided fuzzing adds feedback on which code paths are reached.
flashcards.detail: Blind mutation struggles with checksums and strict formats, where grammar-based generation does better.

flashcards.front: Failure testing: fault injection, stress testing and break testing
flashcards.back: Failure testing checks behavior when things go wrong. Fault injection deliberately causes errors such as failed dependencies, corrupted data or slow networks, stress testing pushes load past limits to see how the system fails, and break testing looks for the point and manner of failure. Chaos engineering applies the idea in production-like environments.
flashcards.detail: Look for failing open, data leaked by error handling and unsafe recovery states, not only for crashes.

flashcards.front: Cryptographic validation: random number generators and entropy
flashcards.back: Cryptographic testing checks that approved algorithms and key sizes are used, that keys come from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator seeded from a strong entropy source (see NIST SP 800-90A and 800-90B), and that validated modules, FIPS 140-3 through the CMVP, are used where required.
flashcards.detail: A predictable generator, such as one seeded from the clock, breaks an otherwise strong algorithm; entropy is the unpredictability that seeds it.

flashcards.back: Continuous testing runs automated tests, including security tests, at every commit, build and deployment so feedback arrives in minutes. It combines unit, static analysis, composition analysis, dynamic and regression suites in the pipeline, with gates that block risky changes.
flashcards.detail: Automation covers known patterns; manual review and penetration testing still catch logic flaws.

flashcards.back: Simulation tests the software against production-like conditions and data patterns, and synthetic transactions are scripted fake user actions run on a schedule against the live system to measure availability, performance and correct behavior.
flashcards.detail: Synthetic transactions reveal a broken login before real users do; use dedicated test accounts, never real customer data.

flashcards.front: Security researcher outreach: disclosure policy, bug bounty and security.txt
flashcards.back: A vulnerability disclosure policy tells outside researchers how to report problems safely and promises good-faith handling, a bug bounty adds rewards, and a security.txt file (RFC 9116) published under /.well-known/ gives contact details. Safe-harbor wording reduces legal risk for researchers.
flashcards.detail: Without a clear reporting path researchers may go public; triage staff and fix deadlines are what make a program work.

flashcards.back: After the design reduces the attack surface, testing confirms it is what was intended by scanning for exposed ports, endpoints, services, accounts and features, comparing them with the documented inventory and checking that unused ones are disabled.
flashcards.detail: The surface grows silently through new endpoints, debug features and cloud misconfigurations, so revalidate after each release.

flashcards.back: Test cases derived from abuse cases try what an attacker or careless user would do, such as skipping steps, replaying or tampering with requests, escalating privileges and exhausting resources, and assert that the system refuses them safely.
flashcards.detail: They turn abuse cases from the requirements phase into executable tests, closing the loop through traceability.

flashcards.front: Operational risk analysis: environments, personnel training, legal compliance and integration
flashcards.back: Before release, analyze the risks of the deployment environment (staging, production and QA differ in their controls), whether administrators and users are trained for their roles, whether the deployment complies with law, privacy rules and licensing, and how the system integrates with others. Findings feed hardening and the operational readiness decision.
flashcards.detail: Administrators and end users need different training, and a QA environment with relaxed controls must never hold production data.

flashcards.front: Version control, patching and documentation practices in operations
flashcards.back: Operations keeps code, configuration and infrastructure definitions in version control with history and review, tracks the versions and patch levels of every deployed component, records baselines for hardware, firmware and software, and maintains current documentation for build, deployment and recovery.
flashcards.detail: You can only patch and roll back what you can identify, so an accurate inventory and version record come first.

flashcards.front: Application security toolchain and build artifact verification
flashcards.back: The toolchain is the set of automated tools around the pipeline, such as static analysis, composition analysis, secret scanning, infrastructure scanning, dynamic testing and signing, that gate releases. Build artifact verification checks that what is deployed is exactly what was built and approved, using hashes, digital signatures and provenance.
flashcards.detail: A hash published beside the file on the same server proves little; verify against a signature or a hash obtained over a separate trusted channel.

flashcards.front: Key, certificate and secret lifecycle management in operations
flashcards.back: Keys and certificates are generated with approved methods, stored in protected stores such as an HSM or managed key service, distributed securely, rotated on schedule, revoked on compromise and destroyed at end of life, with certificate expiry tracked and renewal automated. Configuration that holds credentials is managed the same way.
flashcards.detail: Forgotten keys and expired certificates are among the commonest operational failures, so keep an inventory.

flashcards.front: Secure boot and root of trust
flashcards.back: Secure boot verifies the digital signature of each component in the boot chain (firmware, bootloader, kernel) starting from an immutable hardware root of trust and refuses to run unsigned or altered code. Generating, accessing and managing the signing keys is critical, and measured boot records what ran so it can be attested.
flashcards.detail: Compromised signing keys defeat secure boot, so protect them in an HSM with limited access and a revocation path.

flashcards.back: Provisioning creates systems and accounts in a controlled way: unique credentials issued and delivered securely, configuration applied from an approved baseline, licenses registered and tracked, and environments built from reviewed infrastructure as code.
flashcards.detail: Default or shared credentials and hand-built servers are the typical failures, and automation makes secure provisioning repeatable.

flashcards.front: Security approval to operate and risk acceptance sign-off
flashcards.back: Before go-live a person with authority at the appropriate level reviews residual risk, open findings and compensating controls, and signs an approval or a documented risk acceptance. The level of sign-off rises with the size of the risk.
flashcards.detail: A project team signing off its own work is not independent, and authority must match the risk being accepted.

flashcards.back: ISCM maintains ongoing awareness of vulnerabilities, threats and control effectiveness (NIST SP 800-137) by collecting observable data such as logs, events, telemetry, traces and metrics, correlating it in a SIEM, enriching it with threat intelligence and feeding detection and response. It also tracks regulation and privacy changes that alter requirements.
flashcards.detail: Monitoring only works if the application emits useful security events, and traces and metrics help detect abnormal behavior that logs miss.

flashcards.back: Triage classifies the severity and scope of an incident to decide who responds and how fast, while forensics preserves and analyzes evidence, collecting the most volatile data first, keeping a chain of custody and working on hashed copies, to establish what happened. Remediation and root cause analysis follow.
flashcards.detail: Preserve evidence before wiping or rebuilding systems, and capture volatile data such as memory first.

flashcards.back: The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) program assigns unique identifiers to publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, and the National Vulnerability Database adds severity and metadata. Teams track the CVEs that affect their components, triage by exposure and exploitability, assign owners and deadlines and verify fixes.
flashcards.detail: CVE names one vulnerability in one product, CWE names the weakness type and CVSS scores severity.

flashcards.front: Runtime protection: WAF, ASLR and dynamic execution prevention
flashcards.back: A web application firewall (WAF) filters HTTP traffic for attack patterns in front of the application, address space layout randomization (ASLR) randomizes where code and data sit in memory, and dynamic execution prevention (DEP, the NX bit) marks data memory as non-executable. RASP adds protection from inside the application.
flashcards.detail: These are compensating controls, useful for virtual patching, that make exploitation harder without removing the underlying flaw.

flashcards.front: Continuity of operations: BCP, DRP, archiving and erasure coding
flashcards.back: A business continuity plan (BCP) keeps critical business functions running during disruption, a disaster recovery plan (DRP) restores IT services and data afterward, and backup, archiving and retention rules define which copies exist and for how long. Resilient storage can use erasure coding, which splits data into fragments with parity so it survives the loss of some of them.
flashcards.detail: BCP is about the business and DRP about technology recovery, and both are sized by the RTO and RPO.

flashcards.front: Service level objectives and agreements (SLO, SLA)
flashcards.back: A service level objective (SLO) is a measurable target for a service attribute such as availability or response time, tracked by an indicator, and a service-level agreement (SLA) is the contract that promises levels, remedies and responsibilities for maintenance, performance, availability and qualified personnel.
flashcards.detail: SLA terms must be achievable with the architecture and support model, and an SLA with no monitoring cannot be enforced.

flashcards.back: Supply chain risk management identifies, assesses and treats risks from suppliers and components across the lifecycle: identifying and selecting components, assessing their risk and deciding to mitigate or accept it, maintaining a list of third-party components such as an SBOM, and monitoring for changes and new vulnerabilities. Guidance includes NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 and ISO/IEC 27036.
flashcards.detail: It is continuous: component selection is only the start, and monitoring continues for as long as the component is in use.

flashcards.front: Analyzing third-party software: certifications, assessment reports, origin and support
flashcards.back: Judge a product on independent evidence: certifications such as ISO/IEC 27001 and Common Criteria, assessment reports such as SOC 2 and the Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix questionnaires, the origin of the product (who builds it, where and under which jurisdiction) and its support (maintenance status, community or commercial, end-of-life dates).
flashcards.detail: A certification covers a defined scope and period, so read the scope and the date before relying on it.

flashcards.back: Pedigree is the history and lineage of a component: who wrote it, from which sources and through which versions and changes. Provenance is the verifiable record of how an artifact was built and delivered: source, builder, build process and chain of custody. Together they let a consumer decide whether to trust it.
flashcards.detail: Signed provenance, as in SLSA, can be verified, whereas a vendor claim of origin cannot.

flashcards.front: Secure transfer and chain of custody
flashcards.back: Software delivery must preserve authenticity and integrity from producer to consumer: transport over TLS, digital signatures, hashes obtained over a trusted channel, access-controlled repositories and a documented chain of custody that records who handled the artifact and when.
flashcards.detail: A signed artifact fetched from a mirror is still verifiable, whereas an unsigned file from an official-looking site is not.

flashcards.back: Connecting systems owned by different organizations or at different trust levels needs an agreement and controls, such as an interconnection security agreement that defines the data exchanged, security requirements, responsibilities and incident notification (see NIST SP 800-47 Rev. 1).
flashcards.detail: Interconnected systems inherit each other risk, so scope the connection narrowly and remove it when it is no longer needed.

flashcards.back: A right-to-audit clause lets the buyer, or an independent assessor, inspect a supplier practices, facilities, code or logs to verify its security commitments, normally with notice and scope limits. Without it, assurance rests on supplier statements alone.
flashcards.detail: Large cloud providers usually substitute independent reports such as SOC 2, so the clause matters most for critical custom suppliers.

flashcards.front: Supplier security requirements in the acquisition process
flashcards.back: Acquisition requirements to set and verify include audit of secure development practices and policy compliance, vulnerability and incident notification and coordination terms, the maintenance and support structure (community versus commercial, licensing), the supplier security track record, the scope of testing under the shared responsibility model and integration of supplier logs into the buyer SIEM.
flashcards.detail: Write them into the contract so they are enforceable, then verify with evidence rather than self-attestation alone.

flashcards.front: Contract terms: IP ownership, liability, warranty, EULA and SLA
flashcards.back: Contracts allocate ownership of intellectual property in custom code, arrange code escrow, limit liability, set warranties on security defects and define the end-user license agreement (EULA) and service-level agreement (SLA) terms that govern use and support.
flashcards.detail: Liability caps are often far below the cost of a breach, so security, legal and procurement should negotiate together.

flashcards.front: Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM)
flashcards.back: The CSA Cloud Controls Matrix is a cloud security control framework of 197 control objectives in 17 domains that also shows which party in the cloud supply chain, provider or customer, is responsible for each. It underpins CSA STAR assessments and the CAIQ questionnaire.
flashcards.detail: Use it as assessment evidence when analyzing a cloud supplier, as the outline suggests with its assessment-report example.

flashcards.front: Open design in practice: peer review, open source and crowd sourcing
flashcards.back: Open design means the security of a system rests on keys and secrets, not on a hidden design. In practice it favors published, peer-reviewed algorithms and protocols, and it is supported by internal design review, open-source scrutiny and crowd-sourced efforts such as bug bounties, where many independent reviewers look for flaws.
flashcards.detail: Open source is not automatically secure; many reviewers only help if they actually review, and open design is about not depending on secrecy, not about publishing your keys or configuration.

flashcards.front: Least privilege in practice: need-to-know, run-time privileges and Zero Trust
flashcards.back: Least privilege applies to people (access limited by need-to-know) and to code (the account a process runs as, its file, network and database rights at run time). Zero Trust extends it by granting access per request after evaluating identity, device and context, so nothing is trusted because of its network location.
flashcards.detail: A service running as an administrator violates least privilege even if all users are restricted; check the runtime identity of the code as well as the user roles.

flashcards.front: Complete mediation in practice: cookies, sessions and cached credentials
flashcards.back: Complete mediation is applied by checking authorization on every request on the server, not only at login. Session and cookie management must let a revoked or changed permission take effect promptly, so long-lived cookies carrying roles, cached credentials and permissions cached for hours are typical violations, while short-lived tokens and a fast cached policy that is invalidated on change satisfy the principle.
flashcards.detail: Performance is the usual excuse for caching; the compliant answer keeps the cache but makes it expire or be invalidated when permissions change.

flashcards.front: Psychological acceptability: usable controls and screen layouts
flashcards.back: People bypass controls that are hard to use, so security design considers usability: sensible password rules or passkeys, clear prompts and screen layouts that make the secure choice the easy one, and CAPTCHA alternatives that do not block legitimate users. The goal is a control people apply correctly, not one they work around.
flashcards.detail: A control that users routinely disable has failed this principle; the fix is redesign, not more training or stricter punishment.

flashcards.front: Applying security in agile, waterfall and DevOps methodologies
flashcards.back: Managing security within a methodology means mapping the same activities onto its rhythm: phase gates and formal reviews in waterfall, and in agile or DevOps security stories, acceptance criteria, the definition of done, automated pipeline checks and short feedback loops. The method changes scheduling and automation, not the goals.
flashcards.detail: End-loaded security reviews fit neither style; the best answer embeds security in every iteration or phase.

flashcards.front: Misuse and abuse cases: mitigating controls
flashcards.back: A misuse or abuse case describes how an attacker or careless user could subvert a feature, and it is only complete when it names the mitigating controls, such as rate limiting, single-use tokens or lockout. Each control becomes a security requirement with an owner and a test, tracked in the traceability matrix.
flashcards.detail: Writing only the attack story without controls produces no requirement; the output of an abuse case is a testable mitigation.

flashcards.front: Pervasive computing technologies: RFID, NFC, wireless and sensor mesh
flashcards.back: Pervasive or ubiquitous computing spreads small connected devices through the environment: RFID tags, NFC (very short-range, tap to pay or pair), wireless and location-based services and sensor networks that relay data through a mesh. Their weaknesses are eavesdropping, cloning and relay attacks, weak authentication, tracking of people and difficult patching.
flashcards.detail: Short range is not security: NFC and RFID can be skimmed or relayed, so sensitive exchanges still need cryptographic authentication.

flashcards.front: Programming language environments: CLR, JVM, Python and PowerShell
flashcards.back: Managed runtimes such as the .NET common language runtime and the Java virtual machine provide memory safety, type checking and permission or sandbox features, while scripting environments such as Python and PowerShell run code with the user rights and need controls like signed scripts, constrained language modes, logging and restricted execution. Choosing the environment is a security decision.
flashcards.detail: A managed runtime removes many memory errors but not logic flaws or injection; scripting hosts need logging and restricted execution to limit abuse.

flashcards.front: Software-defined and cloud-native architecture: IaC, hypervisors and containers
flashcards.back: Virtualization lets many workloads share hardware, with a hypervisor separating virtual machines and containers sharing a kernel. Infrastructure as code defines these environments in reviewed, version-controlled templates. Security depends on hypervisor and image patching, isolation, least privilege for the pipeline and scanning templates before deployment.
flashcards.detail: Containers isolate less strongly than virtual machines, and a flaw in a template is deployed repeatedly, so review the template itself.

flashcards.back: Static application security testing analyzes source or binaries without running them, using rules and data flow analysis to find flaws, and linting applies lighter rules for style and common bug patterns early in the editor or build. Automated coverage metrics describe how much code the analysis or tests reach. Both are tuned to limit false positives.
flashcards.detail: Linting and SAST find patterns, not business logic flaws, and coverage numbers show reach, not correctness; manual review remains necessary.

flashcards.front: Penetration test scope: security controls, known vulnerabilities and known malware
flashcards.back: A penetration test can target whether security controls actually stop an attacker, whether known vulnerabilities are exploitable in context, and whether defenses detect and block known malware. The scope, rules of engagement and written authorization define what may be tested, and findings are reported with evidence and remediation advice.
flashcards.detail: A pen test shows what an attacker can do on the day; it is not a complete list of vulnerabilities and does not replace scanning or review.

flashcards.back: Operational resiliency keeps service going through failures and attacks using redundancy, failover, erasure-coded or replicated storage, capacity headroom and denial-of-service protection. Survivability is the ability to keep essential functions running in degraded form while under attack or after a partial loss. These are availability controls and must be tested.
flashcards.detail: Resilience is designed and exercised, not assumed; a redundant system that has never been failed over is an untested assumption.

flashcards.front: Documentation practices and hardware in configuration control
flashcards.back: Secure configuration control covers hardware and firmware as well as software: inventories and approved baselines, version control, patch records and documentation of installation, configuration, recovery and change history. Good documentation lets a new administrator rebuild the system correctly and lets auditors see what changed and why.
flashcards.detail: Undocumented hardware, firmware or manual changes are how drift and unpatched devices go unnoticed.

flashcards.front: Build environment and code repository security as provenance evidence
flashcards.back: Provenance depends on protecting where code is written and built: branch protection, reviewed merges, signed commits, hardened and isolated build systems, short-lived credentials, reproducible builds and signed provenance records. A consumer can then verify that an artifact came from the expected source through the expected process.
flashcards.detail: A signature proves who signed, not that the build environment was clean; protect the build and record provenance as well.

questions.question: A payment API checks the caller token when a session starts but trusts the same session for every later request, even after an administrator revokes the user permissions. Which design principle is being violated?
options: Complete mediation, because every access must be checked each time it occurs
Separation of duties, because one user is performing the whole operation
Economy of mechanism, because the token check has too many steps
Open design, because the revocation logic is not publicly documented
questions.explanation: Complete mediation requires that every access to every object be authorized at the time of the access, so a revoked permission takes effect immediately. A one-time check followed by cached trust breaks that. Separation of duties is about splitting a sensitive process among people, open design is about not relying on secrecy of the design, and economy of mechanism is about keeping mechanisms simple, none of which describes cached authorization.

questions.question: A microservice that reads product images runs under a database administrator account because that was the quickest way to get it working. Which principle most directly calls for changing this?
options: Defense in depth, by adding a second administrator account as a backup
Psychological acceptability, by making the account easier to remember
Least privilege, giving the service only the access it needs
Separation of privilege, by requiring two administrators to approve each query
questions.explanation: Least privilege says each component should hold only the permissions required for its job, which here is read access to one data set. An administrator account lets any bug in the service become a full database compromise. Adding another administrator account, easier credentials or approvals per query do not reduce the excess privilege itself.

questions.question: After a failed deployment, a gateway starts allowing all traffic through because its policy file could not be loaded. Which principle was ignored?
options: Least common mechanism: policy files should never be shared between components
Open design: the format of the policy file must be published publicly
Accountability: every failed deployment must generate a signed audit record
Fail-safe defaults: access should be denied when the system fails or errors
questions.explanation: Fail-safe defaults means that when something goes wrong, the system should end up in a secure state, normally denying access, and permission should be explicitly granted. A gateway that opens up when its policy fails does the reverse. Least common mechanism, open design and accountability are real principles but do not address the failure behavior in this scenario.

questions.question: A team keeps its encryption algorithm secret and treats that as its main protection. A reviewer objects. What is the best basis for the objection?
options: Security should rest on protecting keys, so a public, peer-reviewed algorithm is preferred
Secret algorithms are prohibited by nearly all data protection regulations in force today
Only symmetric algorithms can be kept hidden without any loss of message integrity
Algorithms that are kept secret always execute more slowly than published algorithms do
questions.explanation: The open design principle, which comes from Kerckhoffs, holds that a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public, because secrets about design eventually leak and unreviewed algorithms often hide weaknesses. The other statements are not true: secrecy is generally legal, speed is unrelated, and symmetry has no bearing.

questions.question: A web form needs a security control against automated account takeover but users are already abandoning it because the rules are complicated. Which principle supports the best recommendation?
options: Psychological acceptability: a protective control that people can use correctly
Economy of mechanism: remove the control entirely to cut down the complexity
Fail-safe defaults: block every login until the user proves identity in person
Defense in depth: require each user to pass every possible control available
questions.explanation: Controls that are too hard to use get bypassed or abandoned, so the design should achieve the security goal in a usable way, for example with multi-factor authentication that fits normal workflow. Removing the control gives up the protection, blocking all logins breaks the service, and stacking every control makes usability worse.

questions.question: An application stores a customer record worth about 40,000 dollars. An analyst estimates a successful attack would expose 25 percent of its value and happens twice every ten years. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
options: 10,000 dollars
20,000 dollars
2,000 dollars
8,000 dollars
questions.explanation: Single loss expectancy is 40,000 times 25 percent, which is 10,000 dollars. The annualized rate of occurrence is twice in ten years, or 0.2 per year. Multiplying gives 2,000 dollars per year. A countermeasure costing more than that annually would not be justified on this risk alone.

questions.question: The product owner decides not to fix a moderate vulnerability in a legacy report module this quarter after reading the risk summary and signing a record of the decision. Which risk treatment is this?
options: Risk acceptance, a knowing decision by the accountable owner
Risk avoidance, because the risk is no longer discussed
Risk mitigation, because the owner reviewed the vulnerability
Risk transference, because responsibility moved to the product owner
questions.explanation: Acceptance means the accountable owner, informed of the risk, chooses to tolerate it, and it should be documented and revisited. Transference shifts financial impact to another party such as an insurer, avoidance eliminates the risky activity, and mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact with a control. Reviewing the issue is not itself mitigation.

questions.question: Management wants a feature that would collect customers contact lists even though the product does not use them. Applying privacy by design, what should the architect recommend FIRST?
options: Do not collect the contact lists unless a documented purpose requires them
Collect them and arrange for staff to delete them manually after one year
Collect them and encrypt the stored copy with a strong, current algorithm
Collect them and display a detailed privacy notice on the sign-up screen
questions.explanation: Privacy by design starts with data minimization: data that is never collected cannot leak or be misused, and each collected item needs a defined purpose. Encryption, notices and manual deletion are all weaker than not collecting unnecessary data in the first place.

questions.question: A vendor ships a product with administrator remote access enabled and a default password, and relies on a hardening guide to tell customers to change it. Which concept does this contradict?
options: Risk transference: the customer now owns all of the product risk
Secure by default: the product should ship already hardened
Non-repudiation: actions on the product cannot be tied to a specific person
Accountability: the vendor failed to publish the product access logs
questions.explanation: Secure by default means the out-of-the-box configuration is already safe, so customers do not need extra steps to get protection. Shipping an insecure default and documenting the fix moves the burden to the customer. Non-repudiation and accountability are about tracing actions, and transference is a risk treatment, none of which fits.

questions.question: A threat is described as an attacker with stolen credentials, and a weakness is described as the absence of multi-factor authentication. What is the risk?
options: The stolen credentials themselves, since they are the asset that has been exposed here
The absence of multi-factor authentication, since it is the only item the team controls
The identity of the attacker, since risk is defined by who is carrying out the attack
The chance and impact of the attacker using the credentials against the gap
questions.explanation: Risk is the combination of the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability and the resulting impact. The threat is the attacker, the vulnerability is the missing control, and the credentials are an asset or an attack input. Treating any single element as the risk skips the likelihood and impact analysis.

questions.question: A company wants to compare its software security program with others in the same industry by looking at the activities those organizations actually perform. Which model fits BEST?
options: BSIMM, because it describes what real programs are observed doing
CMMI, because it measures only hardware manufacturing quality
SAMM, because it prescribes the target activities for every organization
The Microsoft SDL, because it was written for Windows products only
questions.explanation: BSIMM is a descriptive measurement of what many organizations actually do, which makes benchmarking against peers possible. SAMM and the SDL are prescriptive, telling you what to do rather than reporting what peers do. CMMI is a general process maturity model, not tied to hardware manufacturing, and the SDL is not limited to Windows.

questions.question: A security lead wants a roadmap with measurable maturity levels across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, tailored to the company risk. Which framework is the BEST fit?
options: STRIDE, which classifies threats against the elements of a system design
Common Criteria, which assigns evaluation assurance levels to evaluated products
OWASP SAMM, which defines five business functions with three maturity levels
NIST SP 800-61, which defines the phases of incident handling and recovery
questions.explanation: SAMM is organized into five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each with security practices and maturity levels, designed for building an improvement roadmap. SP 800-61 is incident response, Common Criteria evaluates products, and STRIDE is a threat classification model.

questions.question: A federal customer asks a software supplier to attest that it follows secure development practices. The practices are grouped as prepare the organization, protect the software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities. Which document is the customer referencing?
options: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, level 2
The NIST Secure Software Development Framework, SP 800-218
The BSIMM report for the supplier industry sector
NIST SP 800-53, the catalog of security and privacy controls
questions.explanation: The SSDF organizes practices into exactly those four groups and is the basis of US federal secure software attestations. ASVS lists verification requirements for applications, BSIMM is a descriptive study, and SP 800-53 is a control catalog for systems rather than a development practice framework.

questions.question: A team is moving from quarterly releases to deploying several times a day. Which approach to security activities is BEST?
options: Automate checks in the pipeline and add security criteria to every story
Keep a single manual security review before the annual external audit
Freeze deployments until every developer completes a security certification
Move all security testing to a separate team that works after release
questions.explanation: Frequent delivery needs security that scales with it: automated static analysis, dependency checks and policy gates in the pipeline plus testable acceptance criteria in each story. Periodic reviews and post-release testing cannot keep pace, and a blanket freeze would stop delivery without fixing the process.

questions.question: A project manager asks what a security champions program contributes to the lifecycle. What is the BEST answer?
options: A mandatory audit role that is independent of each development team
A group that holds the authority to approve or block every release
Embedded developers who promote secure practice and act as local contacts
A replacement for the central security team in smaller organizations
questions.explanation: Champions extend security knowledge and early detection into each team and give the security team a scaled network of contacts. They are not an approval authority, they do not replace specialists, and they are embedded rather than independent auditors.

questions.question: Which security metric BEST shows whether the vulnerability handling process is improving over time?
options: The total number of vulnerabilities that one scanner reported this month
The count of lines of code scanned by static analysis each week
The number of developers who finished the annual training video
The trend in mean time to remediate vulnerabilities, by severity
questions.explanation: A trend in time to remediate by severity shows how effectively the organization responds to findings. A raw count can rise because testing improved, training completion measures activity rather than outcome, and lines scanned says nothing about whether findings are fixed.

questions.question: A high-severity change to a payment module must go live tonight to stop active fraud. What is the BEST way to handle change management?
options: Wait for the next scheduled change board meeting in two weeks time
Let the developer who wrote the fix deploy it without keeping any record
Bypass change management completely because the fix is so urgent
Use the emergency change path with delegated approval and review it later
questions.explanation: Mature change management has an expedited path for emergencies that keeps accountability: delegated approval, a record and a retrospective review. Skipping the process leaves no control, waiting two weeks ignores the urgency, and an unrecorded single-person change breaks separation of duties.

questions.question: A document says all production systems must use approved encryption. Another says AES-256 must be used for data at rest in the customer database. A third suggests developers consider hardware modules where practical. Which are correctly labeled in order?
options: Procedure, standard, policy
Guideline, policy, standard
Standard, guideline, policy
Policy, standard, guideline
questions.explanation: A policy is a high-level mandatory statement of intent, a standard is a mandatory and specific requirement such as a particular algorithm, and a guideline is optional recommended advice. A procedure would be the step-by-step instructions, which none of the three statements is.

questions.question: A requirements document lists detailed features but says nothing about authentication, logging or data protection. What should the secure software professional do FIRST?
options: Wait for penetration testing to show which controls turn out to be missing
Copy the control list from another team without checking whether it applies
Record the missing controls as defects to be fixed during integration testing
Elicit security requirements from data classes, laws and abuse cases
questions.explanation: Security requirements must be defined early so they can be designed, built and tested, and they come from the data classification, applicable regulations, risk and abuse cases. Waiting for testing or treating them as defects makes fixes costly, and copying controls without analysis may miss real needs or add unneeded ones.

questions.question: Which artifact BEST shows that each security requirement has been designed, implemented and tested?
options: A ranked list of the penetration test findings, sorted by severity and component
A security requirements traceability matrix linking requirements to design and tests
A copy of the organization information security policy approved by management
A diagram of the production network topology showing every firewall and subnet
questions.explanation: A traceability matrix maps each requirement to the design elements, implementation and test cases that satisfy it, exposing gaps in coverage. Findings, policy copies and network diagrams do not tie each requirement to its verification.

questions.question: A designer wants to find security requirements by thinking like an attacker who abuses the checkout feature. Which technique does this describe?
options: Creating a business impact analysis
Writing abuse or misuse cases
Calculating the annualized loss expectancy
Writing use cases for the intended user flows
questions.explanation: Abuse and misuse cases describe how an attacker or careless user could subvert a feature and give rise to requirements such as rate limits, validation and lockout. Use cases cover intended behavior, ALE is a quantitative risk figure, and a business impact analysis identifies critical functions and recovery needs.

questions.question: A hospital application stores diagnoses, billing addresses and appointment times. The architect needs a basis for deciding the encryption, access control and retention rules for each field. What should be done FIRST?
options: Classify the data by sensitivity and regulatory scope together with the data owner
Ask the developers to decide which fields happen to be easiest to protect
Select the strongest available encryption algorithm and apply it to every field
Move all of the data to the cloud provider default storage tier immediately
questions.explanation: Classification by the data owner determines sensitivity and applicable rules, which then drive control choices. Applying the strongest encryption everywhere ignores context and cost, a default storage tier does not address requirements, and convenience is not a basis for protection.

questions.question: A product will process personal data of people in the European Union for a new purpose. Which activity should happen during requirements, before design is finalized?
options: A data protection impact assessment of risks to the individuals concerned
A load test that confirms response time targets are met under peak demand
A disaster recovery drill performed at the secondary site over a weekend
A code review focused on the layout and styling of the user interface
questions.explanation: A data protection impact assessment is required under GDPR for high-risk processing and should shape requirements and design before data is collected. Load tests, interface reviews and recovery drills are valuable, but they do not assess privacy risk to individuals.

questions.question: A sprint story states that the system must be secure. How can the team make this testable?
options: Split it into two smaller stories without defining any further criteria
Move it to the project risk register where it will be recorded as an assumption
Replace it with measurable criteria, such as server-side validation of all inputs
Leave it as written and rely on the testers to judge whether it is satisfied
questions.explanation: A requirement can only be verified if it has specific, observable criteria, so security stories need concrete acceptance conditions that become test cases. Judgement-based testing, burying it in a register and splitting it without criteria all leave it unverifiable.

questions.question: The business states that after an outage it can tolerate no more than 15 minutes of lost transactions and must be running within two hours. How should this be recorded?
options: An RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of two hours
An RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of two hours
A generic availability figure of 99 percent without any time values
An ALE of 15 minutes and an SLE of two hours
questions.explanation: Recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, here 15 minutes, and recovery time objective is the maximum time to restore service, here two hours. Reversing them is a frequent error. ALE and SLE are loss figures in money, and a generic percentage does not capture these targets.

questions.question: A system holds low-impact public data, but a failure in its integrity could cause loss of life in a connected process. How does FIPS 199 categorize the overall system?
options: Moderate, because the category is the average of the three impact ratings
Undetermined, because categorization must wait for a penetration test to finish
Low, because the data is public and confidentiality is the main property here
High, because the highest impact among the three properties sets the category
questions.explanation: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark, so a single high-impact property raises the system to high. Averaging or choosing only confidentiality understates the risk, and categorization is a design-time analysis that does not wait for testing.

questions.question: An organization wants to verify web application security requirements at different assurance levels depending on risk, from basic to highly sensitive. Which resource is the BEST source?
options: The OWASP Top 10, which is a ranked awareness list of web application risks
The SPDX standard, which describes formats for software component inventories
The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, which defines three levels
The CVSS specification, which scores the severity of individual vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: ASVS provides detailed testable requirements organized into three levels for different assurance needs. The Top 10 is for awareness and is not a verification standard, CVSS rates findings, and SPDX describes bill of materials formats.

questions.question: Customer data is retained indefinitely in an application because nobody defined a retention period. What is the MAIN risk this creates?
options: Higher licensing costs for the database engine that holds the records
Reduced mathematical accuracy of the encryption algorithm in use
Larger breach impact, and possible violation of laws that limit retention
A noticeably longer response time for the application login function
questions.explanation: Keeping personal data longer than needed enlarges what an attacker can steal and can breach laws requiring deletion once the purpose ends. Licensing cost, encryption accuracy and login speed are not the main security concern.

questions.question: A team is asked to find what could go wrong in a new design, classifying threats as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Which method is it using?
options: STRIDE
CVSS
DREAD
PASTA
questions.explanation: STRIDE is the threat classification scheme named by those six categories. DREAD scores severity, PASTA is a seven-stage risk-centric process, and CVSS scores the severity of known vulnerabilities, so none of those is a classification of threat types.

questions.question: After threats are identified, the team needs to rank them by damage potential, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users and discoverability. Which technique applies?
options: STRIDE
DREAD
An attack tree
LINDDUN
questions.explanation: DREAD rates threats using those five factors so the team can prioritize. STRIDE categorizes rather than ranks, LINDDUN is a privacy-focused threat method, and an attack tree models paths to an attacker goal.

questions.question: An architect wants a threat modeling approach that begins with business objectives, defines technical scope, simulates attacks and ends with risk and countermeasure analysis. Which should be chosen?
options: Trike, which excludes any attacker perspective
