questions.explanation: Secure transfer relies on authenticity and integrity checks plus a record of who handled the item. Assurances by phone, shared passwords and brochures are not cryptographically verifiable.

questions.question: An auditor reviewing the supplier code repository finds that any developer can push directly to the release branch, and the build runs on a shared workstation with a long-lived administrator account. Which part of pedigree and provenance is weak?
options: Right to audit clauses written into the supplier contract terms
End-user license agreement terms and conditions
Code repository security and build environment security
Software escrow deposit completeness and testing
questions.explanation: Provenance depends on controlling who can change source and on running builds in protected, isolated environments. Contract clauses, license terms and escrow do not make the repository or build environment trustworthy.

questions.question: A supplier objects to an on-site review of its development practices by the buyer. Which contract mechanism should have been negotiated?
options: A larger warranty period on the delivered software
A right-to-audit clause with agreed notice and scope
A copy of the supplier source code in escrow only
A promise from the supplier to follow best practice in all of its development work
questions.explanation: The right to audit lets the buyer or an independent assessor verify security claims. Warranties, escrow and general promises do not give verification access.

questions.question: A supplier is to host a service that processes customer data and will run its own penetration tests. Which acquisition requirement best addresses the scope of testing in the shared responsibility model?
options: An assumption that the supplier tests everything, so the buyer does not need to test
A written statement of which layers each party tests, with buyer permission
A ban on any testing by the buyer, to prevent disruption to other tenants
A requirement to test only the marketing web site of the supplier
questions.explanation: The shared responsibility model divides responsibilities, so testing scope must say who tests what and what is permitted. Assuming the supplier covers everything, banning all buyer tests and testing only the brochure site leave the buyer layers unexamined.

questions.question: The contract with a software vendor requires that security incidents affecting the buyer be reported within 24 hours and that vulnerability notices include a coordinated fix timeline. Which element of supplier requirements is this?
options: Vulnerability and incident notification and coordination
Maintenance and support structure, including licensing terms
Security track record, including past breaches of the supplier
Log integration into the buyer SIEM
questions.explanation: The terms define how and how fast the supplier tells the buyer and works with it on issues, which is the notification and coordination requirement. The others are different elements in the same outline objective.

questions.question: Which supplier requirement lets a buyer detect an attack on a hosted component using its own security tooling?
options: Delivery of the component security logs into the buyer SIEM in an agreed format
A supplier statement that attacks are unlikely because the product is popular
A requirement that logs be kept privately by the supplier for one year
A contract clause that forbids the buyer from using monitoring tools
questions.explanation: Log integration gives the buyer visibility and correlation across its estate. Statements about popularity, supplier-only logs and a ban on monitoring all remove or prevent that visibility.

questions.question: Which contract provision addresses who owns the code that a contractor writes specifically for the buyer, and who is liable for defects?
options: A schedule showing when the contractor teams will attend security training
A list of the encryption algorithms used in the supplier internal network
A statement of the supplier preferred programming languages
Terms covering intellectual property ownership, warranty and liability
questions.explanation: Contractual requirements settle ownership of intellectual property, the warranty on the delivered work and who bears liability, along with items such as escrow, EULA and SLAs. Training schedules, internal algorithms and language preferences do not.

questions.question: A vendor release is delivered together with a statement that a listed vulnerability in an included library is not exploitable in the product because the vulnerable function is never invoked. What should the buyer do?
options: Treat the statement as final and remove the component from the inventory
Record the VEX statement, verify it and keep monitoring the component
Reject all future vendor statements because they cannot be trusted
Delete the SBOM entry since the vulnerability does not apply
questions.explanation: A VEX statement helps prioritize but is a supplier assertion, so it is tracked, checked where practical and revisited if the product changes. Removing the component from inventory or discarding the entry loses information.

questions.question: Which TWO belong in a secure CI/CD pipeline used for release? (Choose two.)
options: Long-lived administrator credentials stored in the pipeline settings
Signing and verification of build artifacts before deployment
A rule that anyone can edit the pipeline definition without review
Automated static, dependency and secret scanning with defined break criteria
questions.explanation: Automated checks with gates and signed artifacts are core release controls. Long-lived powerful credentials and unreviewed pipeline edits make the pipeline an attack path.

questions.question: Which TWO are correct statements about key and certificate management in operations? (Choose two.)
options: Keys and certificates have lifecycles that need inventory, rotation, revocation and expiry monitoring
A single key can safely be used for every environment to reduce administration
Private keys are best kept in a hardware security module or managed key service
Expired certificates are only a cosmetic problem for users
questions.explanation: Lifecycle management prevents outages and compromise, and protected key stores reduce theft. Expired certificates cause failures or warnings that users ignore, and shared keys across environments mean a test leak exposes production.

questions.question: Which TWO items should a buyer verify when assessing the origin and support of third-party software? (Choose two.)
options: Whether support is commercial or community-based, and its end-of-life dates
The number of staff who attended the vendor annual conference
The color scheme used in the vendor user interface
Who develops and maintains it, and under what jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Origin and support determine how quickly issues are fixed and who can compel the supplier. Interface colors and conference attendance have no bearing.

questions.question: Which THREE are valid purposes of a software bill of materials? (Choose three.)
options: Supporting license compliance reviews
Letting buyers see the third-party components and versions delivered
Replacing the need for supplier security assessments
Proving that every listed component is free of vulnerabilities
Identifying affected products when a component vulnerability is announced
questions.explanation: An SBOM is an inventory that supports vulnerability response, license review and transparency. It says nothing about whether the components are vulnerable and does not replace assessment.

questions.question: Release approval should rest on a security sign-off by the accountable owner as well as functional acceptance.
questions.explanation: A product may satisfy its functional requirements and still carry unacceptable residual security risk, so approval to operate is a separate decision with documented sign-off at the appropriate level.

questions.question: Erasure coding stores data as fragments with redundancy, so the original can be rebuilt even if some fragments are lost.
questions.explanation: Erasure codes split data and add parity-like pieces, so loss of a node does not lose the data, which supports operational resilience with less storage than full replicas.

questions.question: Patching should always be performed immediately in production, without testing, so that the vulnerability window is as short as possible.
questions.explanation: Untested patches can break production. A risk-based process tests quickly, uses an expedited path for exploited flaws and applies compensating controls while testing proceeds.

questions.question: Information security continuous monitoring covers only technical data such as logs, and not regulatory or privacy changes.
questions.explanation: Monitoring in the outline includes observable data, threat intelligence, intrusion detection and response, regulation and privacy changes, and integration analysis such as a SIEM.

questions.question: A supplier SOC 2 report from three years ago for a different service is adequate evidence for a current purchase.
questions.explanation: Assessment reports cover a defined scope and period, so stale reports or ones for another service do not provide assurance about the service being bought.

questions.question: Code signing is useful in a supply chain because consumers can verify the publisher and detect alteration after signing.
questions.explanation: A signature binds the artifact to the signer and breaks if the file changes. It does not prove the code is free of flaws, and a compromised signing process can still sign bad code.

questions.question: Chain of custody for delivered software means documenting who held the artifact and how its authenticity and integrity were preserved during transfer.
questions.explanation: The record, combined with cryptographic checks, supports confidence that what arrived is what was built.

questions.question: Software escrow guarantees that the buyer can maintain the product even if the deposit has never been tested.
questions.explanation: An escrow deposit has value only if it is complete and can be built, so verification of the deposit matters as much as the agreement.

questions.question: Over several years an employee moves through four roles and keeps the access rights granted in each. An access review finds the employee can now both create and approve payments. Which problem and which control apply?
options: Privilege creep, addressed by entitlement review and removal on role change
Fail-safe defaults, addressed by denying the employee all access for a trial period
Open design, addressed by publishing the list of who holds each entitlement
Economy of mechanism, addressed by merging all four roles into one broader role
questions.explanation: Entitlements accumulate unless they are reviewed and removed when duties change, and the combination here also breaks separation of duties. Blanket denial, publication and a merged broader role either overreact or enlarge the access.

questions.question: A company replaces eleven separate application logins and a spreadsheet of passwords with single sign-on and a password vault. Which design principle does this most directly serve?
options: Least common mechanism, because users now share one login across the applications
Economy of mechanism, by using one small, well-reviewed mechanism rather than many
Open design, because the vault design is available to any employee who asks
Complete mediation, because the login now occurs only once per day
questions.explanation: Consolidating authentication into one proven component reduces complexity and the number of places to get it wrong, which is economy of mechanism and a form of component reuse. The statement about sharing a login would actually describe a tension with least common mechanism, and a single daily check does not satisfy mediation.

questions.question: Multi-tenant software keeps each customer data in a separate schema, runs each customer batch jobs in isolated containers and uses an allow list for the internal addresses that services may call. Which principle is mainly applied?
options: Fail-safe defaults, because every call is blocked when the service is idle
Psychological acceptability, because the customers see no differences between tenants
Least common mechanism, using compartmentalization and isolation instead of shared resources
Defense in depth, because the schemas and containers are the same layer of control
questions.explanation: Limiting what tenants share reduces leakage paths and limits the effect of one tenant failure, and allow lists restrict reachable destinations. The other principles are not what the isolation and allow list achieve.

questions.question: An application records every approval in an append-only, blockchain-style ledger whose entries are chained by hash and signed by each approver. Which two properties does this primarily support?
options: Availability and scalability
Confidentiality and data minimization
Non-repudiation and accountability
Authentication and single sign-on
questions.explanation: Signed, hash-linked entries make it hard to deny or rewrite an action and give an audit trail that can be traced to the person. A ledger does not itself provide secrecy or capacity, and signing entries is not the same as logging in.

questions.question: Which TWO changes would improve availability without weakening integrity or confidentiality? (Choose two.)
options: Turn off input validation to reduce processing time per request
Run the service in a cluster across separate failure domains with automatic failover
Replicate the production database to a public test site for easy access
Add horizontal scaling that adds instances when demand rises
questions.explanation: Redundancy, clustering, failover and elastic scaling support availability. Copying production data to a public site breaks confidentiality, and disabling validation reduces integrity protection.

questions.question: Passwordless authentication with a phishing-resistant authenticator can improve both security and psychological acceptability.
questions.explanation: Removing memorized secrets reduces phishing and reuse, and sign-in becomes simpler for users, so people are less tempted to work around the control.

questions.question: A new compliance manager asks which security documents the project should produce and maintain. Which collection is most appropriate?
options: Marketing plans, sales forecasts, office layouts and travel policies
Requirements, threat model, review and test records, risk acceptances
A single page stating that the software follows industry best practice
Only the final penetration test report, kept by the testing firm
questions.explanation: Security documentation records decisions and evidence across the lifecycle so that others can build, verify, operate and audit the software. A slogan, unrelated business papers or a single report do not.

questions.question: A program tracks the number of vulnerabilities found each month, and the number rose after the team adopted better scanners. How should the metric be interpreted and improved?
options: The rise proves the developers are getting worse, so the scanners should be removed
The count is useless, so metrics should not be used to manage the program
The count may reflect better detection, so add trends like time to remediate
The count should be hidden from management to avoid unnecessary concern
questions.explanation: Metrics must be interpreted in context and paired with outcome measures such as time to fix, criticality distribution and recurring weakness types, and tied to objectives and key results. Removing tools, abandoning measurement and hiding data remove insight.

questions.question: An application is being retired at the end of its life. The credentials, DNS records and API keys it used are still active, and a license subscription renews automatically. Which decommissioning activities were missed?
options: Threat modeling and misuse case writing for the retired application
Fuzzing and regression testing of the released build
Tokenization and obfuscation of the stored data
Credential and configuration removal, and license cancellation
questions.explanation: End-of-life policies include removing credentials and configuration, cancelling licenses, archiving and meeting service level obligations, so no active access paths or costs remain. The other items are development-time activities.

questions.question: A security lead wants a dashboard for executives and a separate feedback loop for developers. Which design best meets both needs?
options: Executives see risk trends, and developers get findings in their tools
Both audiences receive the same weekly spreadsheet of raw scanner output
Executives receive nothing, and developers get a quarterly report
Developers see the dashboard, and executives read the commit logs directly
questions.explanation: Reporting is tailored to its audience: summarized risk for decision makers and actionable detail for the people who fix the problems, with feedback to improve processes. Raw output, no reporting and swapped audiences are ineffective.

questions.question: The business owner argues that a technical weakness in a back-office module is acceptable because it affects no revenue. The architect responds that the weakness allows access to the payroll database. What is the best way to frame the decision?
options: Overrule the owner, since technical risk is always greater than business risk
Express the technical risk in business impact terms for the owner
Accept the owner view, since business risk alone drives every decision
Remove the module from the risk register until it is exploited
questions.explanation: Technical risk becomes a business decision when its consequence is stated in business terms, and the accountable owner then accepts, mitigates or transfers it. Overruling, ignoring technical risk and deleting the entry skip proper risk management.

questions.question: A team following an agile method works in two-week sprints. Which approach best integrates security compared with a phase-gated waterfall method?
options: Embed security tasks in every sprint, with acceptance criteria
Run one large security phase after the last sprint is complete
Skip security until the product backlog is empty
Hand all security work to a separate team that never meets the developers
questions.explanation: In agile and DevOps the security goals do not change, but activities are scheduled in short cycles and automated, while waterfall maps them to phase gates. End-loaded or isolated security does not match the cadence.

questions.question: A change to an authentication service has passed unit tests and is ready for production. The change board needs to include the Assessment and Authorization process. What does this process contribute?
options: Control assessment and formal risk acceptance by an official
A rewrite of the code by the assessors to remove any defects found
A guarantee, issued by the vendor, that the system has no vulnerabilities
An automatic approval whenever all unit tests pass
questions.explanation: Assessment tests the controls and authorization is the risk acceptance decision made on that evidence, repeated when the system changes. Assessors do not rewrite code, no one can guarantee no vulnerabilities, and passing tests is not authorization.

questions.question: The team asks the difference between verification and validation. Which statement is correct?
options: Verification checks the specification, and validation checks real user needs
Verification checks that users are satisfied, and validation checks the source code against standards
Verification is done only by developers, and validation is done only by auditors
Verification is performed once at release, and validation is performed once at design
questions.explanation: Verification asks whether we built the product right, and validation asks whether we built the right product. The other statements mix up the terms or invent restrictions.

questions.question: An organization wants a software security standard for application security processes that auditors can assess, and a separate reference for payment software. Which pair fits?
options: OWASP Top 10 and the CVSS scoring specification
SPDX and CycloneDX as machine-readable inventory formats
ISO/IEC 27034 and the PCI Software Security Framework
STRIDE and DREAD as threat modeling aids
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27034 covers application security and the PCI Software Security Framework covers payment software. The other pairs are an awareness list and a scoring system, two SBOM formats, and two threat modeling aids.

questions.question: Which TWO are appropriate inputs when defining the security metrics and reporting for a software program? (Choose two.)
options: Criticality levels of applications, so results can be weighted by business importance
The total number of lines of code written by the team
The number of meetings held about security each quarter
Objectives that link measures to program goals, such as fixing critical findings within a set time
questions.explanation: Metrics should connect to objectives and take criticality into account. Meeting counts and code volume measure activity, not security outcomes.

questions.question: Decommissioning an application requires attention to data disposition, including retention duties, destruction and dependencies on the data.
questions.explanation: Retired systems still hold data subject to retention and privacy rules, and other systems may depend on it, so archiving or destruction must be planned and recorded.

questions.question: Technical risk and business risk are the same thing, so the same people always make both decisions.
questions.explanation: Technical risk describes weaknesses and threats in the system, while business risk describes the consequences for the organization, and accountable business owners make the risk acceptance decisions informed by technical analysis.

questions.question: A story reads As a customer I can reset my password, and another says Password reset links must expire within 15 minutes and be single-use. How should these be classified?
options: The first is functional, the second non-functional security
The first is non-functional, the second is a use case
Both are functional, because both concern the same feature of the system
Both are non-functional, because they mention passwords
questions.explanation: Functional requirements say what the system does, and security, operational and continuity qualities are non-functional constraints. The expiry and single-use rule constrains how the feature must behave.

questions.question: A defense contractor builds a patient scheduling tool for a hospital that takes card payments, using the contractor approved libraries only. Which list covers the compliance requirement sources?
options: Only the company library standards, because they are the closest to the developers
Only the payment card industry standard, because it is the only one with fines
Health regulation, card industry standard, contract and company standards
The marketing requirements, because they define the customers and markets
questions.explanation: Compliance comes from regulators, law, industry-specific obligations and company standards, and all that apply to the data and market must be identified. Single-source answers miss obligations.

questions.question: A company labels documents Public, Internal, Confidential and Restricted, and attaches each label to the data as it is created. Which requirement does this support?
options: Avoiding any need for access control, because the label alone stops disclosure
Eliminating the need for data retention rules, because labels apply forever
Removing the data owner role, because the system now classifies by itself
Consistent handling rules driven by sensitivity and impact
questions.explanation: Labels make sensitivity visible to people and systems so rules apply consistently, but they do not enforce anything on their own and do not replace owners or retention rules.

questions.question: A new application will collect birth date, home address and employer to register users, though the features need only an e-mail address. Which privacy requirement is most appropriate?
options: Collect all fields now in case they are useful in the future
Limit collection to what the stated purpose needs
Collect everything and encrypt it with the strongest algorithm
Collect everything and delete it manually after a year
questions.explanation: Defining the data collection scope and purpose is the first privacy control, since data not collected cannot be breached or misused. Encryption and later deletion cost more and carry residual risk.

questions.question: A misuse case for a checkout feature describes an attacker replaying a discount code many times. Which element should the team add to complete it?
options: A description of the colors used on the checkout page
A list of the developers who wrote the feature
The date by which the case will be removed from the backlog
Mitigating controls, such as single-use codes
questions.explanation: A useful misuse case names how the abuse is prevented or detected, and the controls become requirements and tests. Presentation details, authorship and backlog dates do not.

questions.question: A requirement states that every login failure be logged. The team cannot show the reviewer which design element or test covers it. Which artifact should have provided the answer?
options: The data flow diagram without any requirement identifiers
The list of open source licenses in the project
The security requirements traceability matrix
The change advisory board meeting minutes
questions.explanation: An SRTM links each requirement to its source, design, implementation and test, exposing gaps. A diagram without identifiers, license lists and meeting minutes do not trace requirements.

questions.question: A company is outsourcing the development of a module to a contractor. When should vendor security requirements be defined?
options: Before selection, in the requirements
After delivery, when the module is available to test
Only if the contractor asks for them
After the first security incident involving the module
questions.explanation: Vendor requirements, such as secure development practices, vulnerability handling and audit rights, belong in the baseline before selection, and verifying them follows in the supply chain domain.

questions.question: Which TWO are good examples of non-functional security requirements? (Choose two.)
options: The user sees a confirmation page after ordering
The user can search products by name
The service must resume within two hours of a regional failure
All administrator actions must be logged and the logs retained for one year
questions.explanation: Logging, retention and recovery targets are qualities and constraints on how the system behaves. Searching and confirmation pages are functional behaviors.

questions.question: Which TWO belong in the data lifecycle requirements for personal data? (Choose two.)
options: A policy that backups are exempt from every privacy rule
A secure and verifiable disposal method at the end of its life
A plan to keep all data forever as a source of future analysis
Rules for how long data is retained and where it is stored
questions.explanation: Lifecycle requirements span collection, storage, use, sharing, retention and disposal. Keeping data forever and exempting backups violate retention and privacy principles.

questions.question: Fully anonymized data that cannot reasonably be re-identified generally falls outside privacy regulations that apply to personal data.
questions.explanation: Anonymization removes identifiability, whereas pseudonymization does not. The determination depends on whether re-identification is reasonably possible, including by combining data sets.

questions.question: A data dictionary is the document that records which users hold access to each data store.
questions.explanation: A data dictionary describes data elements, their meaning, format and sometimes classification. Access is recorded in access control lists, provisioning records and review reports.

questions.question: A third-party processor that receives personal data from the application relieves the application owner of requirements for that data.
questions.explanation: The organization stays accountable for the data it shares and must flow down requirements and verify them, including for retention, deletion and security.

lessons.title: Secure Software Concepts and Design Principles
lessons.summary: The core security properties, the classic secure design principles, and the risk and privacy ideas that every other domain builds on.
lessons.reading:
Secure software starts from a small set of ideas. The first is the CIA triad: confidentiality (only the right people see the data), integrity (the data is only changed in authorized ways) and availability (the system works when it is needed). Every threat you will ever model attacks one of these, and every control you will ever choose protects one of these. Next to the triad sit the AAA steps. Authentication proves who is asking, authorization decides what that identity may do, and accountability records what it actually did. A very common exam trap is to treat a valid login as permission. Being authenticated says nothing about whether you may read a particular record.

The secure design principles come largely from a famous 1975 paper by Saltzer and Schroeder, and they are still the vocabulary of the exam. Least privilege means every user and every piece of code gets only the access it needs. Separation of duties means one person cannot complete a sensitive process alone. Defense in depth means several independent controls, so one failure is not a disaster. Fail-safe defaults means that access is denied unless it is explicitly granted and that a failing component ends up closed, not open. Complete mediation means every access is checked every time, not just once at the start of a session. Economy of mechanism says keep security mechanisms small and simple, because simple things can be verified. Open design says do not rely on keeping the design secret, only the keys. Psychological acceptability says that if a control is painful, people will route around it.

Two more are worth knowing. Least common mechanism says to minimize shared components between users, because shared state is a path for leaks. Separation of privilege says that sensitive actions should need more than one condition to be satisfied. A service running as an administrator breaks least privilege. A gateway that opens when its configuration fails breaks fail-safe defaults. An API that checks permission only when a session begins breaks complete mediation.

The next layer is risk. A threat is something that could cause harm, a vulnerability is a weakness it could exploit, and risk is the combination of likelihood and impact. Organizations can mitigate a risk with controls, transfer it with insurance or contract, avoid it by dropping the activity, or accept it knowingly. Acceptance is a decision by an accountable owner, written down, not what happens when nobody acts. For quantitative questions, remember that single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor, and annualized loss expectancy is that figure times the annual rate of occurrence. A safeguard is worth buying when it reduces the expected annual loss by more than it costs per year.

Finally, modern secure software work includes privacy and product responsibility. Privacy by design means collecting only what you need, making privacy the default, and protecting data through its entire life. Secure by design and secure by default shift responsibility toward the vendor: the product should be built with security in its architecture and ship hardened, rather than shipping insecure and publishing a guide for customers to fix it.

The outline widens each of these ideas, so be ready to apply them in concrete form. Availability is engineered with redundancy, replication, clustering, scalability and resiliency, but replication copies bad writes as well as good ones, so it is not a backup. Authentication covers multi-factor authentication (factors must be of different kinds), identity and access management, single sign-on, federation and biometrics, which are probabilistic and cannot be reissued if a template leaks. Authorization is expressed as permissions and entitlements, which accumulate unless they are reviewed. Non-repudiation comes from digital signatures and tamper-evident records such as an append-only ledger or blockchain. Governance, risk and compliance ties these to regulatory, legal and industry obligations, and compliance is a baseline, not proof of security.

The design principles also have concrete forms. Separation of duties is enforced through multi-party control, secret sharing and split knowledge, where no one person knows the whole secret. Defense in depth gains independence through technical and geographic diversity. Resiliency means no single point of failure, with failover that still fails secure. Economy of mechanism and component reuse favor one reviewed mechanism, such as single sign-on or a password vault, over many. Complete mediation shows up in cookie and session management and in caching of credentials or permissions, which must expire or be invalidated when rights change. Open design is Kerckhoffs principle and is supported by peer review, open source and crowd-sourced scrutiny. Least common mechanism favors compartmentalization, isolation and allow lists. Psychological acceptability covers passwordless sign-in, sensible password rules, usable screen layouts and alternatives to CAPTCHA that do not block real users.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to secure design principles? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a well-run bank branch. Tellers can only open the drawer they are assigned (least privilege), large withdrawals need a second signature (separation of duties), and there is a door, a camera, a vault and an alarm instead of one lock (defense in depth). If the power fails, the vault stays locked (fail-safe defaults) and every withdrawal is checked against the account at the moment it is made, not because the customer was recognized at the door (complete mediation). The vault design is not secret, since the safety rests on the combination (open design), and the procedures are simple enough that staff actually follow them (economy of mechanism and psychological acceptability).
commonTraps: Authentication is not authorization: a successful login does not grant access to every function or record.
Fail safe protects human life (doors unlock in a fire), while fail secure protects data (doors lock); software questions normally mean fail secure, which is the default-deny idea.
Least privilege trims each role to the minimum, whereas separation of duties splits a single sensitive process across roles; they are often swapped in distractors.
Risk acceptance is a documented decision by an informed accountable owner, not a lack of action, and transfer shifts financial impact but not accountability.
Replication protects availability but copies corruption, so it does not replace point-in-time backups.
Split knowledge means no one knows the whole secret, while dual control means two people must act together; the terms are swapped in options.
lessons.scenario: A team ships a reporting service that runs under a database owner account, caches each user permissions at login for the whole day, and reveals a full stack trace to anyone who triggers an error. Naming the principles at play makes the remediation obvious: reduce the account to read-only access on the views it needs (least privilege), check authorization on each request (complete mediation), and show a generic message while logging the detail (fail-safe handling and open design, since the system should not depend on attackers not seeing its internals).
lessons.onTheJob: Practitioners rarely cite Saltzer and Schroeder by name, but the principles are the shared language in design reviews: saying this call path lacks complete mediation gets a faster fix than saying it feels insecure. Keep a short list of the principles in your review checklist and map every finding to one. When you present risk to management, always attach an owner and a decision (mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept) to each item, because a risk list with no owners becomes a graveyard. And remember that the exam rewards the answer that fixes the root cause by design over the answer that adds a compensating control after the fact.

lessons.title: Secure Lifecycle Management: Models, Maturity and Governance
lessons.summary: How security is built into the software development lifecycle, the main frameworks and maturity models, and the governance that keeps them running.
lessons.reading:
A secure software development lifecycle (secure SDLC) is not a separate process bolted onto development. It is the practice of placing security activities inside every phase: security requirements during planning, threat modeling during design, secure coding and review during implementation, security testing before release, and monitoring and response afterward. The guiding idea is shift left. A defect found while requirements are being written costs a conversation to fix, while the same defect found in production costs an emergency patch, customer notification and possibly a breach. That cost curve is the standard justification you will see behind exam answers that favor earlier activities.

Several frameworks give structure, and the exam expects you to tell them apart. The Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) is a prescriptive set of practices from training through requirements, design, implementation, verification, release and response. The NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF, SP 800-218) groups practices into four sets, Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software and Respond to Vulnerabilities, and it works with any lifecycle model. OWASP SAMM, the Software Assurance Maturity Model, is also prescriptive and organizes work into five business functions: governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, each with three practices and three maturity levels. BSIMM is different in kind: it is descriptive. It records what real organizations do, so you use it to compare your program with peers, not to learn what you should do.

The development model changes how security is scheduled, not whether it happens. In waterfall, security activities map to phase gates. In agile, security must be expressed as user stories and acceptance criteria, tested within the sprint, and automated wherever possible. In DevOps and DevSecOps, security checks such as static analysis, dependency scanning and policy checks run in the delivery pipeline, and ownership of security is shared between development, operations and security staff.

Governance is what makes the practices stick. A policy states management intent and is mandatory, a standard states specific mandatory requirements, a guideline offers optional advice, and a procedure lists steps. Role-based training makes sure developers, testers, architects and operators each know what they need. Gates define criteria that must be met before work moves on, and an exception to a gate needs a documented risk acceptance from the accountable owner.

Finally, programs must be measured and changes controlled. Useful metrics are trends, such as mean time to remediate by severity, the percentage of code covered by scanning and the number of open findings by severity, because a raw count of vulnerabilities can rise when testing improves. Change management ensures that every change, including security fixes, is assessed, approved, tested and recorded. Emergencies get an expedited path with delegated approval and a review afterward, not a bypass.

The outline adds several management activities. Security standards and guidance come from many sources, and you should know what kind each is: ISO/IEC 27034 for application security, the PCI Software Security Framework for payment software, the NIST SSDF and SP 800-53, OWASP resources such as SAMM and ASVS, the industry group SAFECode for practical development guidance, and BSIMM as a descriptive measurement. A strategy and roadmap turns these into security milestones and control gates with break/build criteria set in advance, and security documentation (requirements, threat models, review and test records, procedures and risk acceptances) is the evidence that the gates were met.

Metrics and reporting close the loop. Useful measures include criticality levels, average time to remediate, complexity and key performance indicators, and objectives and key results (OKRs) that link them to goals. Reports and dashboards are tailored to the audience, with feedback loops returning findings to developers. Decommissioning follows end-of-life policies: remove credentials and configuration, cancel licenses, archive what must be kept, honor service level agreements and dispose of data according to retention duties and dependencies. Integrated risk management distinguishes technical risk (weaknesses and threats in the system) from business risk (the consequence for the organization), considers legal matters such as intellectual property and breach notification (for example GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, and the HIPAA rule requires individual notice within 60 days), and finally feeds secure operation practices: change management, an incident response plan, verification and validation (building the product right and building the right product) and the assessment and authorization process in which an authorizing official accepts residual risk.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to secure lifecycle models? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Building secure software is like building a house. You do not inspect the electrical wiring only after the walls are plastered; the inspector visits at the foundation, framing and wiring stages, and each visit has criteria that must pass before the next trade starts (gates). A building code states what is required (standards), best-practice guides suggest more (guidelines), and the contractor follows detailed instructions (procedures). A maturity model is like grading the contractor on how repeatable their process is, and a benchmark study such as BSIMM is like a survey of what other contractors in town actually do.
commonTraps: BSIMM is descriptive (what others do) while SAMM, the SDL and the SSDF are prescriptive (what to do); questions often hinge on that single word.
The SSDF has four groups: prepare, protect, produce and respond; it is outcome-based and is not a lifecycle model in itself.
A higher maturity level means the process is managed and repeatable, not that the resulting software is secure.
Emergency changes still follow an expedited process with approval and later review; skipping change management is never the best answer.
Verification checks against the specification and validation checks against the real need; the words are often reversed.
A rising count of findings can mean better testing; pair it with trends such as mean time to remediate.
lessons.scenario: A company moving to continuous delivery asks what to do about its annual manual security review. A good answer keeps the review for architecture and risk questions but moves repeatable checks into the pipeline: static analysis and dependency scanning on every commit, security acceptance criteria in every story, and a gate that blocks release when critical findings are open without an approved exception. It then measures mean time to remediate by severity and uses SAMM to plan the next maturity step.
lessons.onTheJob: Programs fail from friction more often than from missing tools. Introduce checks in advisory mode first, tune them until developers trust the findings, then turn them into gates. Pick a small number of metrics tied to outcomes, such as time to fix critical findings, and review them with engineering leaders each quarter. Use BSIMM or SAMM to justify budget by showing the gap to peers and a concrete roadmap, not to chase a score. Keep a written exception process, because there will always be a launch with an open finding, and you want the business owner, not the security team, to be the one accepting that risk in writing.

lessons.title: Secure Software Requirements: Security, Privacy and Compliance
lessons.summary: How to elicit, classify and document security, privacy and compliance requirements, including abuse cases and traceability.
lessons.reading:
Requirements are where security either gets specified or gets forgotten. Functional requirements describe what the software does, and non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, availability and security. A control that is not written down will rarely be designed, built or tested, which is why the exam keeps returning to the idea that missing security requirements should be elicited first, before anyone argues about tools. Good requirements are specific and testable. The statement that the system must be secure cannot be tested, but a statement such as all inputs are validated on the server and every request is authorized for the specific object can be.

Sources of security requirements include the data classification, the laws and contracts that apply, the organization policies and standards, the results of threat modeling, and abuse cases. Data classification assigns levels such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, and it is decided by the data owner, not by developers. The level then drives encryption, access control, logging, retention and handling rules. For federal systems FIPS 199 rates the impact of losing confidentiality, integrity and availability as low, moderate or high and uses the high-water mark, so one high rating makes the overall system high. The data lifecycle matters too: create, store, use, share, archive and destroy are all stages with requirements, and backups and test copies are the places where data most often escapes.

Abuse and misuse cases flip a use case around. Where a use case says a customer places an order, an abuse case says an attacker places thousands of orders with stolen cards, or changes the order number to read someone else's order. They produce requirements such as rate limiting, fraud checks and object-level authorization, and later become negative test cases. A security requirements traceability matrix links each requirement to its source, design element, code and test, so you can show coverage and see what a change affects.

Privacy and compliance are requirements too. Privacy requirements include data minimization (collect only what you need), purpose limitation (use data only for the declared purpose), retention limits and deletion, and a privacy or data protection impact assessment performed early for high-risk processing. Laws and standards differ: GDPR governs personal data of people in the EU, HIPAA covers US health information, PCI DSS is an industry standard for payment card data enforced by contract, and SOX concerns controls over financial reporting. The first step is to determine which apply, then map them to concrete controls.

Finally, availability and recovery needs belong in requirements. The recovery time objective is the longest tolerable time to restore service, and the recovery point objective is the longest tolerable window of data loss. Remember the reversal trap: RTO is time to recover, RPO is how far back data may go. Logging requirements say which events are recorded, what each record contains, how long logs are kept and how they are protected, and they exclude secrets such as passwords.

Several finer points in the outline deserve attention. Compliance requirements come from four sources: regulators, law, the industry sector (defense, healthcare, financial, payment cards) and the company itself, such as approved languages, frameworks and tools. Data classification needs a data owner who decides the label and a data custodian who protects the data, a data dictionary that describes each element, labels for sensitivity and impact, and different handling for structured data (fields can be classified one by one) and unstructured data (documents and messages, where discovery comes first).

Privacy requirements fix the collection scope and lawful basis, state whether data is pseudonymous (the link can be restored, so it is still personal data) or anonymous, honor user rights such as access, correction and erasure and marketing preferences, set retention limits and address cross-border requirements: data residency, jurisdiction and lawful transfer mechanisms. Data access provisioning covers users, service accounts (each needs an owner, narrow rights and rotation) and periodic reapproval. A misuse or abuse case is only complete when it names mitigating controls, which become requirements, and a traceability matrix links each requirement to design and test. Finally, when part of the system will be built or run by a supplier, third-party vendor security requirements are written before selection and carried into the contract.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security requirements? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Writing security requirements is like writing the brief for a new office building. Saying the building should be safe is useless to the architect. A good brief says which rooms hold valuables (data classification), which fire and accessibility codes apply (compliance), who must be able to enter which floors (access requirements), how long the building may be closed after a flood (recovery objectives) and what a burglar might try, such as using the loading dock or tailgating (abuse cases). A checklist that ties each line of the brief to a drawing and an inspection is the traceability matrix.
commonTraps: RTO is the time allowed to restore service and RPO is the amount of data loss allowed; the two are swapped constantly in answer options.
Data classification is performed by the data owner and drives controls; it is not chosen by whichever team finds a control cheapest.
Pseudonymized data is generally still personal data under GDPR; only truly anonymized data is outside it.
PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard, not a statute, yet compliance is still mandatory for organizations that handle card data.
Pseudonymized data can be re-linked, so it stays personal data; only data that cannot reasonably be re-identified is anonymous.
Service accounts are provisioning subjects too: each needs an owner, minimal rights, rotation and periodic reapproval.
lessons.scenario: A health-tech startup is building a mobile app that stores diagnoses and appointment times for users in several countries. Before design begins the team has the data owner classify each field, identifies the health and privacy laws that apply, runs a data protection impact assessment, writes abuse cases such as one patient reading another record, and records requirements for encryption, access control, logging and retention. Each requirement is entered in a traceability matrix with an owner and a planned test.
lessons.onTheJob: The most valuable skill is turning vague demands into testable statements and getting them into the backlog before sprint planning, not after. Ask what is the worst thing that could happen to this data, then write that as an abuse case. Keep a short mapping from each regulation to the controls that satisfy it, so audits become a lookup instead of an investigation. Watch for requirements that conflict, such as retention for legal hold versus a deletion request, and get legal and the data owner to resolve them in writing. Finally, make sure logging requirements name the data that must never be logged, because log files are one of the most common places secrets and personal data leak.

lessons.title: Secure Architecture and Design: Threat Modeling and Patterns
lessons.summary: Threat modeling methods, attack surface reduction, zero trust and the security design of APIs, microservices, cloud, containers and AI-enabled systems.
lessons.reading:
Design is the cheapest and most powerful place to remove vulnerabilities, because a flaw in the architecture cannot be patched away by coding carefully. The central design activity is threat modeling: a structured way to ask what we are building, what can go wrong, what we will do about it, and whether we did a good job. Most methods start from a data flow diagram, which shows processes, data stores, external entities and the flows between them, plus trust boundaries where data moves between zones of different trust. The flows that cross a trust boundary are where you look first.

You need to distinguish the main methods. STRIDE classifies threats as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege, and each maps to a security property: authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorization. DREAD ranks threats by scoring Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability. STRIDE classifies, DREAD prioritizes. PASTA, the Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis, is a seven-stage risk-centric method that starts from business objectives and uses attack simulation.

Architecture then applies design principles at scale. Attack surface reduction removes features, ports and accounts nobody needs. Zero trust, described in NIST SP 800-207, abandons trust based on network location: every request is authenticated, authorized and evaluated using identity, device state and context, with a policy decision point and policy enforcement points. In microservices, services authenticate each other, often with mutual TLS, and every service authorizes its callers, because an attacker who gets inside the network could otherwise call any service. APIs must authenticate callers, authorize at the object and function level, validate input against a schema, limit rates and avoid over-sharing data. Broken object level authorization, where changing an identifier reaches another user's data, is the leading API risk.

Cloud, container and serverless designs change who is responsible for what. Under the shared responsibility model the provider secures the infrastructure and the customer is always responsible for its own data, identities, configuration and code, with the split shifting by service model. Containers share the host kernel and so isolate less strongly than virtual machines: use minimal scanned images, run as non-root, keep secrets out of images and apply network policies. Identity architecture uses federation: SAML or OpenID Connect carry authentication, while OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, a distinction exams love.

Two further design topics round this out. Cryptographic architecture means using vetted algorithms, protecting data in transit, at rest and where needed in use, and managing keys through their lifecycle in a dedicated key service or hardware module apart from the data. AI-enabled software adds threats such as prompt injection, training data poisoning, model theft and leakage of sensitive data through outputs. Treat model output as untrusted input, give any tools the model can call the least privilege, and require human approval for high-impact actions.

The architecture objective names many styles, and each has a typical weakness. SABSA derives controls from business requirements, and the security chain of responsibility passes verified identity along each hop. Distributed designs (client-server, peer-to-peer, message queuing, n-tier) add trust boundaries at every broker and tier. Service-oriented architecture and enterprise service buses centralize policy but must not replace authorization in each service. Rich internet applications run in an untrusted client, so the server stays authoritative. Pervasive computing (IoT, RFID, NFC, sensor meshes) and embedded software need secure boot, secure memory and signed secure update. Cloud (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS) shifts responsibilities, mobile apps raise implicit data collection concerns, hardware needs side-channel and speculative-execution mitigations, secure elements and trustworthy firmware and drivers, and cognitive and immersive technologies and industrial or medical IoT add safety and privacy concerns.

Interface design covers management and out-of-band interfaces, log interfaces, upstream and downstream dependencies, including keys and data shared between applications, and protocol and API choices. Reusable technologies to evaluate include credential management with X.509 certificates, flow control through proxies, firewalls and queues, data loss prevention, virtualization, infrastructure as code and containers, trusted computing with the Trusted Platform Module and trusted computing base, database security (encryption, views, triggers, privileges and secure connections), language runtimes such as the common language runtime and Java virtual machine, operating system controls, and secure backup, retention and destruction. Threat modeling adds hybrid methods, CVSS for scoring, common threats such as advanced persistent threats, insiders and suppliers, attack surface evaluation and threat intelligence. Architectural risk assessment and design reviews, modeling of non-functional properties and constraints, and a secure operational architecture (deployment topology, operational interfaces and the CI/CD pipeline) complete the picture.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to threat modeling? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Threat modeling a design is like a burglar-minded walk-through of a house plan before it is built. You mark where people legitimately come and go (flows), where the property line and the front door are (trust boundaries), then at each door and window ask how it could be forced, faked, hidden behind or overloaded (STRIDE). You rank which break-ins would hurt most (DREAD) or sketch the easiest route to the jewelry box (attack tree). Zero trust is like checking a visitor badge at every door inside the building, not just at the lobby. Zero trust means being in the lobby does not mean you can open the server-room door.
commonTraps: STRIDE classifies threats and DREAD ranks them; options that swap the two are wrong.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework; authentication of the user comes from OpenID Connect or SAML.
A gateway that authenticates users does not remove the need for each microservice to authorize its callers.
The customer always owns its data, identities and configuration in the cloud; misconfigured storage is a customer failure.
Obscurity, such as long random identifiers, does not replace an object-level authorization check.
A trusted bus or gateway does not remove the need for each service to authorize and validate what it receives.
Short-range technologies such as NFC and RFID can still be skimmed or relayed, so sensitive exchanges need cryptographic authentication.
lessons.scenario: A retailer is designing an order API behind a gateway, with several microservices in containers talking to a payment service and a customer database. The team draws a data flow diagram, marks the gateway and the database as trust boundaries, and runs STRIDE on each flow. It finds that internal services trust any caller, orders can be fetched by changing an identifier, and database keys sit beside the data. The design is changed to use mutual TLS between services, object-level authorization in every service, a separate key service and narrowly scoped identities for each workload.
lessons.onTheJob: Do threat modeling in short, regular sessions with developers in the room, not as a heavyweight document written by security alone. Start with a whiteboard data flow diagram, spend most of the time at trust boundaries, and track every threat as a ticket with an owner so it is mitigated or explicitly accepted. Prefer removing a feature over hardening it, and prefer a standard pattern, such as an established identity provider, over a custom design. In cloud work, review identity and access policies as carefully as code, because over-broad roles are the most common root cause of serious incidents. When AI features appear in a design, ask what the model is allowed to do on behalf of a user and what happens if its output is hostile.

lessons.title: Secure Implementation: Coding Defenses and Safe Practices
lessons.summary: The coding practices that prevent injection, scripting, memory and access control flaws, plus secrets, cryptography, review and repository security.
lessons.reading:
Implementation is where design intentions meet real code, and most exploited vulnerabilities come from a small set of recurring mistakes. The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web application risk categories for awareness. Broken access control has been first in both the 2021 and 2025 editions, followed in the 2025 list by security misconfiguration and software supply chain failures, with cryptographic failures, injection and insecure design also present.

The foundation of defending against injection and scripting attacks is to keep data and code separate. Input validation checks that data has the expected type, length, range and format, and it works best as an allow-list of what is acceptable, enforced on the server because client checks are trivially bypassed. SQL injection is prevented primarily by parameterized queries, which tell the database that input is always a value, never syntax. Cross-site scripting is prevented primarily by output encoding that matches the context, whether HTML body, attribute, JavaScript or URL, with a content security policy as a backstop. Cross-site request forgery abuses the browser attaching cookies automatically, and anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies stop it. Server-side request forgery makes your server fetch an attacker-chosen address, so you allow-list destinations and block internal ranges.

Access control must be enforced on the server, for every request, with default deny. Hiding a link or a button is not access control, and neither is a hard-to-guess identifier. Changing an identifier to reach another user record is an insecure direct object reference, and the fix is an ownership check on the object. Error handling follows the same logic: users see a generic message while detail goes to protected logs, because stack traces and queries reveal internals to attackers.

Memory-related flaws dominate in languages such as C and C++. A buffer overflow writes past the end of a buffer, and use-after-free uses memory that has been released. Mitigations such as stack canaries, data execution prevention and address space layout randomization make exploitation harder, but only bounds checking, careful coding or a memory-safe language removes the bug.

Cryptography and secrets deserve their own discipline. Never invent algorithms: use vetted libraries, current algorithms and a cryptographically secure random number generator. Store passwords with a unique salt and a slow algorithm such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2, because passwords are checked, never recovered. Keep keys and secrets out of source code and images and hold them in a secrets manager with rotation and audit. A secret that was ever committed must be treated as compromised and rotated. Finally, protect the pipeline that carries code: secure code review combining human review and tools, hardening to a baseline such as a CIS Benchmark, and repository protections such as branch protection with independent review and signed commits.

The implementation objective lists more practices than the common web flaws. Security can be declarative (roles and rules configured outside the code) or programmatic (checks in code that handle object-specific decisions). Concurrency flaws such as race conditions need atomic operations, locking or optimistic version checks. Sanitization means canonicalizing input before validating it and encoding output for its context, and obfuscation is not encryption. Secure logging records enough for accountability without secrets or unnecessary personal data. Session management regenerates identifiers at login, uses unpredictable values and protective cookie attributes, and invalidates sessions on the server. Untrusted APIs and libraries get verified sources and minimal privilege, resource management bounds memory, compute, storage and connections and releases them reliably, tokenization replaces values with surrogates held in a vault, and isolation (sandboxing, virtualization, containers and separation kernels) contains compromised parts.

Cryptography is applied at field, payload, transport and storage levels with agile algorithm choices. Access control models include discretionary, mandatory and role-based control plus trust zones. Processor microarchitecture extensions provide hardware isolation, and secure code reuse means shared, owned and versioned components. Vulnerability lists such as the OWASP Top 10, the CWE Top 25 and CVE help focus review. Code analysis combines SAST and linting with manual peer review and inspection for malicious code such as backdoors, logic bombs and high-entropy hidden payloads. Controls such as watchdogs, file integrity monitoring and anti-malware address runtime risks, and identified risks are treated with a documented strategy. Integration of components needs trust contracts and software composition analysis, and the build applies anti-tampering techniques such as code signing, compiler switches and fixing compiler warnings instead of silencing them.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to secure coding? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Injection attacks are like a restaurant order slip where a customer is allowed to write in the notes field. If the kitchen treats everything on the slip as instructions, a customer who writes "and give me the cash from the register" gets it. Parameterized queries are a slip with a fixed form: the notes box can only ever be read as a request for ingredients, never as an instruction to the staff. Output encoding is like printing the customer name on the receipt in a way that cannot be read as a command, and access control is the manager checking, at every request, that the person asking is allowed to ask.
commonTraps: Client-side validation is a usability feature; the server must enforce validation and authorization.
ASLR and similar mitigations make memory exploits harder but do not remove the bug; fixing the code or changing language does.
Passwords are hashed with a unique salt and a slow algorithm, not encrypted; there is no reason to recover them.
XSS abuses a site trust in the content it serves; CSRF abuses a site trust in the requests a browser sends.
A secret removed from the latest commit is still exposed in history and clones, so it must be rotated.
Obfuscation slows analysis but does not protect secrets; keep keys in protected storage, not in the binary.
Silencing a compiler warning leaves the underlying defect; fix the code rather than suppress the message.
lessons.scenario: A security review of an internal portal finds a search page that concatenates user input into SQL, a comments page that echoes input into HTML, an export endpoint that accepts any record number, and an API key in a repository from a year ago. The remediation is to switch to parameterized queries, apply context-aware output encoding, add an ownership check to the export, rotate the key and add secret scanning to the pipeline. Each fix removes a root cause rather than filtering symptoms.
lessons.onTheJob: Make the safe way the easy way. Provide teams with vetted libraries and framework defaults for output encoding, query building, authentication and cryptography, then review deviations, instead of expecting every developer to remember every rule. Put secret scanning and dependency checks in pre-commit and in the pipeline so mistakes are caught in minutes. In code review, focus effort on authentication, authorization, input parsing, cryptography and anything touching money or personal data. Avoid the temptation to block-list: attackers find the encoding or variant you did not list, so prefer allow-lists and structural defenses such as parameterization.

lessons.title: Secure Software Testing: Tools, Techniques and Release Criteria
lessons.summary: Static, dynamic and interactive testing, fuzzing, penetration testing, test data, and how test results feed release decisions.
lessons.reading:
Security testing answers a different question from functional testing. Functional tests ask whether the software does what it should, while security tests ask whether it refuses to do what it should not do. A security test plan therefore derives its cases from security requirements, abuse cases and the threat model, not just from the feature list. Negative testing, which supplies invalid, unexpected or hostile input and actions, is central: boundary values, wrong data types, tampered tokens, repeated guesses and attempts to skip steps.

The automated tool families are distinguished by what they can see. Static application security testing (SAST) analyzes source code, bytecode or binaries without running the application. It can start as soon as code exists and points to the exact line, but it can produce false positives and cannot see runtime or configuration problems. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) attacks a running application from the outside with no need for source code. It finds runtime and configuration issues, but cannot identify the line and covers only the paths it reaches. Interactive application security testing (IAST) places sensors inside the running application while tests exercise it, which gives accurate findings tied to code, but only for the paths the tests reach. Runtime application self-protection (RASP) is not primarily a test: it sits inside the application and blocks attacks in production.

Fuzz testing deserves special mention. A fuzzer feeds large volumes of malformed or random input to a program to provoke crashes, hangs and memory errors, and coverage-guided fuzzers evolve inputs to reach new code. It is the best technique for unknown input-handling and memory-safety flaws, especially in parsers and protocol handlers. Penetration testing is a different kind of activity: an authorized, scoped, time-boxed attempt to exploit weaknesses, often chained together, to show real impact. It needs written authorization and rules of engagement before it starts. A vulnerability scan is automated, broad and repeatable but only lists potential weaknesses, whereas a penetration test proves exploitability.

Good test practice supports everything above. Code coverage shows what code ran during tests but not whether the assertions were meaningful. Regression tests rerun existing checks after every change, and each fixed vulnerability should get its own regression test so it cannot silently return. Test data must not be production personal data: use synthetic data or data that has been masked or anonymized, because test systems are usually less protected.

Testing ends in a decision. Exit criteria, such as no open critical or high vulnerabilities and all required scans completed, define when software may be released. If the business wants to release with an open finding, the correct path is documented risk acceptance by the accountable owner with compensating controls and a remediation date. It is not a quiet exception by the project team, a reclassification of severity or the omission of the finding from the report.

The testing objective is broader than tool names. The strategy comes from the risk assessment and requirements, and the plan states scope, environments, data, roles, entry and exit criteria and reporting, drawing on standards such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 and the Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual. Techniques are described by what testers know (known-environment versus unknown-environment testing), by what they check (functional security logic versus nonfunctional reliability, performance and scalability) and by where they run (a production-like environment with a test harness for interoperability). Security researcher outreach through a disclosure policy and bug bounties complements internal work, and attack surface validation confirms that what is exposed matches what was intended.

Further techniques include penetration tests aimed at controls, known vulnerabilities and known malware, fuzzing (generated from a format model or mutated from valid samples), simulation with synthetic transactions, failure testing such as fault injection, stress and break testing, and cryptographic validation of random number generators and entropy. Unit tests with code coverage, regression, integration and continuous testing are layered, and misuse and abuse cases produce negative tests. Testers also verify documentation (installation steps, error messages, user guides, release notes) and hunt for undocumented functionality. Results are analyzed for their effect on product management, prioritization and break/build criteria, security defects are classified and tracked with a score such as CVSS and restricted visibility, test data is generated with referential integrity and production-like quality, or reused only after obfuscation, sanitization, anonymization or tokenization while watching for aggregation risk, and independent verification and validation and acceptance testing give the final assurance.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security testing? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of testing a new car. Reading the engineering drawings for mistakes is static analysis, because nothing is moving yet. Driving it around a track and trying to break it is dynamic testing. Putting sensors inside the engine while someone drives is interactive testing. Slamming the controls with random, absurd inputs to see what fails is fuzzing, and hiring a professional thief with written permission to actually steal it is a penetration test. The final inspection checklist that must all be green before the car leaves the factory is the exit criteria.
commonTraps: SAST needs code and can name the line; DAST needs only a running application and cannot; the two are often reversed in distractors.
A vulnerability scan lists possible weaknesses while a penetration test actually exploits them.
Penetration testing requires written authorization and rules of engagement first, never just a verbal agreement.
Real production personal data does not belong in test environments, even on an internal network.
Releasing with an open critical finding needs documented risk acceptance from the accountable owner, not a project-level exception.
Unknown-environment (black-box) testing mirrors an outside attacker but explores less than known-environment testing in the same time.
Documentation, error messages and release notes are in scope for verification because they can instruct unsafe actions or leak details.
lessons.scenario: A team is about to release a service that parses uploaded documents. Static analysis runs on every commit, dependency scanning runs in the pipeline, and a coverage-guided fuzzer has been running against the document parser for a week and found two crashes, both fixed with regression tests. A dynamic scan runs against staging, and an outside firm performs a penetration test under written rules of engagement. One medium finding remains, and the product owner signs a risk acceptance with a remediation date.
lessons.onTheJob: Do not drown developers in raw scanner output. Triage first, deduplicate, rank by exploitability and exposure, and send actionable tickets with the line of code and a suggested fix. Run quick checks on every commit and slower deep scans nightly or per release. Treat fuzzing as continuous infrastructure for anything that parses untrusted data, because it keeps finding bugs as the code changes. Before a penetration test, agree on scope, hours, contacts and what to do if something breaks, and give testers realistic accounts and architecture documentation so they spend time on depth instead of discovery. Keep the release criteria written down so decisions on the deadline day are not improvised.

lessons.title: Secure Deployment, Operations and Maintenance
lessons.summary: Release and configuration management, pipeline security, vulnerability and patch management, incident response for software, and end of life.
lessons.reading:
Software is not finished at release, and a large part of its security is decided in how it is built, shipped, run and eventually retired. Release management controls how a build moves into production through approvals, versioning, tested packages and rollback plans, and code signing lets recipients verify the publisher and that the artifact has not been altered. Remember what a signature does not prove: it does not show that the code is free of vulnerabilities, and if the build itself is compromised the malicious output will be signed too. Configuration management identifies each configuration item, defines an approved baseline and detects drift from it.

The delivery pipeline has become a prime target, because whatever it builds gets trusted. Protect it with short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, isolated and ephemeral build runners, protected secrets, signed artifacts, reviewed changes to the pipeline definition and logging of all of the above. The SolarWinds compromise inserted malicious code during the build, not in the source repository, which is why build integrity matters. Before go-live an operational readiness review confirms secure defaults, hardening, monitoring, tested recovery and a signed security acceptance.

Once running, vulnerability management is a continuous cycle: discover, assess and prioritize, remediate or mitigate, verify and report. Prioritization uses CVSS severity together with context, such as whether the system is internet-facing, whether exploit code exists and whether the flaw appears in the CISA known exploited vulnerabilities catalog or has a high EPSS score. A CVSS base score measures intrinsic severity, not the risk to you. Patch management, described in NIST SP 800-40, tests and deploys updates on a risk-based schedule with an expedited path for actively exploited flaws, and uses compensating controls such as virtual patching or restricted access when a patch cannot yet be applied.

Software incident response follows the familiar sequence: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate and recover, then review lessons learned. Product teams also need a way to receive vulnerability reports, usually through a product security incident response team and a published contact, and they practice coordinated disclosure with the reporter, agreeing a timeline so a fix exists before details become public. After any serious event, root cause analysis fixes the class of problem and updates requirements, tests and training.

Finally, software has an end. When a vendor stops issuing patches the product is at end of life, and continuing to run it means living with flaws that can never be fixed.
