Retirement should be planned: notify users, migrate or archive data under retention rules, remove accounts, credentials and network access, and sanitize media following NIST SP 800-88 using clear, purge or destroy as appropriate, since deleting files or quick formatting leaves recoverable data.

The deployment objective begins before release with an operational risk analysis that considers the target environment (QA, staging, production), personnel training for administrators and users, legal compliance and system integration. Secure configuration and version control cover hardware and firmware as well as software, approved baselines, patch records and documentation. Releases flow through a secure CI/CD pipeline with an application security toolchain and build artifact verification by signatures and hashes. Credentials, secrets, keys, certificates and configurations are stored in managed vaults with inventory, rotation, revocation and expiry monitoring. Secure installation uses a verified boot chain with controlled key generation, least privilege, environment hardening and secure provisioning, including infrastructure as code, and implements the security policy. A system goes live only after approval to operate: risk acceptance and sign-off at the appropriate level by the accountable owner.

Operations add information security continuous monitoring of logs, events, telemetry, traces and metrics, fed with threat intelligence and correlated in a SIEM, together with intrusion detection and response and attention to regulation and privacy changes. Incident response executes triage, forensics, remediation and root cause analysis. Patch management tests and releases updates, vulnerability management tracks and triages by CVE and exploitability, and runtime protection such as a web application firewall, runtime application self-protection, ASLR and dynamic execution prevention reduces exploitation without fixing the flaw. Continuity covers backup, archiving, retention, the disaster recovery and business continuity plans and resiliency (operational redundancy, erasure coding, survivability and denial-of-service resistance), while service level objectives and agreements set targets for maintenance, performance, availability and qualified personnel. Note that NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (September 2025) now governs media sanitization and SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) aligns incident response with the CSF 2.0 functions.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to deployment and operations? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Running software in production is like running a restaurant after the grand opening. The recipe card that cooks must follow is the configuration baseline, and a change to it goes through the head chef (change control). Trying a new dish on a few tables first is a canary release. A recall notice when a supplier ingredient turns out to be unsafe is a vulnerability disclosure, and deciding which fridges to check first, the ones with the suspect batch that serve the most customers, is prioritization. When the restaurant finally closes you do not simply lock the door: you empty the storage, shred the order books and cancel the supplier accounts, which is decommissioning.
commonTraps: A digital signature proves publisher and integrity, not that the software is free of vulnerabilities.
CVSS base score is severity, not risk; exposure and active exploitation can make a lower score more urgent.
Emergency patches still follow an expedited, recorded process, and unsupported end-of-life software needs migration plus compensating controls.
Deleting files, emptying the recycle bin or a quick format is not sanitization.
Preserve evidence and contain before cleaning up during incident response; lessons learned feed back into requirements and tests.
A WAF, ASLR or RASP makes exploitation harder but is a compensating control, not a fix for the flaw.
The accountable owner, not the developer, tester or project manager, signs approval to operate and any risk acceptance.
lessons.scenario: A critical flaw is announced in a library used by a company internet-facing service, and the exploit is already seen in the wild. The team queries its inventory to find affected products, ranks the internet-facing one first, applies a virtual patch at the web application firewall within hours, tests and deploys the vendor fix through a canary release the next day, and records a short post-incident review. Months later it retires an old report server by migrating its data, removing its accounts and purging its disks under NIST SP 800-88.
lessons.onTheJob: Know what you run. Keep an accurate inventory of applications, versions and dependencies, because every other process depends on it, and a vulnerability announcement with no inventory means days of guesswork. Agree service-level targets for fixing flaws by severity and exposure, and review exceptions regularly. Treat the pipeline like production: separate its credentials, review its definitions and watch its logs. Rehearse recovery and incident response with tabletop exercises, including how to reach the reporter of a vulnerability. Put end-of-life dates on a calendar at purchase time, so retirement is planned and funded long before support stops.

lessons.title: Secure Software Supply Chain: Components, Suppliers and Assurance
lessons.summary: Third-party and open-source risk, SBOMs and VEX, supply chain attacks and defenses, licensing, supplier contracts and assurance schemes.
lessons.reading:
Modern applications are mostly assembled, not written. A typical product includes hundreds of open-source libraries, a build system, container images and cloud services, all supplied by others. A software supply chain attack compromises something that a victim already trusts, such as a dependency, a build server, an update channel or a vendor, so that malicious or vulnerable code arrives through a legitimate path. SolarWinds in 2020 showed tampering inside a vendor build that was then delivered as a signed update. Log4Shell in 2021 showed a single flaw in a ubiquitous logging library affecting thousands of products at once.

The first defense is knowing what you have. A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the components in a product, with names, versions and suppliers, and it lets you find affected products quickly when a new vulnerability is announced. The main formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, and the NTIA minimum elements define the baseline data. An SBOM is an inventory, not an assessment: it does not say whether a component is exploitable in your product. A Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) statement is the supplier assertion that a known vulnerability does or does not affect a product, for example because the vulnerable function is never reached. Software composition analysis (SCA) tools find open-source components in a codebase, report vulnerabilities and licenses, and can generate SBOMs, and they should run continuously because new vulnerabilities are disclosed for components already shipped.

Several specific attacks are named on the exam. Dependency confusion publishes a public package with the same name as an internal one and a higher version so build tools fetch the attacker copy. Typosquatting relies on package names that resemble popular ones. Defenses include reserving or scoping internal names and resolving them only from a private registry, pinning versions with lock files, verifying hashes, reviewing updates for critical dependencies and limiting build network access. Build integrity frameworks such as SLSA define increasingly strong requirements for provenance, which is a verifiable record of the source, process and builder that produced an artifact.

Licensing is also supply chain risk. Permissive licenses such as MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 allow broad reuse, while copyleft licenses such as the GPL require derivative works to be distributed under the same terms, and the AGPL extends that to software offered over a network.

Suppliers are managed through due diligence and contracts. Assess a supplier's security practices, vulnerability history, maintenance activity and independent reports such as SOC 2, then continue monitoring after selection for new vulnerabilities, ownership changes and end of support. Contracts make assurance enforceable: security requirements, breach notification, the right to audit, vulnerability handling timelines and exit terms. For product assurance, Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) evaluates a product against a Security Target and reports an evaluation assurance level from EAL1 to EAL7. A higher level reflects a more rigorous evaluation, not more features and not a guarantee of security.

The supply chain objective reads as a lifecycle. Supply chain risk management begins with identifying and selecting components, assessing their risk and deciding to mitigate or accept it, maintaining a list of third-party components such as an SBOM, and monitoring for changes and new vulnerabilities, using guidance such as ISO/IEC 27036 and NIST SP 800-161. Analyzing third-party software relies on independent evidence: certifications, assessment reports such as SOC 2 and the Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix, and the origin and support of the product, always checking scope and dates.

Verifying pedigree and provenance means secure transfer with chain of custody, authenticity and integrity, controlled system sharing and interconnections, code repository and build environment security, cryptographically hashed and digitally signed components, and a right to audit. In acquisition, buyers verify audits of the supplier secure development practices, vulnerability and incident notification, maintenance and support structure (community or commercial, licensing), security track record, the scope of testing under the shared responsibility model and log integration into the buyer SIEM. Contractual requirements settle intellectual property ownership, code escrow, liability, warranty, the end-user license agreement and service level agreements.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to supply chain security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a food manufacturer. Every ingredient comes from a supplier, who gets theirs from another supplier. A recall can start three links away. The ingredient list on the package is the SBOM, and the note saying the recalled flour is not in the product you bought is the VEX. Checking suppliers before signing, putting inspection rights into the contract and testing deliveries continuously are the controls. A rogue supplier shipping a look-alike flour in the same sack is a dependency confusion or typosquatting attack, and a tamper-evident seal and a record of which plant made each batch is provenance.
commonTraps: An SBOM lists components; it does not state whether they are vulnerable or exploitable, which is the job of vulnerability data and VEX.
SAST analyzes the code you wrote while SCA analyzes the open-source and third-party code you imported.
Dependency confusion exploits a higher version number across registries; typosquatting exploits a misspelled name.
A higher EAL means a more rigorous evaluation, not more security features or a guarantee of no vulnerabilities.
A questionnaire is evidence, but a contract term is what makes a supplier security commitment enforceable.
A supplier report covers a stated scope and period, so read the scope and date before relying on it.
A signature shows who signed, not that the build environment was clean; provenance and build security matter too.
lessons.scenario: A vendor announces a critical flaw in a widely used open-source library. The company queries its SBOM inventory and finds the library in four products. VEX statements from its own product teams show that two are not affected because the vulnerable function is never called, so remediation focuses on the other two. Afterward the team pins dependency versions, scopes internal package names to its private registry, adds SCA to every build and updates supplier contracts to require breach notification and an audit right.
lessons.onTheJob: Generate SBOMs automatically at build time and store them with each release, because a document written by hand at audit time will be wrong. Ask suppliers for SBOMs and VEX data as part of procurement, and treat a supplier that cannot provide them as a risk factor. Prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies and review the health of critical ones: how many maintainers, how recent are releases, how quickly are issues fixed. Mirror critical packages in a private registry and block direct downloads from the public internet during builds. Keep a decision record for licenses, with legal review for any copyleft component that will be distributed.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam facts and domain weights (ISC2 outline effective 15 September 2023)
points: CSSLP: 125 items (multiple choice and advanced item types), 3 hours, 700 out of 1000 points to pass, English, delivered at Pearson VUE test centers.

Domain weights: 1 Secure Software Concepts 12%, 2 Secure Software Lifecycle Management 11%, 3 Secure Software Requirements 13%, 4 Secure Software Architecture and Design 15%, 5 Secure Software Implementation 14%, 6 Secure Software Testing 14%, 7 Secure Software Deployment, Operations, Maintenance 11%, 8 Secure Software Supply Chain 10%.

Experience: at least four years cumulative, full-time experience in one or more of the eight domains. A bachelor or master degree in computer science, IT or a related field may satisfy up to one year; part-time work and internships may also count.
Without the experience you can pass the exam and become an Associate of ISC2, then have five years to earn the four years of experience.
Design, implementation and testing together are 43% of the exam, so spend study time there; the outline names the CSSLP accreditation as ISO/IEC 17024 through ANAB.

cheatSheet.heading: Secure design principles
points: Least privilege, separation of duties, defense in depth, fail-safe defaults (default deny), complete mediation, economy of mechanism, open design, least common mechanism, psychological acceptability, separation of privilege.
Complete mediation = check every access every time; fail-safe defaults = failure results in denial; open design = only keys are secret.
Fail secure protects data, fail safe protects life; software questions normally want fail secure.

STRIDE maps each threat to the property it breaks: spoofing breaks authentication, tampering breaks integrity, repudiation breaks non-repudiation, disclosure breaks confidentiality, denial of service breaks availability, elevation of privilege breaks authorization.

Concrete forms: split knowledge, dual control and secret sharing enforce separation of duties; technical and geographic diversity make layers independent; SSO and password vaults serve economy of mechanism; cached credentials and long-lived role cookies violate complete mediation; passwordless sign-in serves psychological acceptability.

cheatSheet.heading: Lifecycle models and maturity
points: Microsoft SDL, NIST SSDF (SP 800-218) and OWASP SAMM are prescriptive; BSIMM is descriptive and used for peer comparison.
SSDF groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities.
SAMM: five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), three practices each, three maturity levels.
Shift left: the earlier a defect is found, the cheaper it is to fix; in agile and DevOps automate checks and write security acceptance criteria.
Policy (mandatory, high level) > standard (mandatory, specific) > guideline (optional) > procedure (steps).

Break/build criteria are set in advance and exceptions go to the accountable owner; decommissioning removes credentials, configuration and licenses, archives or destroys data by retention rules; verification asks "built right", validation asks "right product"; assessment and authorization ends in an authorizing official accepting residual risk; breach clocks start at awareness (GDPR 72 hours to the authority, HIPAA 60 days to individuals).

cheatSheet.heading: Requirements, privacy and compliance
points: Missing security requirements are elicited first from data classification, laws, policies, threat models and abuse cases; make them testable and trace them in an SRTM.
Data classification is set by the data owner; FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark of confidentiality, integrity and availability impact.
RTO is time to restore and RPO is tolerable data loss; do not reverse them.
Privacy: data minimization, purpose limitation, retention limits, impact assessment early; pseudonymized data is generally still personal data.
GDPR (EU personal data), HIPAA (US health), PCI DSS (payment cards, contractual standard), SOX (financial reporting controls).

Data owner decides classification, custodian protects the data, the data dictionary describes elements; pseudonymous data can be re-linked, anonymous data cannot; data residency covers backups, keys and support access; service accounts need an owner, narrow rights and reapproval; an abuse case is complete only with mitigating controls; vendor requirements are written before selection.

cheatSheet.heading: Threat modeling, architecture and design
points: STRIDE classifies, DREAD ranks, PASTA is risk-centric with seven stages, attack trees start from an attacker goal, LINDDUN is for privacy threats; start analysis at trust boundaries on a data flow diagram.
Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207): no implicit trust by network location; authenticate, authorize and evaluate each request.
Microservices: mutual TLS plus authorization inside every service; APIs: object-level authorization first, plus rate limits and schema validation.
OAuth 2.0 = authorization; OpenID Connect and SAML = authentication and federation.
Cloud: customer always owns data, identities, configuration and code; containers share the host kernel; serverless needs per-function least privilege.

Know the weak spot of each style: message queues and buses are extra trust boundaries, rich clients are untrusted, IoT and embedded need secure boot and signed update, management interfaces belong on out-of-band networks, TPM measured boot seals keys to a known state, and hybrid threat modeling blends methods such as STRIDE and attack trees.

cheatSheet.heading: Secure implementation
points: Allow-list validation on the server; parameterized queries for SQL injection; context-aware output encoding for XSS; anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies for CSRF; allow-list destinations for SSRF.
Broken access control is first in the OWASP Top 10 (2021 and 2025); hiding a link is not access control; fix IDOR with object ownership checks.
Memory safety: bounds checking or memory-safe languages remove the bug; ASLR, DEP and canaries only make exploitation harder.
Passwords: unique salt plus Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2; never reversible encryption; never invent cryptography.
Committed secrets are compromised: revoke and rotate, then add a secrets manager and scanning.

Declarative security is configured outside the code, programmatic security lives in it; canonicalize then validate; regenerate the session identifier at login; tokenization replaces a value with a vaulted surrogate; fix compiler warnings instead of silencing them; file integrity monitoring and watchdogs detect tampering and hangs; hidden payloads with high entropy and logic bombs are malicious code indicators.

cheatSheet.heading: Testing and assurance
points: SAST = source, early, names the line, false positives; DAST = running app, no source, runtime issues; IAST = in-app agent during tests; RASP = in-app protection in production.
Fuzzing finds unknown input-handling and memory flaws; penetration tests exploit and need written authorization and rules of engagement; scans list, pen tests prove.
Negative testing and abuse cases derive security test cases; add a regression test for every fixed vulnerability; coverage does not prove meaningful checks.
Never use raw production personal data in test; mask, anonymize or use synthetic data.
Releasing with an open critical finding needs documented risk acceptance by the accountable business owner.

Known-environment testing gives testers internals, unknown-environment testing mimics an outsider; mutation fuzzing alters valid samples and generation fuzzing builds from a format model; fault injection, stress and break testing show how the system fails; predictable seeds break strong cryptography; test data needs referential integrity and aggregation checks; independent verification and validation reduces bias.

cheatSheet.heading: Deployment, operations and supply chain
points: Sign release artifacts; protect the CI/CD pipeline with short-lived scoped credentials, ephemeral runners and reviewed pipeline changes; scan infrastructure as code before deployment.
CVSS is severity, not risk: weigh exposure and active exploitation (CISA known exploited vulnerabilities, EPSS); NIST SP 800-40 for patching; compensating controls when patching is delayed.

Incident response: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate and recover, post-incident review (SP 800-61 Rev. 2; Rev. 3, April 2025, aligns with the CSF 2.0 functions); coordinated vulnerability disclosure with the reporter.
End of life means no more patches: plan migration; sanitize media per NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (clear, purge, destroy).

SBOM (SPDX, CycloneDX) is an inventory; VEX says whether a vulnerability affects the product; SCA finds third-party components and licenses; SLSA and provenance protect builds; dependency confusion uses a higher version number.
Copyleft (GPL, AGPL) can force source disclosure; permissive (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0) cannot; Common Criteria EAL1 to EAL7 measures evaluation rigor, not features.

Approval to operate is the accountable owner decision on residual risk; ISCM correlates logs, traces and telemetry in a SIEM with threat intelligence and watches regulation changes; WAF, RASP and ASLR are compensating controls; RPO limits data loss and RTO limits downtime; erasure coding and replicas give resilience; read the scope and date of a supplier report; chain of custody, right to audit, code escrow and shared responsibility testing scope are supply chain contract topics.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: 125 questions in 3 hours is about 1 minute 25 seconds per question; do a first pass, flag the hard ones and return, leaving time to review flagged items. Unanswered questions score zero, so never leave one blank.
Scoring is scaled to 1000 with 700 to pass, and an exam can include unscored pretest items, so do not try to count your correct answers during the exam.

Questions ask for the BEST, FIRST or MOST appropriate action. The best answer is usually the one that fixes the root cause earliest in the lifecycle, enforces policy by design and involves the accountable owner.
Eliminate options that bypass process (quiet exceptions, deleting findings), rely on obscurity, or wait for a penetration test to discover a design problem.

Read the scenario for the lifecycle phase: during requirements think classification and abuse cases, during design think threat model and principles, after release think patching, disclosure and end of life.
On multiple-response and advanced item types (such as drag-and-drop ordering and matching), read each instruction carefully and use partial knowledge to eliminate wrong options.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of a basic threat modeling session in the order in which they are normally performed.
steps: Define the scope and draw a data flow diagram with trust boundaries
Identify threats on each element, for example by applying STRIDE
Rate and prioritize the threats, for example with DREAD or risk analysis
Choose mitigations and assign them as tracked work items
Validate that the mitigations work and update the model when the design changes
sequences.explanation: You must know what you are building before you can find threats. Prioritization precedes choosing mitigations so effort goes where risk is greatest, and the model is kept current because designs change.

sequences.prompt: Order the four groups of the NIST Secure Software Development Framework as they naturally build on each other.
steps: Prepare the Organization (people, processes and tools are ready)
Protect the Software (guard code and build assets from tampering)
Produce Well-Secured Software (design, code, review and test with security in mind)
Respond to Vulnerabilities (identify, fix and learn from residual flaws)
sequences.explanation: The SSDF is usually remembered as prepare, protect, produce, respond: organizational readiness first, then protection of the environment, then secure production of the software, and finally handling the vulnerabilities that remain after release.

sequences.prompt: Order the phases of software incident response.
steps: Preparation (policies, tools, contacts and training in place)
Detection and analysis (confirm and scope the incident)
Containment (stop the spread and preserve evidence)
Eradication and recovery (remove the cause and restore service)
Post-incident review (lessons learned feed requirements, tests and training)
sequences.explanation: Preparation comes first so the team can act fast, detection confirms what happened, containment limits damage before cleanup begins, and the review closes the loop by improving the earlier lifecycle phases.

sequences.prompt: A critical vulnerability is reported in a shipped product by an outside researcher. Order the vulnerability handling steps.
steps: Acknowledge the report and validate the issue
Assess severity and affected versions and decide priority
Develop and test a fix
Release the fix and publish an advisory, coordinated with the reporter
Verify deployment, monitor and record lessons learned
sequences.explanation: Coordinated disclosure means the fix exists and the timing is agreed with the reporter before details are published, and verification afterward confirms that customers are actually protected.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for responsibly adopting a new open-source component.
steps: Identify the need and shortlist candidate components
Assess maintenance health, vulnerability history and license
Approve and pin the exact version in the private registry or lock file
Record the component in the SBOM and scan it with software composition analysis
Monitor continuously for new vulnerabilities, changes and end of support
sequences.explanation: Assessment comes before adoption so risky or incompatible components never enter the code. Pinning and recording make the choice reproducible and findable, and monitoring continues for the life of the dependency.

sequences.prompt: Put the main steps of decommissioning an application in the order in which they are normally performed.
steps: Announce the end-of-life date and notify users and dependent systems
Archive the data that retention rules require and record where it is kept
Remove accounts, credentials, configuration and access, and cancel licenses
Destroy the remaining data and media with an approved method and record it
Verify that nothing depends on the system and close it formally
sequences.explanation: Users and dependent systems need notice first, retention duties are met before anything is destroyed, access and licenses are removed so no live paths or costs remain, destruction is recorded as evidence, and a final check confirms nothing still relies on the system.

sequences.prompt: Order the activities of analyzing and handling a security defect found in testing.
steps: Record it in the tracker with restricted visibility and a risk score
Triage by exploitability, exposure and business impact against release criteria
Assign an owner and a deadline, and fix or mitigate the defect
Retest to verify the fix and add a regression test
Review the cause and update requirements, training or standards
sequences.explanation: A tracked record comes first, triage then sets priority against the break/build criteria, an owner fixes it, retesting proves the fix and prevents recurrence, and root cause review feeds the class of problem back into the process.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of safely handling untrusted user input on the server before it is used in a query.
steps: Receive the input and decode it to a canonical form
Validate it against an allow list of type, length, range and format
Reject input that fails validation and log the event without secrets
Pass accepted values to the database through a parameterized query
Encode the result for the output context when it is displayed
sequences.explanation: Canonicalizing first stops disguised variants from slipping past the check, validation uses an allow list, rejection is preferred to repair, parameterization keeps data from becoming SQL, and context-aware output encoding protects the page that displays it.

sequences.prompt: Arrange the steps of turning a new feature into verified security requirements.
steps: Classify the data the feature handles with its owner
Identify compliance and privacy obligations that apply
Write misuse and abuse cases with mitigating controls
Record the security requirements with measurable criteria
Trace each requirement to design elements and test cases
sequences.explanation: Classification and obligations determine what must be protected, abuse cases reveal what attackers would try, requirements are written so they can be tested, and traceability proves each was designed and verified.

caseStudies.title: HarborView Health Patient Portal
caseStudies.scenario: HarborView Health is building a patient portal as a set of containerized microservices behind an API gateway. Patients view lab results and message clinicians, and the service stores diagnoses and appointment history for people in several countries. The architect's first design has the gateway authenticate users with an identity provider, after which internal services trust any request that arrives from the cluster network. Results are fetched with a URL such as /results/48213, where the number is the record identifier. Encryption keys for the database are kept in a configuration table in the same database. The team plans a single penetration test just before launch and has not yet produced a threat model or a privacy assessment. The product owner wants to add an AI assistant that summarizes lab results and can book appointments on a patient's behalf by calling internal services. Delivery is in two-week sprints, and legal has confirmed that health privacy laws apply to the data.

questions.question: Which weakness in the first design is the MOST serious from a design standpoint?
options: The gateway uses an identity provider rather than a locally built login system
The portal is deployed as containers instead of virtual machines
The team uses two-week sprints for delivery
Internal services trust any request from the cluster network, so one foothold exposes every service
questions.explanation: Services that trust any caller on the network allow lateral movement after a single compromise, so each service needs authenticated callers (for example with mutual TLS) and its own authorization. Using an identity provider is good practice, containers are acceptable with proper hardening, and sprint length is not a security design issue.

questions.question: A tester changes 48213 to 48214 in the results URL and sees another patient record. What control is missing?
options: Encryption of the database column that holds the lab results
A web application firewall rule that blocks numeric identifiers
A longer and more random record identifier format
An object-level authorization check that confirms the caller owns the requested record
questions.explanation: This is broken object-level authorization: the API authenticates the caller but never checks ownership of the object. Random identifiers only make guessing harder, a firewall rule cannot know who owns a record, and database encryption does not stop the application from returning the data to an unauthorized caller.

questions.question: Which TWO actions should happen EARLY, before more design and coding work is done? (Choose two.)
options: Move the encryption keys into the application configuration file
Wait for the pre-launch penetration test to show what the threats are
Run a threat model on the data flows, focusing on trust boundaries
Add a fixed tracking identifier to every user for marketing analytics
Perform a data protection impact assessment of how patient data is collected and shared
questions.explanation: Threat modeling and a privacy impact assessment shape the architecture while changes are cheap. Waiting for a penetration test discovers design flaws late, and the other options either weaken key handling or add privacy exposure.

questions.question: For the AI assistant that can book appointments by calling internal services, which design control is the BEST?
options: Log the assistant prompts and responses and review them after the next release
Allow the assistant full access to every internal service so it can handle any request
Trust the model to refuse malicious instructions without further checks
Give the assistant the least privilege needed, treat its output as untrusted input and require patient confirmation before actions
questions.explanation: AI components can be manipulated by prompt injection, so their capabilities are limited to what is needed, their output is validated like any untrusted input, and consequential actions need explicit approval. Full access, blind trust and after-the-fact log review do not prevent harm at the time of the action.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Logistics Build Pipeline Review
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Logistics ships a customer-facing shipment tracking application and a mobile client. After a widely reported library vulnerability, leadership asks the security team to review the delivery process. The review finds that builds run on long-lived shared runners using one administrator credential for every pipeline. Dependencies are fetched from public registries without version pinning, and the team also publishes several internal packages whose names are not reserved on the public registry. No inventory of third-party components exists, so it took six days to find which products used the vulnerable library. Release packages are not signed. A third-party route optimization component is supplied by a small vendor under a contract that has no security clauses, and the vendor holds the only copy of the source code. Northwind also copied its production shipment database into the staging environment for realistic testing. The CISO wants a prioritized plan that improves supply chain security without halting delivery.

questions.question: Which finding should be addressed FIRST to reduce the chance that a malicious package reaches production builds?
options: Pin dependency versions with hash verification and reserve or scope internal package names to a private registry
Ask developers to review every library by hand once a year
Increase the number of runners so builds finish faster
Move the mobile client to a different development framework
questions.explanation: Unpinned public fetches and unreserved internal names enable dependency confusion and malicious updates, and pinning with hashes plus controlled resolution closes that path. Changing frameworks, annual manual reviews and more runners do not stop a malicious package from being fetched.

questions.question: The team could not tell which products used the vulnerable library for six days. What is the BEST control to fix this?
options: Generate an SBOM for every build and keep a searchable inventory, with software composition analysis
Add a note to the release process that developers should remember which libraries they use
Retain the penetration test reports from previous years
Block all open-source libraries from future builds
questions.explanation: An SBOM produced automatically at build time, combined with SCA, answers where a component is used within minutes. Relying on memory is unreliable, banning all open-source is impractical, and old penetration test reports do not list dependencies.

questions.question: Which TWO changes best reduce the risk from the shared administrator credential and unsigned packages? (Choose two.)
options: Issue short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials to isolated, ephemeral build runners
Send release packages by email to customers instead of publishing them
Keep the shared credential but rename it so that it is less obvious
Disable pipeline logging to remove sensitive values from records
Digitally sign release artifacts and verify the signatures before installation
questions.explanation: Scoped temporary credentials limit what a compromised build can do, and signing lets recipients verify origin and integrity. Renaming a credential is obscurity, emailing packages adds risk, and disabling logging destroys evidence.

questions.question: Which action best addresses the risk of depending on the small vendor that holds the only copy of the route optimization source code?
options: Remove the component and write a replacement within the current sprint
Ask the vendor to send an informal security assurance by email
Negotiate security clauses and a software escrow arrangement, with the deposit verified to build
Accept the situation because the vendor has not had a problem so far
questions.explanation: Contract terms make security duties enforceable, and a verified escrow deposit preserves the ability to maintain the component if the vendor fails. Informal assurances are not enforceable, doing nothing leaves the risk open and an immediate rewrite is rarely realistic.

questions.question: Copying the production shipment database into staging is acceptable as long as the staging environment is only reachable from the internal network.
questions.explanation: Test environments usually have weaker controls, so real customer data should be replaced by synthetic data or masked and anonymized before use. An internal network does not remove the breach and compliance exposure.

compare.scenario: A finance application checks a user entitlements when a session starts and keeps them for eight hours for performance. Which improvement is the better recommendation?
compare.optionA: Shorten the session timeout from eight hours to four hours so cached entitlements go stale more quickly.
compare.optionB: Check authorization on every request, using a fast cached policy that is invalidated when permissions change.
compare.why: Checking each request with an invalidating cache delivers complete mediation and still performs well. Shortening the timeout is the tempting runner-up but only narrows the window in which a revoked permission still works; it does not remove it.

compare.scenario: A team releases several times a day and the security manager needs a control to stop a critical dependency flaw from reaching production. Which is the better answer?
compare.optionA: An automated pipeline gate that fails the build on critical findings unless a documented exception is approved.
compare.optionB: A weekly manual review meeting where the team looks at the dependency report before the next release.
compare.why: The automated gate runs on every build and enforces the criterion at the speed of delivery, with an accountable exception path. The weekly meeting looks thorough but cannot keep pace with several releases a day, so flawed builds ship between meetings.

compare.scenario: A product manager wants the sign-up form to collect birth date and home address, although the product never uses them. What should the security architect recommend?
compare.optionA: Drop those fields from the form and do not collect the data.
compare.optionB: Collect the fields and encrypt them at rest with a strong algorithm and managed keys.
compare.why: Data minimization removes the risk entirely, since data never collected cannot be breached or misused. Encrypting the fields is the tempting runner-up, but it keeps unnecessary data in scope for breach, compliance and retention obligations.

compare.scenario: A team must prove to an auditor that every security requirement was implemented and tested. Which artifact is better?
compare.optionA: The latest penetration test report showing the number of findings by severity.
compare.optionB: A traceability matrix linking each requirement to design elements, code and test cases.
compare.why: Traceability shows coverage requirement by requirement, including gaps. The penetration test report is the tempting runner-up because testing sounds like proof, but it shows what was found, not that each stated requirement was built and verified.

compare.scenario: A company wants a design for internal microservices that remains safe if an attacker gets a foothold on the network. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: A stronger perimeter firewall and an authenticated gateway in front of all the services.
compare.optionB: Mutual TLS between services plus authorization checks inside each service.
compare.why: Service-to-service authentication and local authorization protect against lateral movement after a foothold. The gateway design is the tempting runner-up, but once an attacker is inside the network nothing stops direct calls to services that trust any internal caller.

compare.scenario: A team needs to prioritize a list of already identified threats in a design. Which technique is the better fit?
compare.optionA: DREAD scoring of damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users and discoverability.
compare.optionB: STRIDE classification of each threat into spoofing, tampering and the other categories.
compare.why: DREAD produces a ranking so effort can be ordered. STRIDE is the tempting runner-up because it is the best known method, but it classifies threats rather than ranking them, so it does not tell the team which to fix first.

compare.scenario: A developer must protect against SQL injection in a legacy report that builds queries from user text. Which is the better fix?
compare.optionA: Add a filter that removes quotes and semicolons from the input.
compare.optionB: Rewrite the queries to use parameterized statements.
compare.why: Parameterization addresses the root cause by keeping data separate from SQL syntax. The filter is the tempting runner-up because it is quick, but block-lists miss encodings and variants and leave the query structure injectable.

compare.scenario: A vendor delivers a compiled web application with no source code and the customer wants to find vulnerabilities before go-live. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: A static analysis scan of the vendor repository, which the customer requests through the vendor.
compare.optionB: A dynamic scan and a scoped penetration test against the running application in staging.
compare.why: Dynamic testing needs only a running application, which is what the customer has. Static analysis is the tempting runner-up because it gives line-level findings, but it depends on source the customer does not hold and may never receive.

compare.scenario: A critical vulnerability is being actively exploited in an internet-facing service, and the vendor patch needs two weeks of regression testing. Which is the better interim step?
compare.optionA: Deploy the vendor patch to production immediately without regression testing to close the gap.
compare.optionB: Apply a virtual patch or access restriction now and deploy the vendor fix after testing.
compare.why: Compensating controls reduce exposure immediately while preserving stability. Deploying untested is the tempting runner-up because it feels decisive, but it can break production, and the exposure can usually be reduced faster by a targeted control.

compare.scenario: A company depends on a small vendor for a critical custom application and worries about the vendor failing. Which is the better assurance?
compare.optionA: A clause obliging the vendor to fix defects within thirty days of notice.
compare.optionB: A software escrow agreement with periodic verification that the deposit builds.
compare.why: Escrow gives the customer the means to maintain the application if the vendor disappears. The defect-fix clause is the tempting runner-up, but a vendor that has failed cannot perform it, so it gives no continuity protection in that scenario.

compare.scenario: A critical flaw is exploited in the wild and the vendor patch needs two weeks of regression testing on a legacy system. Which is the better interim plan?
compare.optionA: Add virtual patching or access restrictions now, test the patch on an expedited path and record the exception.
compare.optionB: Apply the patch to production tonight without testing, because a short exposure window matters most.
compare.why: Compensating controls reduce exposure while the fix is validated, and the recorded exception keeps accountability. An untested patch can break the legacy system and turn a security problem into an outage.

compare.scenario: A supplier hands over a report for a cloud service. Which use of the report is better?
compare.optionA: Accept it as proof that the whole supplier product line is secure and skip further assessment.
compare.optionB: Read its scope and period, note exclusions and combine it with contract terms and monitoring.
compare.why: Assessment reports describe a defined scope and period. Treating them as universal proof ignores exclusions, while combining them with enforceable terms and continued monitoring gives real assurance.

compare.scenario: A compiler warns about an unchecked buffer copy in a legacy module. Which response is better?
compare.optionA: Fix the code with bounds checking, and keep the warning treated as an error in the build.
compare.optionB: Suppress the warning for that file because the module has run in production for years.
compare.why: Warnings often mark real defects, and age is not evidence of safety. Fixing the code and keeping the strict build setting prevents the flaw from returning.

compare.scenario: A team wants to know whether a deployed application exposes only the endpoints it intended. Which activity is the better fit?
compare.optionA: A load test that measures how many requests per second the endpoints can handle.
compare.optionB: Attack surface validation that compares reachable endpoints and ports with the design.
compare.why: Attack surface validation looks for unintended exposure such as debug endpoints and leftover services. A load test measures capacity and would not reveal an unplanned entry point.

compare.scenario: A feature collects birth dates that the product does not need. Which requirement is better?
compare.optionA: Do not collect the data element, and document the purpose of every field that is collected.
compare.optionB: Collect it, encrypt it and delete it manually after twelve months.
compare.why: Data never collected cannot be breached or misused, and a documented purpose limits the collection scope. Encrypting and later deleting still carries risk and manual effort.

compare.scenario: Thousands of field sensors will run for ten years with rare physical access. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: Devices verify signed firmware before applying updates, and each has its own credentials.
compare.optionB: Devices accept any update from the vendor server and share one factory password for easy support.
compare.why: Long-lived devices need a trustworthy update path and unique identities so a single compromise does not unlock the fleet. Unsigned updates and a shared password remove both protections.
